uni-ee-circuit-theory.title: Electrical Circuit Theory (full syllabus)
uni-ee-circuit-theory.description: Complete EE circuit-theory subject in six units: DC networks and theorems, AC steady state and power, resonance and coupled circuits, three-phase circuits, transients and Laplace, then practicals and a final exam. Goes deeper than uni-ee-core.

courses.title: Unit 1 · DC network analysis and network theorems
courses.summary: Circuit laws, series-parallel reduction, nodal and mesh analysis, superposition, source transformation, Thevenin, Norton and maximum power transfer, with fully solved numericals.
outcomes: Apply Ohm's law, KCL and KVL to resistive networks

lessons.title: Circuit laws, series-parallel reduction and dividers

scenes.text: Asha's 5 V charger delivers less current than its label says. Her lab teacher asks her to model the cable as a series resistance.
Every circuit problem starts with the same two laws: KCL for currents at a node and KVL for voltages around a loop.

steps.title: Laws and definitions
steps.body:
**Ohm's law:** V = I R (V in volts, I in amperes, R in ohms). Power p = V I = I²R = V²/R (watts).
**KCL:** the algebraic sum of currents at a node is zero (charge is conserved).
**KVL:** the algebraic sum of voltages around any closed loop is zero (energy is conserved).
- Series: R_eq = R1 + R2 + ...; same current.
- Parallel: 1/R_eq = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + ...; same voltage. Two resistors: R_eq = R1R2/(R1+R2).
- Voltage divider: V_k = V·R_k/ΣR. Current divider (two branches): I1 = I·R2/(R1+R2).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 12 V source feeds 4 Ω and 6 Ω in series. R_eq = 10 Ω, I = 12/10 = 1.2 A. V across 6 Ω = 1.2 × 6 = 7.2 V (or 12×6/10 = 7.2 V). Power delivered = 12 × 1.2 = 14.4 W.

**Example 2.** 9 A enters a parallel pair of 6 Ω and 3 Ω. R_eq = 18/9 = 2 Ω, V = 9×2 = 18 V. I(6 Ω) = 9×3/9 = 3 A, I(3 Ω) = 6 A. Check: 3 + 6 = 9 A.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- In the current divider, the branch current uses the OTHER resistor in the numerator.
- Adding resistances in parallel instead of conductances.
- Mixing the sign convention: current enters the + terminal of a passive element.
- Forgetting that a voltmeter in practice loads the circuit.

lessons.title: Nodal analysis

scenes.text: A technician probes node voltages on a sensor board with a multimeter — node voltages are what you can actually measure.
Nodal analysis turns KCL at each non-reference node into a linear equation in node voltages.

steps.title: Method
steps.body:
1. Choose a reference (ground) node.
2. Label the other node voltages V1, V2 ...
3. Write KCL at each node: sum of currents leaving = 0, each as (V_node − V_adjacent)/R.
4. Solve the n−1 equations. For a voltage source between two non-reference nodes, form a **supernode** (KCL for the combined node plus the constraint V_a − V_b = E).
Matrix form: G·V = I, where G is symmetric with positive diagonal (sum of conductances at the node) and negative off-diagonals.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 5 A source feeds a node with 2 Ω and 3 Ω to ground. G = 1/2 + 1/3 = 5/6 S, V = 5/(5/6) = 6 V.

**Example 2.** 12 V source → 2 Ω → node 1; node 1 has 4 Ω to ground and another 4 Ω to ground. KCL: (V1−12)/2 + V1/4 + V1/4 = 0 → V1(0.5+0.25+0.25) = 6 → V1 = 6 V.

**Example 3 (supernode).** A 6 V source joins nodes 1 and 2 (V1 − V2 = 6).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using a source's own node voltage as an unknown when it is fixed by a grounded voltage source.
- Wrong sign for the injected source current.
- Forgetting the constraint equation in a supernode.

activity.prompt: A 10 V source is connected through 5 Ω to a node. From the node, a 5 Ω and a 10 Ω resistor go to ground. Find the node voltage.

lessons.title: Mesh analysis and supermesh

scenes.text: Two loops of a battery charger share one resistor. The current in it is the difference of the two loop currents.
Mesh analysis writes KVL around each window of a planar circuit.

steps.title: Method
steps.body:
1. Assign a clockwise mesh current to each window (planar circuit only).
2. KVL around each mesh: (sum of resistances in the mesh)×I_k − (shared resistance)×I_adjacent = source EMFs rising in the direction of I_k.
3. If a current source lies on a shared branch, form a **supermesh** (KVL around the outer loop, plus I_a − I_b = I_s).
Matrix form: R·I = E, R symmetric with positive diagonal.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
10 V source and 2 Ω in mesh 1; shared 4 Ω; 2 Ω in mesh 2.
Mesh 1: 10 = 2I1 + 4(I1 − I2) → 6I1 − 4I2 = 10.
Mesh 2: 0 = 4(I2 − I1) + 2I2 → −4I1 + 6I2 = 0 → I2 = (2/3)I1.
Substitute: 6I1 − (8/3)I1 = 10 → I1 = 3 A, I2 = 2 A. Current in the shared 4 Ω = 1 A. Power from source = 10×3 = 30 W; losses: 2²... = 2×9 + 4×1 + 2×4 = 18+4+8 = 30 W ✔.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixed mesh directions give wrong signs on the off-diagonal terms.
- Writing KVL across a current source (its voltage is unknown).
- Using mesh analysis on non-planar circuits.

lessons.title: Superposition and source transformation

scenes.text: A load is fed by a battery and a solar panel together. How much does each contribute?
In a linear circuit each source can be treated alone and the effects added.

steps.title: Principles
steps.body:
**Superposition (linear, bilateral circuits only):** response = sum of responses due to each independent source acting alone. Turn off the others: voltage source → short circuit; current source → open circuit. Dependent sources stay. Power is NOT superposable.
**Source transformation:** a voltage source E in series with R ⇔ a current source E/R in parallel with R. Direction: the current source arrow points toward the + terminal of the voltage source.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 12 V source → 2 Ω → node; node → 4 Ω → ground; 3 A current source injects into the node.
Source alone 12 V: V = 12×4/6 = 8 V. Current source alone: V = 3×(2∥4) = 3×4/3 = 4 V. Total V = 12 V. Check by nodal: (V−12)/2 + V/4 = 3 → 0.75V = 9 → V = 12 V ✔.

**Example 2.** 12 V in series with 2 Ω ⇔ 6 A in parallel with 2 Ω.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding powers instead of currents/voltages.
- Opening a voltage source or shorting a current source.
- Transforming a source that has a resistor in parallel (voltage) or in series (current) — the resistor must be in the correct arrangement.

lessons.title: Sinusoids, RMS values and phasors

scenes.text: The mains socket is labelled 230 V, but the voltage actually peaks near 325 V.
The label is the RMS value — the DC voltage that would heat a resistor equally.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
v(t) = V_m sin(ωt + φ), ω = 2πf (rad/s), T = 1/f.
**RMS** = √(mean of v²) = V_m/√2 = 0.707 V_m for a sine. **Average (half-cycle)** = 2V_m/π = 0.637 V_m.
Form factor = RMS/average = 1.11; peak factor = V_m/RMS = 1.414.
**Phasor:** V = V_rms ∠φ (polar) = a + jb (rectangular). Addition in rectangular form; multiplication/division in polar form. Differentiation ⇒ multiply by jω; integration ⇒ divide by jω.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding magnitudes of phasors instead of complex numbers.
- Mixing peak and RMS phasors in power calculations.
- Using degrees and radians together in ωt + φ.
- Quoting the average value of a full sine cycle (it is zero).

activity.prompt: Find the RMS value of a sinusoidal voltage with peak 325 V.

lessons.title: Impedance and series RLC circuits

scenes.text: A tube-light choke is mostly inductive: the current lags the voltage and the supply sees reactive load.
Complex impedance Z = R + jX captures resistance and reactance together.

steps.title: Impedance
steps.body:
X_L = ωL (Ω), X_C = 1/(ωC) (Ω). Z_R = R, Z_L = jωL, Z_C = −j/(ωC).
Series RLC: Z = R + j(X_L − X_C), |Z| = √(R² + X²), φ = tan⁻¹(X/R). I = V/Z. pf = cos φ = R/|Z| (lagging if X_L > X_C).
Voltage across each element = I × its impedance; V_R, V_L, V_C form a phasor diagram with V² = V_R² + (V_L − V_C)².

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating |Z| as R + X.
- Wrong sign of the angle: inductive current lags, capacitive current leads (ELI the ICE man).
- Using f instead of ω in X_L.

lessons.title: Parallel AC circuits and admittance

story.title: Plugging three loads into one socket

scenes.text: A heater, a ceiling fan and a capacitor-start motor share the same 230 V supply — a parallel connection.
Branch currents add as phasors, not as numbers.

steps.title: Admittance
steps.body:
Y = 1/Z = G + jB (siemens). For parallel branches Y_total = ΣY. Conductance G = R/(R²+X²); susceptance B = −X/(R²+X²).
Parallel RLC: I_R = V/R, I_L = V/X_L (lag), I_C = V/X_C (lead). I = √(I_R² + (I_L − I_C)²). pf = I_R/I.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding branch current magnitudes (50 ≠ 30 + 40).
- Forgetting that the inductive and capacitive currents are in opposite directions on the phasor diagram.

lessons.title: Power, power triangle and power-factor correction

scenes.text: A small factory pays a penalty on its electricity bill because its power factor is 0.6 lagging.
Adding a capacitor bank supplies the reactive power locally and lifts the power factor.

steps.title: Power relations
steps.body:
Real power P = VI cos φ (W). Reactive Q = VI sin φ (var; positive for inductive). Apparent S = VI (VA), S² = P² + Q². Complex S = VI* = P + jQ.
PF correction: Q_c = P(tan φ₁ − tan φ₂). Capacitor: C = Q_c/(ωV²) (single-phase, V in rms).
Why correct: for the same P, lower pf means higher current, higher I²R loss and larger conductors/transformers.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 230 V, 10 A, pf 0.8 lag: S = 2300 VA, P = 1840 W, Q = 1380 var. To reach unity: Q_c = 1380 var, C = 1380/(314.16×230²) = 83 µF.

**Example 2.** 10 kW load at 0.6 lag to be improved to 0.9 lag. tan φ₁ = 1.333, tan φ₂ = 0.4843. Q_c = 10 (1.333 − 0.4843) = 8.49 kvar.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using kW and kVA interchangeably.
- Over-correcting (leading pf) which raises voltage and wastes capacity.
- Capacitor calculation with peak instead of rms voltage.

activity.prompt: A 10 kW load runs at 0.6 lagging. How many kvar must a capacitor bank supply to raise pf to 0.9 lagging?

lessons.title: AC network theorems and maximum power transfer

scenes.text: A radio engineer matches the load to the source impedance so the antenna gets the most power.
DC theorems carry over to AC if resistance becomes impedance.

steps.title: Statements
steps.body:
Thevenin, Norton, superposition and reciprocity hold with phasors and impedances. For different frequencies use superposition in the time domain.
**AC max power transfer:** with Z_th = R_th + jX_th, maximum power when Z_L = Z_th* (R_L = R_th, X_L = −X_th); P_max = |V_th|²/(4R_th). If only R_L is variable: R_L = |Z_th|.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
V_th = 100∠0° V, Z_th = 3 + j4 Ω. Z_L = 3 − j4. Total = 6 Ω, I = 100/6 = 16.67 A. P_L = I²R_L = 277.8×3 = 833 W = 10000/(4×3) ✔.
If the load is purely resistive: R_L = |Z_th| = 5 Ω, then Z_total = 8 + j4, |Z| = 8.944, I = 11.18 A, P = 125×5 = 625 W (less than 833 W).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using Z_L = Z_th instead of the conjugate.
- Using R_L = R_th when the load is purely resistive and X_th ≠ 0.

lessons.title: Parallel resonance and the practical tank circuit

scenes.text: An oscillator uses a coil and capacitor in parallel to select its frequency.
At resonance it draws a small current from the source while a large current circulates inside.

steps.title: Parallel resonance
steps.body:
Ideal L ∥ C: ω0 = 1/√(LC); line current is zero (infinite impedance).
Practical coil (R in series with L) ∥ C: ω0 = √(1/LC − R²/L²) ≈ 1/√(LC) for high Q. **Dynamic impedance** Z_d = L/(CR) = Q²R (resistive, maximum, at resonance). Line current is minimum; circulating current is Q times line current. BW = f0/Q.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
L = 100 µH, R = 10 Ω, C = 100 pF.
f0 ≈ 1/(2π√(10⁻⁴×10⁻¹⁰)) = 1/(2π×10⁻⁷) = 1.59 MHz.
Q = ω0L/R = (10⁷×10⁻⁴)/10 = 100.
Z_d = L/(CR) = 10⁻⁴/(10⁻¹⁰×10) = 100 kΩ = Q²R ✔. With 1 V source: line current 10 µA; circulating current ≈ Q×10 µA = 1 mA.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying the series Z = R result to the parallel circuit.
- Using the ideal formula when Q is low (< 10).

lessons.title: Bandwidth, selectivity and half-power frequencies

scenes.text: Two radio stations 10 kHz apart should not leak into each other.
The sharper the resonance peak, the better a circuit rejects neighbours.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
Half-power frequencies f1 < f0 < f2 at which I = I_max/√2 (power = ½ P_max). BW = f2 − f1 = f0/Q = R/(2πL) for series RLC. Selectivity ∝ Q.
Exact: f1,2 = f0[√(1 + 1/(4Q²)) ∓ 1/(2Q)]. For high Q: f1,2 ≈ f0 ∓ BW/2.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling BW the difference in rad/s without converting.
- Taking f0 as the arithmetic mean (only approximately true for high Q).

lessons.title: Mutual inductance, coupling coefficient and dot convention

scenes.text: A phone charger powers the phone through air by magnetic coupling between two coils.
Flux of one coil linking another coil is described by mutual inductance M.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
v1 = L1 di1/dt ± M di2/dt. **Coefficient of coupling** k = M/√(L1L2), 0 ≤ k ≤ 1.
**Dot convention:** if current enters the dotted terminal of one coil, the voltage induced in the other coil is positive at its dotted terminal.
Series: aiding L_eq = L1 + L2 + 2M; opposing L_eq = L1 + L2 − 2M. M = (L_aid − L_opp)/4.
Parallel with common-dot: L_eq = (L1L2 − M²)/(L1 + L2 − 2M).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Ignoring the dot polarity and always adding M.
- Confusing k with M.
- Using M > √(L1L2).

quiz.why: They show the sign of induced voltages.

lessons.title: Coupled circuit analysis, reflected impedance and ideal transformer

scenes.text: An audio transformer matches an 8 Ω speaker to a high-impedance amplifier output.
The load's effect appears in the primary as a reflected impedance.

steps.title: Analysis
steps.body:
Primary mesh: V1 = (R1 + jωL1)I1 − jωM I2. Secondary: 0 = −jωM I1 + (R2 + jωL2 + Z_L)I2.
Define Z22 = R2 + jωL2 + Z_L. Then **Z_in = R1 + jωL1 + (ωM)²/Z22** (reflected impedance).
**Ideal transformer** (k = 1, L → ∞, no loss): V1/V2 = N1/N2 = a, I1/I2 = N2/N1, and impedance reflected to primary Z' = a²Z_L.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** R1 = 2 Ω, X1 = 6 Ω, ωM = 4 Ω, Z22 = 8 Ω (resistive). Reflected = 16/8 = 2 Ω. Z_in = 4 + j6 Ω, |Z_in| = 7.21 Ω.

**Example 2.** Ideal transformer 10:1, R_L = 100 Ω on the secondary. Seen at the primary: a²R_L = 100×100 = 10 kΩ. If the primary is 1000 V: secondary 100 V, I2 = 1 A, I1 = 0.1 A. Power = 100 W both sides.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to square the turns ratio when reflecting impedance.
- Sign error: reflected impedance of a coupled pair adds to Z_in (it is (ωM)²/Z22, positive for resistive Z22).
- Using DC across a transformer.

lessons.title: Three-phase systems, star and delta relations

story.title: Why the grid uses three wires

scenes.text: High-voltage lines on pylons come in sets of three conductors, not two.
Three voltages 120° apart deliver constant total power and save copper.

steps.title: Basics
steps.body:
Phase voltages (sequence RYB): V_R = V∠0°, V_Y = V∠−120°, V_B = V∠+120°; their sum is zero.
**Star (Y):** V_L = √3 V_ph (leads phase voltage by 30°), I_L = I_ph.
**Delta (Δ):** V_L = V_ph, I_L = √3 I_ph (lags phase current by 30°).
Advantages over single-phase: constant instantaneous power, smaller conductors for the same power, self-starting rotating field in motors.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 400 V line-to-line star source: V_ph = 400/√3 = 230.9 V.

**Example 2.** Delta load, 10 Ω per phase on 400 V: I_ph = 40 A, I_L = 40√3 = 69.3 A.

**Example 3.** Same 10 Ω resistors in star on 400 V: I_L = 230.9/10 = 23.1 A — delta draws three times the line current of star.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using √3 in the wrong connection.
- Confusing line voltage (between lines) with phase voltage.
- Quoting a 230 V/400 V system as 440 V.

lessons.title: Power in balanced three-phase loads

scenes.text: A workshop engineer reads 400 V, 20 A, pf 0.8 on a motor and wants the kW.
Three-phase power uses line values and a factor √3.

steps.title: Formulae
steps.body:
For a balanced load (star or delta): P = √3 V_L I_L cos φ = 3 V_ph I_ph cos φ (W); Q = √3 V_L I_L sin φ; S = √3 V_L I_L. φ is the angle between phase voltage and phase current — not between line quantities.
Per-phase method: analyse one phase using V_ph and Z_ph; multiply power by 3.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using √3 V_ph I_ph (it is 3 V_ph I_ph).

lessons.title: Unbalanced loads and the neutral

story.title: A building where one floor draws more

scenes.text: In a building, single-phase loads are spread across R, Y and B but never perfectly equally.
The neutral wire carries the imbalance.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
4-wire star: each phase sees V_ph even if unbalanced; I_N = −(I_R + I_Y + I_B) (phasor sum).
3-wire star unbalanced: the load star point shifts; use Millman: V_N'N = (ΣV_k Y_k)/(ΣY_k), phase voltage across load k = V_k − V_N'N.
Delta unbalanced: each phase current = V_L/Z_phase; line currents by KCL.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Balanced: 10∠0°, 10∠−120°, 10∠120° ⇒ I_N = 0.

**Example 2.** I_R = 10∠0°, I_Y = 10∠−120°, I_B = 0: sum = 10∠−60°, so I_N = 10 A (magnitude).

**Example 3.** Open neutral with a missing load can overvoltage the lightly loaded phases — a reason neutral breaks are dangerous.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding unbalanced phase currents arithmetically.
- Assuming V_N'N = 0 without a neutral wire.

lessons.title: Two-wattmeter method

scenes.text: A 3-wire motor has no neutral, so a lab uses just two wattmeters instead of three.

steps.title: Theory
steps.body:
Connect two wattmeters in two lines, with their pressure coils returning to the third line. Total P = W1 + W2 (valid for balanced or unbalanced 3-wire loads).
For a balanced load: W1 = V_L I_L cos(30° − φ), W2 = V_L I_L cos(30° + φ). tan φ = √3 (W1 − W2)/(W1 + W2).
Special cases: pf = 1 ⇒ W1 = W2; pf = 0.5 ⇒ one reading zero; pf < 0.5 ⇒ one reading negative; pf = 0 ⇒ W1 = −W2.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:

- Forgetting that reversing connections is needed for a negative reading, and recording it as negative.

steps.title: Transformations

For a balanced Δ load, convert to Y, take the single-phase equivalent (V_ph = V_L/√3), compute I_L, and multiply power by 3.
Star-delta starter: line current and torque during start are 1/3 of the direct-on-line values.

courses.summary: First-order RC and RL natural and step responses, time constants and initial conditions, second-order RLC damping cases, the s-domain circuit method and complete response with network functions.

lessons.title: First-order RC and RL circuits

scenes.text: A camera flash charges a capacitor over a couple of seconds and discharges it in a flash.
How fast depends on a single number: the time constant.

steps.title: Time constant
steps.body:
RC: τ = RC. RL: τ = L/R (seconds). General solution: x(t) = x(∞) + [x(0+) − x(∞)] e^{−t/τ}.
Charging capacitor from 0 to V: v_c = V(1 − e^{−t/τ}); at t = τ it reaches 63.2%; at 5τ it is 99.3% (≈ steady state).
RL with step V: i = (V/R)(1 − e^{−t/τ}). Discharge: x = x(0)e^{−t/τ}.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** R = 10 kΩ, C = 100 µF ⇒ τ = 1 s. Charged from a 12 V step: v_c(1 s) = 12(1 − e⁻¹) = 7.58 V; v_c(3 s) = 12(1 − e⁻³) = 11.40 V.

**Example 2.** R = 20 Ω, L = 0.5 H ⇒ τ = 25 ms. 24 V step: I_final = 1.2 A, i(25 ms) = 1.2×0.632 = 0.759 A.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- τ = R/L (inverted) for RL.
- Using the 5τ rule as exact — it is a practical settling time.
- Using the source resistance only: τ uses the Thevenin resistance seen by the energy-storage element.

lessons.title: Initial conditions and switching

scenes.text: Switching off an inductor can cause a spark because its current cannot change instantly.
Continuity rules tell us what the circuit does right after a switch moves.

steps.title: Rules
steps.body:
- Inductor current is continuous: i_L(0+) = i_L(0−).
- Capacitor voltage is continuous: v_C(0+) = v_C(0−).
- At t = 0+ an inductor with initial current acts as a current source (open if i = 0); a capacitor with initial voltage acts as a voltage source (short if v = 0).
- At t → ∞ in DC: inductor = short, capacitor = open.
Steps: (1) find i_L(0−), v_C(0−) with the old steady state; (2) draw the circuit at 0+; (3) find x(∞); (4) τ; (5) write x(t).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1 (source-free RL).** L = 2 H, i(0) = 3 A, R = 4 Ω: τ = 0.5 s, i = 3e^{−2t}; at t = 0.5 s i = 3×0.3679 = 1.104 A. Initial energy ½Li² = 9 J, all dissipated in R.

**Example 2.** Capacitor 10 µF initially at 10 V discharging through 1 kΩ: τ = 10 ms, v = 10e^{−100t}; at 10 ms 3.68 V.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming inductor voltage or capacitor current is continuous (they can jump).
- Reading the circuit at t = 0− instead of 0+ for the other variables.

lessons.title: Second-order series RLC response

scenes.text: A car's shock absorber can be too bouncy (underdamped), too stiff (overdamped) or just right (critical).
A series RLC circuit behaves the same way.

steps.title: Characteristic equation
steps.body:
Series RLC source-free: s² + (R/L)s + 1/(LC) = 0. Define α = R/(2L) (neper frequency), ω0 = 1/√(LC).
- **Overdamped** α > ω0: s = −α ± √(α² − ω0²) real; i = A₁e^{s₁t} + A₂e^{s₂t}.
- **Critically damped** α = ω0: i = (A₁ + A₂t)e^{−αt}; R = 2√(L/C).
- **Underdamped** α < ω0: s = −α ± jω_d, ω_d = √(ω0² − α²); i = e^{−αt}(A cos ω_d t + B sin ω_d t). Damping ratio ζ = α/ω0.
Parallel RLC: α = 1/(2RC).

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
L = 1 H, C = 0.04 F ⇒ ω0 = 5 rad/s.
- R = 6 Ω: α = 3 ⇒ underdamped, ω_d = √(25 − 9) = 4 rad/s.
- R = 10 Ω: α = 5 ⇒ critically damped (R = 2√(L/C) = 2√25 = 10 ✔).
- R = 12 Ω: α = 6 ⇒ overdamped, s = −6 ± √11 = −2.68, −9.32.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- α = R/L instead of R/(2L).
- Using parallel RLC formula for series.
- Forgetting two initial conditions: i(0) and di/dt(0) (from v_C(0)).

lessons.title: Laplace transform method for circuits

scenes.text: Solving a differential equation by hand for every circuit gets tedious.
The Laplace transform turns differentiation into multiplication by s so circuits become algebra.

steps.title: Transform pairs and models
steps.body:
L{1} = 1/s; L{e^{−at}} = 1/(s+a); L{t} = 1/s²; L{sin ωt} = ω/(s²+ω²); L{cos ωt} = s/(s²+ω²); L{δ(t)} = 1; L{f'} = sF − f(0⁻).
Circuit elements in the s-domain: R; inductor sL in series with a source L·i(0) (or sL ∥ i(0)/s); capacitor 1/(sC) in series with v(0)/s.
Initial value: f(0+) = lim sF(s) as s→∞; final value: f(∞) = lim sF(s) as s→0 (poles in the left half-plane).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Dropping the initial-condition source of L or C.
- Using the final value theorem when poles lie on or right of the jω-axis.
- Partial-fraction coefficient mistakes — check at one value of s.

lessons.title: Complete response, network functions, poles and zeros

scenes.text: A headphone amplifier's low-pass filter smooths an input pulse: its output tells us its time constant.
The poles of the transfer function control the entire transient behaviour.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
Complete response = natural (transient) + forced (steady-state) = zero-input + zero-state.
Transfer function H(s) = Y(s)/X(s) (zero initial conditions). Poles: roots of the denominator (decide stability: all in the left half-plane ⇒ stable); zeros: roots of the numerator. Impulse response h(t) = L⁻¹{H(s)}; step response = L⁻¹{H(s)/s}.
RC low-pass: H(s) = 1/(1 + sRC), a pole at s = −1/RC.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** RC with τ = 2 s, source 10 V DC, v_c(0) = 2 V: v_c = 10 + (2 − 10)e^{−t/2}; at t = 2 s: 10 − 8×0.3679 = 7.06 V.

**Example 2.** 5 V pulse of width 2τ on a low-pass RC: v_c(2τ) = 5(1 − e⁻²) = 4.32 V; afterwards it decays: v_c(t) = 4.32 e^{−(t−2τ)/τ}.

**Example 3.** H(s) = 1/(s² + 3s + 2) = 1/((s+1)(s+2)): poles −1, −2 — stable and overdamped.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Concluding stability from zeros.
- Treating a pole at the origin as unstable in every sense (it is marginally stable).
- Ignoring the initial condition term in the complete response.

lessons.title: Formula and key-point sheet

scenes.text: Ravi has one hour to revise a whole semester of circuit theory.
A one-page sheet of formulae with units and conditions is the best last-minute tool.

steps.title: DC and theorems
steps.body:
- Divider: V_k = V R_k/ΣR; I_1 = I R_2/(R_1+R_2).
- Loops = b − n + 1; independent nodes = n − 1.
- Thevenin: V_th = V_oc, R_th = V_oc/I_sc. P_max = V_th²/(4R_th) at R_L = R_th.
- Superposition: linear, not for power.

steps.title: AC, resonance, power
steps.body:
- V_rms = V_m/√2; form factor 1.11.
- Z = R + jX; X_L = ωL; X_C = 1/ωC.
- S² = P² + Q²; Q_c = P(tan φ₁ − tan φ₂); C = Q_c/(ωV²).
- Resonance: f0 = 1/(2π√LC); Q = ω0L/R; BW = f0/Q; Z_d = L/CR.
- Coupled: k = M/√(L1L2); L_series = L1 + L2 ± 2M.
- Max power AC: Z_L = Z_th*.

steps.title: Three-phase and transients
steps.body:
- Star V_L = √3V_ph; delta I_L = √3I_ph.
- P = √3 V_L I_L cos φ; two-wattmeter: tan φ = √3(W1 − W2)/(W1 + W2).
- τ_RC = RC; τ_RL = L/R; x = x∞ + (x0 − x∞)e^{−t/τ}.
- α = R/2L; ω0 = 1/√LC; critical R = 2√(L/C).
- Final value: lim sF(s).

steps.title: Exam habits
steps.body:
- Always write units.
- State the sign convention.
- Check results with a second method (e.g. power balance).

lessons.title: Lab: Three-phase power by two wattmeters (with viva)

scenes.text: A balanced three-phase inductive load is fed from a 415 V supply through two wattmeters.

steps.title: Procedure
steps.body:
1. Connect the current coils of W1 and W2 in two lines and the pressure coils between those lines and the third.
2. Switch on the supply and apply the load.
3. Record W1, W2 (use the reversing switch if a reading is negative and treat it as negative).
4. Compute P = W1 + W2 and pf from tan φ = √3(W1 − W2)/(W1 + W2).
Observation: W1 = 1200 W, W2 = 600 W ⇒ P = 1800 W, tan φ = √3×600/1800 = 0.577 ⇒ φ = 30°, pf = 0.866 lagging.

steps.body:
- Three-phase supply: use insulated probes and check the phase sequence.
- Never open the current-transformer secondary.

lessons.title: Network graphs, trees and matrices

scenes.text: SPICE-type simulators turn a schematic into matrices automatically.
They use graph theory: nodes, branches, trees and loops.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
Graph: nodes (n) and branches (b). Tree: connected subgraph with all nodes and no loops — has n − 1 twigs; remaining l = b − n + 1 branches are links (co-tree).
Incidence matrix A (reduced, (n − 1) × b): +1 branch leaving node, −1 entering. KCL: A·I_b = 0.
Tie-set (fundamental loop) matrix B: one loop per link ⇒ KVL: B·V_b = 0. Cut-set matrix Q: one cut-set per twig ⇒ KCL: Q·I_b = 0.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** A bridge network: n = 4, b = 6 ⇒ twigs 3, links 3 ⇒ 3 independent loop (mesh) equations, 3 independent node equations.

**Example 2.** Number of trees of a complete graph with 4 nodes (Cayley): 4^(4−2) = 16. In general, number of trees = det(A·Aᵀ).

**Example 3.** For n = 5, b = 8: independent KVL equations = 4; KCL = 4.

steps.title: Link with analysis
steps.body: Loop analysis: Z_loop = B Z_b Bᵀ. Node analysis: Y_node = A Y_b Aᵀ. Choosing a tree well (voltage sources in twigs, current sources in links) simplifies equations.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Counting the reference node in the incidence matrix size.
- Forming a loop when choosing twigs.
- Sign conventions inconsistent between A and branch currents.

activity.prompt: A network has 6 nodes and 10 branches. Number of links (independent loops)?

quiz.q: Twigs in a tree with n nodes
quiz.why: A tree connects all n nodes without forming a loop, which needs n − 1 branches. These tree branches are called twigs.
Links are the branches not in the tree. With b total branches and n − 1 twigs, links = b − (n − 1) = b − n + 1.
By the matrix-tree theorem, the number of trees of a graph equals det(A Aᵀ), where A is the reduced incidence matrix. The other options are not the correct matrix product.

quiz.q: Each fundamental cut-set contains exactly one
quiz.why: A fundamental cut-set is formed by removing one tree branch (twig) and the links needed to separate the graph. So it contains exactly one twig.

quiz.q: Each fundamental loop contains exactly one
quiz.why: A fundamental loop is formed by adding one link to the tree. So it contains exactly one link and the rest are twigs.

lessons.title: Dependent sources in nodal and mesh analysis

scenes.text: A transistor's small-signal model contains a current source g_m·v_π controlled by another voltage.
Circuits with dependent sources need one extra relation per controlled source.

steps.title: Types
steps.body: VCVS (μv_x), VCCS (g v_x), CCVS (r i_x), CCCS (β i_x). Treat them like independent sources when writing equations, then add the controlling equation (express v_x or i_x in terms of the unknowns).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1 (nodal with VCCS).** Node V₁: 10 V source through 2 Ω, to ground through 4 Ω, and a VCCS injecting 0.5V₁ into the node... KCL: (V₁ − 10)/2 + V₁/4 − 0.5V₁ = 0 ⇒ V₁(0.5 + 0.25 − 0.5) = 5 ⇒ V₁ = 20 V.

**Example 2 (mesh with CCVS).** Single loop: 12 V source, 2 Ω, 4 Ω and a CCVS of 3i opposing the current: 12 = 6i + 3i ⇒ i = 1.33 A.

**Example 3.** If the CCVS aids the source: 12 + 3i = 6i ⇒ i = 4 A.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Deactivating dependent sources when finding R_th (never do that).
- Missing the controlling-variable equation.
- Sign of the dependent source relative to the loop direction.

activity.prompt: Dependent source → controlled by

quiz.q: Dependent sources are deactivated when finding R_th?
quiz.why: A dependent source is controlled by a voltage or current in the circuit, so it must stay in place when finding R_th. Only independent sources are turned off (voltage sources shorted, current sources opened).

quiz.q: Unit of g in a VCCS
quiz.why: In a VCCS, the output current is g times a control voltage, so g = A/V, which is siemens. It is a conductance.

quiz.q: Unit of r in a CCVS
quiz.why: In a CCVS, the output voltage is r times a control current, so r = V/A, which is ohm. It is a transresistance.
This refers to a worked example in the lesson. Solving its equations gives V₁ = 20 V. The other values come from errors in the sums.
The hybrid-π model of a BJT has a current source g_m·v_π controlled by the base–emitter voltage. A current controlled by a voltage is a VCCS.

sources: Standard Network Analysis / Circuit Theory syllabus (EE core)

lessons.title: Thevenin and Norton with dependent sources

scenes.text: An amplifier datasheet lists output impedance.
With dependent sources inside, we find it by applying a test source.

steps.title: Methods
steps.body:
1. V_oc and I_sc ⇒ R_th = V_oc/I_sc.
2. **Test-source method:** deactivate independent sources only, apply V_t at the terminals, find I_t ⇒ R_th = V_t/I_t. R_th may even be negative (active circuits).
If the circuit has only dependent sources, V_th = 0 and you must use a test source.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 10 V source, 2 Ω series, terminals A–B across a 4 Ω resistor in parallel with a CCCS 0.5i (i = current in the 2 Ω, injecting into node A).
V_oc: (V − 10)/2 + V/4 − 0.5(10 − V)/2 = 0 ⇒ 0.5V − 5 + 0.25V − 2.5 + 0.25V = 0 ⇒ V = 7.5 V.
I_sc: V = 0 ⇒ i = 5 A ⇒ I_sc = 5 + 2.5 = 7.5 A ⇒ R_th = 1 Ω.

**Example 2 (test source).** Only a resistor 3 Ω and a VCVS 2v_x in series where v_x is the voltage across the 3 Ω: V_t = v_x + 2v_x = 3v_x, I_t = v_x/3 ⇒ R_th = 9 Ω.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Use both methods on an exam if time permits — they must agree.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Setting dependent sources to zero.
- Using V_oc/I_sc when both are zero (no independent sources) — use the test source.
- Wrong sign of the controlling variable after short-circuiting.

activity.prompt: Test-source method
items: Deactivate independent sources only
Apply a test voltage V_t (or current I_t) at the terminals
Write KCL/KVL including dependent sources
Solve for the other test quantity
R_th = V_t/I_t

quiz.q: If a network has only dependent sources, V_th =
quiz.why: With no independent source there is nothing to drive the network, so all voltages and currents are zero and the open-circuit voltage V_th = 0. Dependent sources alone cannot start a response.

quiz.q: R_th from open- and short-circuit tests
quiz.why: R_th is the Thevenin voltage divided by the Norton current: R_th = V_oc/I_sc. It is a ratio of voltage to current, so the units are ohm.
With dependent sources, a network can supply power. Then the ratio V/I at the terminals can be negative, so R_th can be negative in active circuits. A passive network cannot do this.
This refers to a worked example in the lesson. With a dependent source present, the test-source method gives R_th = V_t/I_t = 9 Ω. The other values come from ignoring the dependent source.
The test source is applied after only the independent sources are deactivated. The dependent sources stay active, so the ratio V_t/I_t gives R_th.

sources: Standard Network Analysis / Circuit Theory syllabus (EE core)

lessons.title: Millman, reciprocity, Tellegen and substitution theorems

scenes.text: Three batteries with different EMFs feed a common bus.
Millman's theorem gives the bus voltage in one step.

steps.title: Theorems
steps.body:
- **Millman:** parallel branches each with source Eₖ and admittance Yₖ: V = ΣEₖYₖ/ΣYₖ.
- **Reciprocity:** in a linear bilateral network without dependent sources, the ratio of response to excitation is unchanged if their positions are interchanged.
- **Tellegen:** Σ vₖiₖ = 0 over all branches (any network satisfying KCL/KVL, even non-linear) — power conservation.
- **Substitution:** any branch with known v and i can be replaced by an equivalent source.
- **Compensation:** a change ΔZ in a branch carrying I produces changes as if a source IΔZ were inserted.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1 (Millman).** 12 V/2 Ω, 10 V/2 Ω, 0 V/4 Ω (a load) in parallel: V = (6 + 5 + 0)/(0.5 + 0.5 + 0.25) = 11/1.25 = 8.8 V.

**Example 2 (reciprocity).** A 10 V source in branch 1 gives 2 A in branch 2; moving the 10 V source to branch 2 gives 2 A in branch 1.

**Example 3 (Tellegen check).** Source 10 V delivering 2 A (−20 W absorbed) and two resistors absorbing 12 W and 8 W: Σvi = −20 + 12 + 8 = 0 ✔

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying reciprocity to circuits with dependent sources.
- Forgetting zero-EMF branches (pure loads) in Millman's denominator.
- Using associated-reference signs inconsistently in Tellegen.

activity.prompt: Millman: branches 6 V/3 Ω and 12 V/6 Ω in parallel (no load). Common voltage (V)?

quiz.why: Millman's theorem gives the common voltage of parallel branches as V = ΣEY/ΣY, where each branch has source E and admittance Y. The weights are the branch admittances.
Reciprocity holds only for linear bilateral networks. Dependent sources and non-linear devices break it, since the network is then no longer bilateral.
options: linear bilateral network, no dependent sources

quiz.why: Tellegen's theorem says that the sum of v·i over all branches is zero. That means power delivered equals power absorbed, so it expresses conservation of power.
Tellegen's theorem depends only on KVL and KCL (the network topology), not on what the elements are. So it holds for non-linear networks too.
If a branch impedance changes by ΔZ while carrying current I, the compensation theorem replaces the change with a voltage source of IΔZ in series with the branch. Units: A × Ω = V.

sources: Standard Network Analysis / Circuit Theory syllabus (EE core)

questions.q: Branches b, nodes n: KVL equations
questions.why: Independent KVL equations equal the number of links: b − (n − 1) = b − n + 1. The n − 1 count is for KCL node equations.

questions.q: VCCS output is
questions.why: A voltage-controlled current source (VCCS) has a current as its output, and its input is a voltage. The name gives output last: voltage-controlled, current source.

questions.q: Tellegen's theorem sum Σvᵢiᵢ =
questions.why: Tellegen's theorem states that Σvᵢiᵢ = 0 over all branches, for any network, since power supplied equals power absorbed. It is not the total power, which is the sum of absorbed power taken as positive.

questions.q: Trees of a complete graph with 3 nodes
questions.why: Cayley's formula gives nⁿ⁻² trees for a complete graph with n nodes. For n = 3: 3¹ = 3 trees (each pair of the three branches).

questions.q: Millman: 10 V/1 Ω and 20 V/1 Ω parallel
questions.why: Millman: V = (10/1 + 20/1)/(1/1 + 1/1) = 30/2 = 15 V, the average of the two sources since the resistances are equal.

questions.q: Twigs for n = 7
questions.why: Twigs = n − 1 = 7 − 1 = 6. A tree needs one fewer branch than nodes.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Dependent sources must not be deactivated when finding R_th.  Reason (R): Their values depend on circuit variables, not on external excitation.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both are true. A dependent source's value is set by a circuit variable, not by external excitation, so turning it off would change the circuit itself. This is why they stay in when finding R_th, so R explains A.

questions.q: Loop: 20 V, 4 Ω, 6 Ω, CCVS 5i opposing: i
questions.why: With the CCVS opposing the source, KVL gives 20 = 4i + 6i + 5i = 15i. So i = 20/15 ≈ 1.33 A. The CCVS acts like an extra 5 Ω in series.

questions.q: Test source: V_t = 2 V gives I_t = 0.5 A. R_th
questions.why: R_th = V_t/I_t = 2 V/0.5 A = 4 Ω. The test-source method gives the Thevenin resistance directly, as a ratio.

questions.q: Case: Three solar strings 36 V/1.2 Ω, 35 V/1.0 Ω, 34 V/1.5 Ω are paralleled on an unloaded bus. Bus voltage
questions.why: Millman with E/R terms: 36/1.2 = 30, 35/1.0 = 35, 34/1.5 = 22.67; the sum is 87.67. The conductances add to 0.833 + 1 + 0.667 = 2.5. So V = 87.67/2.5 ≈ 35.1 V, a weighted average of the three source voltages.

questions.q: Network with n = 5, b = 9: independent node and loop equations
questions.why: Independent KCL equations = n − 1 = 5 − 1 = 4. Independent KVL equations = b − n + 1 = 9 − 5 + 1 = 5. So the answer is 4 node and 5 loop equations.

questions.q: Circuit: 3 Ω in series with VCVS 2v_x, v_x across the 3 Ω. R_th
questions.why: Apply a test source V_t. The current I through the 3 Ω gives v_x = 3I and the VCVS adds 2v_x = 6I, so V_t = 3I + 6I = 9I. So R_th = V_t/I = 9 Ω. The dependent source makes the circuit look like a larger resistance.

questions.q: V_oc = 15 V, I_sc = −5 A (active network): R_th
questions.why: R_th = V_oc/I_sc = 15/(−5) = −3 Ω. A negative value is possible because the active network (with dependent sources) supplies power at its terminals.

questions.q: Compensation: branch with 2 A has R increased by 1 Ω. Compensating source
questions.why: By the compensation theorem, the source equals IΔR = 2 A × 1 Ω = 2 V. It opposes the current because an extra resistance causes an extra drop.

lessons.title: Initial and final conditions

scenes.text: A camera flash charges a capacitor, then dumps it into the lamp in microseconds.
What happens at t = 0⁺ depends on which quantities cannot jump.

steps.title: Continuity rules
steps.body:
- Capacitor voltage cannot change instantaneously: v_C(0⁺) = v_C(0⁻).
- Inductor current cannot change instantaneously: i_L(0⁺) = i_L(0⁻).
At t = 0⁺: uncharged C acts as a short; charged C as a voltage source; un-energised L acts as open; L carrying I₀ as a current source.
At steady DC (t → ∞): C open, L short.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 12 V, 2 Ω, L in series, switch closes at 0 (i_L(0⁻) = 0): i(0⁺) = 0, v_L(0⁺) = 12 V, i(∞) = 6 A.

**Example 2.** 10 V through 5 Ω charges C (uncharged): i(0⁺) = 2 A, v_C(0⁺) = 0, i(∞) = 0, v_C(∞) = 10 V.

**Example 3.** di/dt at 0⁺ in Example 1: v_L/L = 12/L.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Letting capacitor voltage jump.
- Treating an inductor as open in DC steady state (it's a short).
- Using pre-switching circuit at t = 0⁺ for everything except the continuous quantities.

activity.prompt: At t = 0⁺ (initially de-energised) the element behaves as

quiz.why: The energy in a capacitor is ½CV². Energy cannot change instantly, so the voltage across a capacitor cannot jump. Its current can change suddenly.
The energy in an inductor is ½LI². Energy cannot change instantly, so the inductor current cannot jump, while its voltage can.
At DC steady state the current is constant, so di/dt = 0 and v = L·di/dt = 0. A component with zero voltage is a short circuit.

quiz.q: Uncharged capacitor at t = 0⁺ acts as
quiz.why: An uncharged capacitor has v = 0 at t = 0⁺, because the voltage cannot jump. Zero voltage with any current is a short circuit.
At steady state the inductor is a short, so i(∞) = V/R = 12/2 = 6 A for the lesson's circuit. The other values come from using the wrong resistance.

sources: Standard Network Analysis / Circuit Theory syllabus (EE core)

lessons.title: First-order RL and RC circuits

scenes.text: A car's dome light fades out slowly after the door closes.
An RC timer controls the fade — a first-order transient.

steps.title: General solution
steps.body:
x(t) = x(∞) + [x(0⁺) − x(∞)]e^(−t/τ), τ = RC or L/R (R = Thevenin resistance seen by C or L).
After 1τ: 63.2% of the change; 5τ ≈ 99.3% (considered steady).
Natural (source-free) response decays to zero; forced response follows the source; complete = natural + forced.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** RC: R = 10 kΩ, C = 100 µF, 12 V step, v_C(0) = 0: τ = 1 s; v_C = 12(1 − e^(−t)); v_C(2 s) = 10.4 V.

**Example 2.** RL: R = 4 Ω, L = 2 H, 20 V step: τ = 0.5 s; i = 5(1 − e^(−2t)) A; time to reach 4 A: e^(−2t) = 0.2 ⇒ t = 0.80 s.

**Example 3.** Capacitor charged to 10 V discharges through 2 kΩ, C = 50 µF: τ = 0.1 s; v = 10e^(−10t); energy released = ½ × 50µ × 100 = 2.5 mJ.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using a component R instead of the Thevenin R seen by C or L.
- Using τ = R/L.
- Forgetting that the switch may change the circuit (and thus τ) for t > 0.

activity.prompt: RC charging: τ = 2 s, V_s = 10 V, v_C(0) = 0. v_C at t = 2 s (V, 2 decimals)?

quiz.why: The time constant of a series RL circuit is τ = L/R. For RC it is RC. A larger L slows the current change, and a larger R speeds it up.

quiz.q: Fraction of change completed after one τ
quiz.why: For a first-order response, the fraction completed after t = τ is 1 − e⁻¹ = 1 − 0.368 = 0.632, i.e. 63.2%. The 36.8% is what is left.

quiz.q: Steady state is reached after about
quiz.why: After 5τ, the response is within e⁻⁵ ≈ 0.7% of its final value, so by the usual rule it is at steady state. After 1τ it is only 63% done.

quiz.q: τ for R = 1 MΩ, C = 1 µF
quiz.why: τ = RC = 10⁶ Ω × 10⁻⁶ F = 1 s. The mega and micro prefixes cancel.
The complete response is the natural (transient) part plus the forced (steady-state) part. This follows from the linear differential equation: the sum of the homogeneous and particular solutions.

sources: Standard Network Analysis / Circuit Theory syllabus (EE core)

lessons.title: Second-order RLC circuits

scenes.text: An RLC circuit rings like a car suspension after a bump.
Damping decides whether it oscillates or settles smoothly.

steps.title: Series RLC (source-free)
steps.body:
L d²i/dt² + R di/dt + i/C = 0. Characteristic: s² + (R/L)s + 1/(LC) = 0.
α = R/(2L) (neper frequency), ω₀ = 1/√(LC). Roots s = −α ± √(α² − ω₀²).
- α > ω₀: overdamped (two real roots)
- α = ω₀: critically damped (R = 2√(L/C))
- α < ω₀: underdamped — i = e^(−αt)(A cos ω_d t + B sin ω_d t), ω_d = √(ω₀² − α²)
Parallel RLC: α = 1/(2RC).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** R = 10 Ω, L = 1 H, C = 0.01 F: α = 5, ω₀ = 10 ⇒ underdamped; ω_d = √75 = 8.66 rad/s.

**Example 2.** Critical resistance for L = 1 H, C = 0.01 F: R = 2√100 = 20 Ω.

**Example 3.** R = 50 Ω: α = 25 > 10 ⇒ overdamped; roots −25 ± √525 = −2.09, −47.9.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using α = R/(2L) for a parallel RLC (it is 1/(2RC)).
- Forgetting two initial conditions are needed (i(0) and di/dt(0)).
- Taking ω_d = ω₀ when damping is present.

activity.label: Series resistance for L = 1 H, C = 0.01 F (R_crit = 20 Ω)

bands.text: R = 0: undamped — oscillates forever at ω₀ = 10 rad/s.
Near 20 Ω: critically damped — fastest settling without overshoot.

quiz.why: For a series RLC, α = R/(2L) and ω₀ = 1/√(LC). Critical damping needs α = ω₀, so R = 2√(L/C). Larger R is overdamped and smaller R is underdamped.
The damping factor of a series RLC is α = R/(2L). The 1/(2RC) form is for the parallel RLC, and 1/√(LC) is ω₀.
An underdamped system has complex roots −α ± jω_d, which gives a sinusoid whose amplitude decays exponentially, i.e. a decaying sinusoid.

quiz.q: ω₀ for L = 4 H, C = 1/16 F
Initial conditions needed for second order
quiz.why: A second-order circuit has two arbitrary constants in its response, so two initial conditions are needed, such as v(0) and dv/dt(0) (or i(0)).

lessons.title: Laplace-domain circuit analysis

scenes.text: Instead of differential equations, engineers draw the s-domain circuit.
Initial conditions become small extra sources.

steps.title: s-domain models
steps.body:
- R → R
- L → sL in series with voltage source L·i(0⁻) (aiding the original current direction appropriately), or sL ∥ current source i(0⁻)/s
- C → 1/(sC) in series with v(0⁻)/s, or 1/(sC) ∥ current source C·v(0⁻)
Apply KVL/KCL/theorems to impedances, solve, invert.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Series RC, R = 1 Ω, C = 1 F, step 1 V, v_C(0) = 0: I(s) = (1/s)/(1 + 1/s) = 1/(s + 1) ⇒ i = e^(−t).

**Example 2.** Series RL, R = 2 Ω, L = 1 H, i(0) = 3 A, no source: (s + 2)I = 3 ⇒ i = 3e^(−2t).

**Example 3.** Series RLC, R = 3, L = 1, C = 0.5, step 1 V, zero ICs: I = (1/s)/(s + 3 + 2/s) = 1/(s² + 3s + 2) = 1/(s + 1) − 1/(s + 2) ⇒ i = e^(−t) − e^(−2t).

steps.title: Initial/final value theorems
steps.body: f(0⁺) = lim (s→∞) sF(s); f(∞) = lim (s→0) sF(s) (if poles of sF are in the LHP) — quick checks.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Wrong polarity of initial-condition sources.
- Forgetting the 1/s of a step input.
- Using the final value theorem when poles are on the jω-axis.

activity.prompt: s-domain impedances
activity.text: An inductor becomes ___ and a capacitor becomes 1/(___).

quiz.why: In the s-domain, a capacitor has impedance 1/(sC), found by transforming i = C dv/dt. An inductor has sL.

quiz.q: Inductor initial current appears as a series source
quiz.why: v = L di/dt transforms to V = sL·I − L·i(0⁻). The initial current therefore appears as a series voltage source of value L·i(0⁻).
Final value theorem: f(∞) = lim(s→0) sF(s), valid if all poles of sF(s) are in the left half-plane. The s→∞ limit gives the initial value.
The transform pair is 1/(s + a) ↔ e^(−at). So 2/(s + 4) ↔ 2e^(−4t). The constant 2 is just a multiplier and 4 is the decay rate.
Initial value theorem: f(0⁺) = lim(s→∞) sF(s) = lim 5s/(s + 1) = 5. This matches f(t) = 5e^(−t) at t = 0.

sources: Standard Network Analysis / Circuit Theory syllabus (EE core)

questions.q: Capacitor at DC steady state
questions.why: At DC steady state the voltage is constant, so i = C dv/dt = 0. A branch with no current is an open circuit.

questions.q: τ = RC for 2 kΩ, 5 µF
questions.why: τ = RC = 2×10³ × 5×10⁻⁶ = 10×10⁻³ s = 10 ms. Check the prefixes, since kΩ × µF gives milliseconds.

questions.q: Inductor current is
questions.why: The inductor current cannot change instantly, since that would need infinite voltage (v = L di/dt). So it is continuous, though it need not be zero at t = 0⁺.

questions.q: RL: 24 V, 6 Ω, 3 H: final current
questions.why: At steady state the inductor acts as a short, so I = V/R = 24/6 = 4 A. The 3 H only affects how fast it gets there.

questions.q: Time constant of that RL
questions.why: τ = L/R = 3 H/6 Ω = 0.5 s. Multiplying L by R (18) is wrong because the units would not be seconds.

questions.q: v_C after 3τ (charging to 10 V)
questions.why: v_C = V(1 − e^(−t/τ)). At t = 3τ: 10(1 − e⁻³) = 10 × 0.95 = 9.5 V, so it is about 95% charged.

questions.q: Assertion (A): A series RLC with R = 0 oscillates indefinitely.  Reason (R): With no resistance there is no energy loss (α = 0).
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both are true. With R = 0 there is no resistor to dissipate energy, so α = R/(2L) = 0 and the energy swaps between L and C forever (undamped oscillation). So R explains A.

questions.q: Series RLC R = 4, L = 1, C = 0.25: damping
questions.why: α = R/(2L) = 4/2 = 2. ω₀ = 1/√(LC) = 1/√0.25 = 2. Since α = ω₀, the circuit is critically damped.

questions.q: Time for RC charging to reach 90% of final
questions.why: For charging, 0.9 = 1 − e^(−t/τ), so e^(−t/τ) = 0.1 and t = τ·ln 10 ≈ 2.3τ.

questions.q: Parallel RLC: R = 500 Ω, L = 1 H, C = 1 µF: α
questions.why: For a parallel RLC, α = 1/(2RC) = 1/(2 × 500 × 10⁻⁶) = 1/(10⁻³) = 1000 s⁻¹. Do not confuse with the series formula R/(2L).

questions.q: Case: A 1000 µF capacitor charged to 400 V in a welder discharges through 0.1 Ω. Peak current and τ
questions.why: Peak current is V/R = 400/0.1 = 4000 A at the start. τ = RC = 0.1 × 1000×10⁻⁶ = 10⁻⁴ s = 0.1 ms. The big current is why such discharges are dangerous.

questions.q: Underdamped ω_d for α = 3, ω₀ = 5
questions.why: ω_d = √(ω₀² − α²) = √(25 − 9) = √16 = 4 rad/s. This is the damped oscillation frequency, lower than ω₀.

questions.q: I(s) = 10/(s(s + 5)) final value of i(t)
questions.why: By the final value theorem, i(∞) = lim(s→0) s·I(s) = 10/(0 + 5) = 2. The pole at s = −5 is in the left half-plane, so the theorem applies.

questions.q: RL with i(0) = 2 A, R = 10 Ω, L = 0.5 H discharging: energy dissipated in R
questions.why: All the energy stored in the inductor is dissipated in R: ½LI² = ½ × 0.5 × 2² = 1 J. The value of R changes only the speed, not the total energy.

questions.q: Series RLC R = 6, L = 1, C = 0.2, unit step, zero ICs: I(s) =
questions.why: With zero initial conditions, I(s) = V(s)/Z(s) where V = 1/s and Z = R + sL + 1/(sC) = 6 + s + 5/s. So I(s) = (1/s)/((s² + 6s + 5)/s) = 1/(s² + 6s + 5). Note 1/C = 5.

lessons.title: Phasor-domain analysis and AC theorems

scenes.text: A speaker crossover splits audio into woofer and tweeter paths using L and C.
Mesh and nodal analysis with complex impedances predict each branch's current.

steps.title: Method
steps.body: Replace sources with phasors and elements with impedances (R, jωL, 1/(jωC)); all DC techniques (KCL, KVL, mesh, nodal, superposition, Thevenin) apply with complex arithmetic. For sources at different frequencies use superposition in the time domain.

steps.title: AC maximum power transfer
steps.body: Load Z_L = Z_th* (complex conjugate) ⇒ P_max = |V_th|²/(4R_th) (RMS V_th). If only a resistive load is allowed: R_L = |Z_th|.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** V_th = 10∠0° V (RMS), Z_th = 3 + j4 Ω: Z_L = 3 − j4 ⇒ P_max = 100/12 = 8.33 W.

**Example 2.** Same source, resistive load only: R_L = 5 Ω ⇒ I = 10/|8 + j4| = 1.118 A ⇒ P = 6.25 W.

**Example 3.** Node voltage: 10∠0° V through 5 Ω into a node with −j5 Ω to ground: V = 10 × (−j5)/(5 − j5) = 7.07∠−45° V.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding phasors of different frequencies.
- Using Z_L = Z_th instead of the conjugate.
- Mixing peak and RMS phasors in power formulas.

activity.prompt: V_th = 20 V RMS, Z_th = 4 + j3 Ω. Maximum power with conjugate match (W)?

quiz.why: For maximum power transfer in AC, the load impedance must be the complex conjugate of the source (Thevenin) impedance, Z_L = Z_th*. This cancels the reactance and matches the resistance.
A capacitor's impedance as a phasor is Z_C = 1/(jωC), i.e. a reactance that falls as the frequency rises. The jωC form is the admittance.
Phasors only make sense at a single frequency. With sources at different frequencies, solve for each separately and add the results in the time domain (superposition).
If the load must be purely resistive, the best choice is R_L = |Z_th| = √(R_th² + X_th²). It cannot cancel the reactance, so it is only a compromise match.
This refers to a worked example in the lesson. Using the phasor divider rule gives 7.07∠−45° V. A resistor–capacitor divider gives a lagging phase, so the minus sign is right.

sources: Standard Network Analysis / Circuit Theory syllabus (EE core)

lessons.title: Magnetically coupled circuits

scenes.text: A wireless charger transfers power between two coils that never touch.
Mutual inductance M links them.

steps.title: Mutual inductance and dot convention
steps.body:
v₁ = L₁ di₁/dt ± M di₂/dt. If both currents enter (or leave) the dotted terminals, the mutual voltage adds (+); otherwise subtracts.
k = M/√(L₁L₂), 0 ≤ k ≤ 1 (k = 1 perfect coupling).
Series aiding: L = L₁ + L₂ + 2M; series opposing: L₁ + L₂ − 2M.
Energy w = ½L₁i₁² + ½L₂i₂² ± Mi₁i₂.

steps.title: Ideal transformer and reflected impedance
steps.body: Ideal (k = 1, no losses): V₂/V₁ = N₂/N₁ = n, I₂/I₁ = 1/n (sign by dot convention). Load Z_L referred to primary: Z_L/n². Linear transformer: reflected impedance Z_r = ω²M²/(Z₂₂).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** L₁ = 4 H, L₂ = 9 H, k = 0.5 ⇒ M = 3 H; aiding 19 H; opposing 7 H.

**Example 2.** Series aiding measured 1.2 H, opposing 0.8 H ⇒ 4M = 0.4 ⇒ M = 0.1 H.

**Example 3.** 8 Ω speaker through a 10:1 transformer appears as 800 Ω at the primary.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Ignoring the dot convention sign.
- Using k > 1.
- Referring impedance with n instead of n².

activity.prompt: Coils: L₁ = 2 H, L₂ = 8 H, k = 0.75. Mutual inductance M (H)?

quiz.why: The coefficient of coupling is k = M/√(L₁L₂). It measures how much of one coil's flux links the other.
When the coils are connected in series aiding, the mutual flux adds to the self-flux, so L = L₁ + L₂ + 2M. For opposing it is L₁ + L₂ − 2M.

quiz.q: Impedance referred through turns ratio n = N₂/N₁ to primary
quiz.why: An ideal transformer refers an impedance by the square of the turns ratio. Going from secondary to primary with n = N₂/N₁ gives Z_L/n². The load looks bigger on the primary if n < 1.
The maximum value of k is 1, which means all flux of one coil links the other (perfect coupling). Real coils have k < 1.
Aiding L = L₁ + L₂ + 2M and opposing L = L₁ + L₂ − 2M. The difference is 4M = 10 − 6 = 4, so M = 1 H.

sources: Standard Network Analysis / Circuit Theory syllabus (EE core)

lessons.title: Unbalanced three-phase loads

scenes.text: Flats on one phase run more air-conditioners than others.
The load becomes unbalanced — neutral current flows, and a broken neutral can damage appliances.

steps.title: Star with neutral (4-wire)
steps.body: Each phase current I = V_ph/Z_ph independently; neutral current I_N = I_R + I_Y + I_B (phasor sum).

steps.title: Star without neutral and delta
steps.body:
Without neutral: load star point shifts. Neutral-shift voltage V_N′N = (V_R Y_R + V_Y Y_Y + V_B Y_B)/(Y_R + Y_Y + Y_B) (Millman). Phase voltages of the load = supply phase voltage − V_N′N.
Unbalanced delta: phase currents = V_L/Z_ph for each line voltage; line currents by KCL at each corner.
Power: two-wattmeter method still gives total power for any 3-wire load.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 4-wire 230 V/phase, resistive loads 23 Ω, 46 Ω, 23 Ω: currents 10∠0°, 5∠−120°, 10∠120° A. I_N = 10 + (−2.5 − j4.33) + (−5 + j8.66) = 2.5 + j4.33 = 5∠60° A.

**Example 2.** Same loads, neutral broken: Y = 1/23, 1/46, 1/23; V_N′N = (230/23·1∠0 + 230/46∠−120 + 230/23∠120)/(0.1087) — numerator = (10 + 5∠−120° + 10∠120°) = 2.5 + j4.33 (A) ⇒ V_N′N = 5∠60°/0.1087 = 46∠60° V — phase voltages become unequal (≈ 211 V, 276 V, 211 V), stressing appliances on the lightly loaded phase.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding neutral current magnitudes instead of phasors.
- Assuming the star point stays at zero without a neutral.
- Using phase sequence inconsistently (RYB vs RBY).

activity.prompt: Unbalanced star without neutral — steps
items: Write supply phase voltages as phasors
Find admittances of each load phase
Compute neutral shift V_N′N by Millman's theorem
Find load phase voltages V − V_N′N
Compute currents and powers

quiz.q: Neutral current in a balanced 4-wire system
quiz.why: In a balanced system the three phase currents have equal size and are 120° apart, so their phasor sum is zero. Hence the neutral carries no current.

quiz.q: Broken neutral with unbalanced load causes
quiz.why: If the neutral breaks while the load is unbalanced, the star point moves (neutral shift). The phase voltages then become unequal: some loads see more and some less than normal.
The neutral-point voltage is the weighted average of the phase voltages with weights equal to the load admittances. That is Millman's theorem.
In a delta connection, each phase load is connected directly across a line voltage. So each phase current = line voltage/phase impedance, whatever the other phases do.

quiz.q: Total power of unbalanced 3-wire load measured by
quiz.why: Blondel's theorem says that for N wires, N − 1 wattmeters can measure total power. For a 3-wire system, two wattmeters give the total even if the load is unbalanced.

sources: Standard Network Analysis / Circuit Theory syllabus (EE core)

lessons.title: Power in AC circuits and power-factor engineering

scenes.text: A data centre's power bill depends on kWh and on kVA demand.
Complex power S = P + jQ is the bookkeeping tool.

steps.title: Complex power
steps.body: S = V I* = P + jQ; |S| = V_rms I_rms. Conservation: total complex power supplied = sum absorbed (P and Q separately). Inductive loads absorb +Q, capacitors supply Q (absorb −Q).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Loads in parallel: 10 kW at 0.8 lag (Q = 7.5 kVAR) + 5 kW at 0.6 lead (Q = −6.67 kVAR): total S = 15 + j0.83 kVA ⇒ pf ≈ 0.998 lag.

**Example 2.** V = 230∠0°, I = 10∠−30°: S = 2300∠30° = 1992 + j1150 VA.

**Example 3.** Capacitor to raise 15 kW from 0.75 to 0.95 lag: Q_C = 15(0.882 − 0.329) = 8.3 kVAR.

steps.title: Billing intuition
steps.body: Utilities size cables and transformers by kVA; improving pf cuts kVA demand for the same kW.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the conjugate in S = VI*.
- Adding pf values of loads (add P and Q instead).
- Treating leading Q as positive.

statements.s: S = VI* gives P + jQ.
Power factors of loads can be added directly.
A capacitor bank supplies reactive power.
kVA demand is unaffected by pf.

quiz.why: Complex power is S = VI*, with the complex conjugate of the current. Its real part is P and its imaginary part is Q. Using VI would give the wrong sign for Q.
S = P/pf = 10/0.8 = 12.5 kVA. Q = √(S² − P²) = √(156.25 − 100) = 7.5 kVAR. A 3-4-5 style triangle also works: 10 : 7.5 : 12.5.
A capacitor supplies reactive power, so the Q it absorbs is negative (an inductor absorbs positive Q). That is why capacitors are used to cancel the lagging Q of inductive loads.
S = VI* = 100∠0° × 5∠+60° = 500∠60° VA. The current's angle flips sign when the conjugate is taken. Unit is VA, not W, because it is complex power.
S = P/pf. For the same real power P, raising pf lowers apparent power S (kVA), so the line current falls. Real power stays the same.

sources: Standard Network Analysis / Circuit Theory syllabus (EE core)

questions.q: Impedance of L at ω
questions.why: The phasor impedance of an inductor is Z_L = jωL, a positive imaginary reactance that rises with frequency. The 1/(jωL) form is its admittance.

questions.q: Coefficient of coupling range
questions.why: k = M/√(L₁L₂) is zero for no coupling and 1 for perfect coupling. It cannot exceed 1, because the mutual flux cannot exceed the total flux.

questions.q: Neutral current with balanced load
questions.why: For a balanced load, the three equal currents 120° apart add to zero, so the neutral current is zero.

questions.q: 8 Ω load through 5:1 step-down appears as
questions.why: Referring through the turns ratio multiplies by n² = 5² = 25. So 8 Ω × 25 = 200 Ω seen from the input side. For a step-down transformer, loads look larger from the primary.

questions.q: M for L₁ = L₂ = 5 H, k = 0.6
P_max for V_th = 12 V RMS, Z_th = 6 + j8 Ω
questions.why: P_max = V_th²/(4R_th) = 144/(4 × 6) = 6 W, for a load Z_th* with V_th in RMS. The reactance is cancelled by the conjugate.

questions.q: Assertion (A): With a broken neutral, a lightly loaded phase sees higher voltage.  Reason (R): The load star point shifts toward the heavily loaded phases.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both are true. When the neutral is open, the star point shifts toward the phases with the heavier load (lower impedance). The lightly loaded phase is then left with a higher voltage, so R explains A.

questions.q: Series opposing: L₁ = 3 H, L₂ = 5 H, M = 1 H
questions.why: Series opposing: L = L₁ + L₂ − 2M = 3 + 5 − 2 = 6 H. Opposing connection reduces the total inductance.

questions.q: Total S for 6 kW at 0.6 lag and 4 kW at unity
questions.why: Load 1: P = 6 kW, S = 6/0.6 = 10 kVA, Q = 8 kVAR. Load 2 has Q = 0. Total S = (6 + 4) + j(8 + 0) = 10 + j8 kVA. Add P and Q separately, not the kVA magnitudes.
I_N = −(sum of the phase currents). 10∠0° + 10∠−120° cancels to 10∠60° ... the pair of equal currents leaves the unbalance of 10 A, as 20∠120° minus 10∠120° gives 10∠120°. So |I_N| = 10 A.

questions.q: Case: A 5 kW, 230 V motor at 0.7 lag runs with a 3 kVAR capacitor. New pf
questions.why: Q of the motor = P·tan(cos⁻¹0.7) = 5 × 1.02 ≈ 5.1 kVAR. After the 3 kVAR capacitor it is 2.1 kVAR. S = √(5² + 2.1²) = √29.41, so pf = 5/5.42 ≈ 0.92 lag. It is still lagging since net Q is positive.

questions.q: Resistive-only load for max power with Z_th = 6 + j8
questions.why: For a purely resistive load, R_L = |Z_th| = √(6² + 8²) = √100 = 10 Ω. A resistor alone cannot cancel the j8 reactance, so it matches the magnitude.

questions.q: Reflected impedance ω²M²/Z₂₂ for ωM = 10, Z₂₂ = 5 + j5
questions.why: Z_r = ω²M²/Z₂₂ = 100/(5 + j5) = 100(5 − j5)/50 = 10 − j10 Ω. The reflected impedance has the opposite reactive sign to Z₂₂.

questions.q: Energy in coupled coils L₁ = 2, L₂ = 4, M = 1 H, i₁ = 1, i₂ = 2 A (aiding)
questions.why: Aiding energy: ½L₁i₁² + ½L₂i₂² + Mi₁i₂ = ½·2·1 + ½·4·4 + 1·1·2 = 1 + 8 + 2 = 11 J. The mutual term adds because the fluxes aid.

questions.q: Node: 12∠0° through 4 Ω into node with j4 Ω to ground: V
questions.why: A voltage divider: V = 12∠0° × j4/(4 + j4). The magnitude is 12 × 4/5.657 = 8.49 V. The angle is 90° − 45° = 45°. So V = 8.49∠45° V.

lessons.title: Z and Y parameters

scenes.text: A filter module arrives with two terminals in and two out — no schematic.
Four measured parameters describe it completely.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
Z (open-circuit impedance): V₁ = z₁₁I₁ + z₁₂I₂; V₂ = z₂₁I₁ + z₂₂I₂. z₁₁ = V₁/I₁ with I₂ = 0, etc.
Y (short-circuit admittance): I₁ = y₁₁V₁ + y₁₂V₂; I₂ = y₂₁V₁ + y₂₂V₂; y₁₁ = I₁/V₁ with V₂ = 0.
Y = Z⁻¹. Reciprocal: z₁₂ = z₂₁ (y₁₂ = y₂₁). Symmetric: also z₁₁ = z₂₂.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1 (T-network).** Series arms Z_a (port 1), Z_b (port 2), shunt Z_c: z₁₁ = Z_a + Z_c, z₂₂ = Z_b + Z_c, z₁₂ = z₂₁ = Z_c.
With Z_a = 2, Z_b = 3, Z_c = 4 Ω: Z = [[6, 4],[4, 7]].

**Example 2 (π-network).** Shunt Y_a (port 1), Y_b (port 2), series Y_c: y₁₁ = Y_a + Y_c, y₂₂ = Y_b + Y_c, y₁₂ = y₂₁ = −Y_c.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the minus sign of y₁₂ in a π network.
- Measuring z parameters with the other port shorted (should be open).
- Inverting the matrix element by element.

activity.prompt: Parameter → test condition

quiz.why: A network is reciprocal when the transfer impedances are equal, z₁₂ = z₂₁. This holds for passive networks without dependent sources or gyrators.
In a T-network, the shunt (middle) arm is common to both ports, so z₁₂ = z₂₁ = Z_c. The series arms only appear in the self-impedances.
The admittance matrix is the inverse of the impedance matrix, Y = Z⁻¹, because V = ZI and I = YV.
In a π-network, y₁₂ is the negative of the admittance of the arm between the two ports: y₁₂ = −Y_c. The negative sign comes from the current direction convention.
A symmetric network looks the same from both ports, so z₁₁ = z₂₂ in addition to reciprocity z₁₂ = z₂₁.

sources: Standard Network Analysis / Circuit Theory syllabus (EE core)

lessons.title: h and ABCD parameters

scenes.text: Power engineers describe long lines with ABCD parameters.
Transistor datasheets used h-parameters.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
h (hybrid): V₁ = h₁₁I₁ + h₁₂V₂; I₂ = h₂₁I₁ + h₂₂V₂ — h₁₁ input impedance (Ω), h₁₂ reverse voltage ratio, h₂₁ forward current gain, h₂₂ output admittance (S). Reciprocal: h₁₂ = −h₂₁.
ABCD: V₁ = AV₂ − BI₂ (or AV₂ + BI₂′ with I₂′ = −I₂ out of port 2); I₁ = CV₂ − DI₂. Reciprocal: AD − BC = 1; symmetric: A = D.
Cascade: [ABCD]_total = [ABCD]₁ × [ABCD]₂.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Series impedance Z: A = 1, B = Z, C = 0, D = 1 (AD − BC = 1 ✔).

**Example 2.** Shunt admittance Y: A = 1, B = 0, C = Y, D = 1.

**Example 3.** L-section: series 10 Ω then shunt 0.1 S: [[1,10],[0,1]]·[[1,0],[0.1,1]] = [[2, 10],[0.1, 1]]; AD − BC = 2 − 1 = 1 ✔.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Sign convention of I₂ in ABCD (current leaving port 2).
- Multiplying cascade matrices in the wrong order.
- Mixing units of h parameters.

activity.prompt: ABCD facts
activity.text: A series impedance Z has B = ___, and a reciprocal network satisfies AD − BC = ___.

quiz.why: h₂₁ = I₂/I₁ with the output shorted, which is the forward current gain. It is the β of a transistor in the h-parameter model.
h₁₁ = V₁/I₁ with the output shorted. It is a voltage over a current, so the unit is ohm (an input impedance).
In a cascade the output of the first becomes the input of the second, so the ABCD matrices multiply in order. Z, Y and h parameters are added only for series and parallel connections.
A symmetric two-port has the same behaviour from both ends, so A = D. A reciprocal one has AD − BC = 1.
A shunt admittance has ABCD = [[1, 0],[Y, 1]], so C = Y. A series impedance has [[1, Z],[0, 1]].

sources: Standard Network Analysis / Circuit Theory syllabus (EE core)

lessons.title: Interconnections and parameter conversion

scenes.text: Complex filters are built by joining simple sections.
Series, parallel and cascade joins each favour a different parameter set.

steps.title: Rules
steps.body:
- **Series** (inputs in series, outputs in series): Z = Z₁ + Z₂.
- **Parallel:** Y = Y₁ + Y₂.
- **Series–parallel:** h = h₁ + h₂.
- **Cascade:** T = T₁T₂ (ABCD).
Valid when port conditions are preserved (Brune's test / ideal isolating transformers).

steps.title: Conversions
steps.body:
Z → Y: Y = Z⁻¹ = (1/ΔZ)[[z₂₂, −z₁₂],[−z₂₁, z₁₁]].
Z → ABCD: A = z₁₁/z₂₁, B = ΔZ/z₂₁, C = 1/z₂₁, D = z₂₂/z₂₁.
Z → h: h₁₁ = ΔZ/z₂₂, h₁₂ = z₁₂/z₂₂, h₂₁ = −z₂₁/z₂₂, h₂₂ = 1/z₂₂.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding ABCD matrices for a cascade.
- Forgetting the determinant in conversions.
- Ignoring validity conditions in parallel connections.

activity.prompt: Z = [[5, 2],[2, 4]]. Determinant ΔZ?

quiz.why: When two-ports are connected in series, the port currents are the same and voltages add, so the Z matrices add.
In a parallel connection the port voltages are shared and currents add, so the Y matrices add.
A = V₁/V₂ with I₂ = 0 equals z₁₁/z₂₁ = 6/4 = 1.5. Use the Z-to-ABCD conversion with z₂₁ as the divisor.
With the series–parallel connection (series at the input, parallel at the output), the h parameters add. Z adds for series–series, Y for parallel–parallel.
Y = Z⁻¹, so y₁₁ = z₂₂/ΔZ. ΔZ = 6×7 − 4×4 = 42 − 16 = 26. So y₁₁ = 7/26.

sources: Standard Network Analysis / Circuit Theory syllabus (EE core)

lessons.title: Network functions, poles, zeros and filters

scenes.text: A guitar amplifier hums at 50 Hz from the mains.
A notch filter places a zero exactly at that frequency.

steps.title: Network functions
steps.body: Driving-point function (same port): Z(s) or Y(s). Transfer function (different ports): V₂/V₁, I₂/I₁, V₂/I₁… H(s) = K Π(s − zᵢ)/Π(s − pⱼ). Poles determine natural response; zeros shape frequency response. Passive RLC network poles lie in the closed LHP.

steps.title: Simple filters
steps.body:
- RC low-pass: H = 1/(1 + sRC), pole −1/RC, f_c = 1/(2πRC).
- RC high-pass: H = sRC/(1 + sRC), zero at 0.
- Series RLC band-pass (output across R): H = (R/L)s/(s² + (R/L)s + 1/LC), centre ω₀, BW = R/L.
- Band-stop (notch) output across LC: zeros at ±jω₀.
At the cut-off: |H| = 1/√2 (−3 dB); first-order roll-off 20 dB/decade.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** RC LPF R = 1.6 kΩ, C = 0.1 µF: f_c ≈ 995 Hz.

**Example 2.** Series RLC band-pass L = 10 mH, C = 1 µF, R = 20 Ω: ω₀ = 10⁴ rad/s (1.59 kHz), BW = 2000 rad/s, Q = 5.

**Example 3.** Notch at 50 Hz with C = 10 µF: L = 1/(ω₀²C) = 1/((314.16)² × 10⁻⁵) ≈ 1.01 H.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing driving-point and transfer functions.
- Reading −3 dB as half amplitude (it is half power).
- Using f and ω interchangeably in cut-off formulas.

activity.prompt: Filter type

items.text: Output across R of series RLC
Output across series LC of an RLC

quiz.q: Poles of a passive RLC network lie in
quiz.why: A passive RLC network cannot create energy, so its poles must lie in the closed left half-plane (poles on the jω axis must be simple). A right-half-plane pole would grow without limit.
A first-order system has one pole. Beyond the corner frequency, the gain falls at 20 dB per decade (6 dB per octave).
The bandwidth of a series RLC band-pass is B = R/L rad/s. Together with ω₀, it gives the quality factor Q = ω₀/B.
A notch filter blocks one frequency. It has zeros on the jω axis at ±jω₀, so the output is zero at that frequency.

quiz.q: f_c of RC LPF with R = 10 kΩ, C = 10 nF

sources: Standard Network Analysis / Circuit Theory syllabus (EE core)

questions.q: z₁₁ is measured with
questions.why: z₁₁ = V₁/I₁ with I₂ = 0, so port 2 must be open. Open circuit at the other port sets its current to zero.

questions.q: Reciprocal ABCD condition
questions.why: For reciprocal networks, the ABCD parameters have a determinant of 1: AD − BC = 1. A = D is the condition for symmetry, which is stronger.

questions.q: Driving-point impedance relates
questions.why: A driving-point function relates the voltage and current at the same port (for example, input impedance). A transfer function relates quantities at different ports.
options: voltage and current at the same port

questions.q: T-network Z_a = 1, Z_b = 1, Z_c = 2: z₁₁
questions.why: In a T-network, z₁₁ = Z_a + Z_c, the series arm at port 1 plus the common arm: 1 + 2 = 3 Ω.

questions.q: Cascade of series Z = 5 and shunt Y = 0.2: A
questions.why: For series Z followed by shunt Y, A = 1 + ZY = 1 + 5 × 0.2 = 2. The product ZY is dimensionless.

questions.q: h₂₂ unit
questions.why: h₂₂ = I₂/V₂ with I₁ = 0. A current over a voltage is an admittance, so its unit is siemens.

questions.q: Assertion (A): For reciprocal networks, h₁₂ = −h₂₁.  Reason (R): Reciprocity implies z₁₂ = z₂₁, which maps to h₁₂ = −h₂₁.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both are true. Reciprocity (z₁₂ = z₂₁) is a property of the network, and converting Z to h gives h₁₂ = −h₂₁, so R explains A.
Y = Z⁻¹ = (1/ΔZ)[[z₂₂, −z₁₂],[−z₂₁, z₁₁]]. With ΔZ = 16 − 4 = 12, Y = (1/12)[[4, −2],[−2, 4]]. The off-diagonals change sign.
B = ΔZ/z₂₁. With ΔZ = 4×4 − 2×2 = 12 and z₂₁ = 2, B = 12/2 = 6 Ω.

questions.q: Series RLC band-pass L = 0.1 H, R = 50 Ω, C = 1 µF: Q
questions.why: For series RLC, Q = (1/R)√(L/C) = (1/50)√(0.1/10⁻⁶) = √(10⁵)/50 = 316/50 ≈ 6.32. The Q is moderate, so the filter is fairly selective.

questions.q: Case: A 60 Hz notch needs C = 4.7 µF. L required
Two identical π-networks with Y = [[2, −1],[−1, 2]] S in parallel
questions.why: In a parallel connection, the Y matrices add. Two identical networks double each element: [[4, −2],[−2, 4]] S.

questions.q: L-section series 10 Ω then shunt 0.1 S: input impedance with port 2 open
questions.why: Input impedance with port 2 open is Z_in = A/C. For a series 10 Ω and shunt 0.1 S: A = 1 + ZY = 2 and C = 0.1, so Z_in = 2/0.1 = 20 Ω. Check: 10 Ω in series with 1/0.1 = 10 Ω gives 20 Ω.

questions.q: Gain of first-order LPF at 10f_c
questions.why: A first-order low-pass falls at 20 dB per decade above f_c. One decade above (10f_c), the gain is about −20 dB (precisely −20.04 dB).

questions.q: Transfer function with poles −1 ± j2: natural response
questions.why: Complex poles at −1 ± j2 give the natural response e^(−t)·(a cos 2t + b sin 2t). It is a sinusoid at 2 rad/s inside a decaying e^(−t) envelope, i.e. underdamped.

lessons.title: Formula sheet: topology, theorems, transients

scenes.text: Ananya has one evening to revise Network Analysis.
She works through a one-page sheet, then tests herself.

steps.title: Topology and theorems
steps.body:
- Twigs n − 1; links b − n + 1; trees = det(AAᵀ)
- Dependent sources stay active; R_th = V_oc/I_sc or V_t/I_t
- Millman V = ΣEY/ΣY; Tellegen Σvi = 0; reciprocity (no dependent sources)

steps.title: Transients
steps.body:
- x(t) = x(∞) + [x(0⁺) − x(∞)]e^(−t/τ); τ = RC, L/R
- Series RLC α = R/2L; parallel α = 1/2RC; ω₀ = 1/√LC; ω_d = √(ω₀² − α²)
- s-domain: sL with Li(0⁻); 1/sC with v(0⁻)/s; FVT lim sF(s)

steps.title: How to use this sheet
steps.body:
- Cover the right-hand side of each formula and try to recall it.
- For every formula, say its conditions of validity aloud (units, assumptions, ranges).
- Re-solve one worked example from the matching unit without looking.

steps.title: Common slips to avoid
steps.body:
- Mixing units (kN vs N, mm vs m, km/h vs m/s, degrees vs radians).
- Using a formula outside its assumptions.
- Dropping signs or factors such as 2, ½, π or √3.

quiz.why: For an RL circuit τ = L/R = 2 H/5 Ω = 0.4 s. Inverting the ratio (R/L = 2.5) is a common mistake.
Twigs = n − 1 = 8 − 1 = 7, since a tree joins n nodes with n − 1 branches.

quiz.q: ω₀ for L = 1 mH, C = 1 µF

lessons.title: Formula sheet: AC, coupled, two-ports

scenes.text: Ananya has one evening to revise Network Analysis.
She works through a one-page sheet, then tests herself.

steps.title: AC and coupling
steps.body:
- S = VI* = P + jQ; P_max = |V_th|²/4R_th
- k = M/√(L₁L₂); aiding L₁ + L₂ + 2M; opposing −2M; Z referred Z_L/n²
- Neutral shift by Millman; I_N = phasor sum

steps.title: Two-ports
steps.body:
- Z (open), Y (short), h (hybrid), ABCD (chain)
- Reciprocal z₁₂ = z₂₁, h₁₂ = −h₂₁, AD − BC = 1; symmetric z₁₁ = z₂₂, A = D
- Series → Z add; parallel → Y add; cascade → ABCD multiply

steps.title: How to use this sheet
steps.body:
- Cover the right-hand side of each formula and try to recall it.
- For every formula, say its conditions of validity aloud (units, assumptions, ranges).
- Re-solve one worked example from the matching unit without looking.

steps.title: Common slips to avoid
steps.body:
- Mixing units (kN vs N, mm vs m, km/h vs m/s, degrees vs radians).
- Using a formula outside its assumptions.
