statements.s: Cascade adds ABCD matrices.
k can exceed 1.
Inductor current is continuous.

quiz.q: M for aiding 14 H, opposing 6 H
quiz.why: Aiding minus opposing = 4M, so 4M = 14 − 6 = 8 and M = 2 H.

lessons.title: Mock paper 1 (timed practice)

scenes.text: Set a 30-minute timer and attempt every question before checking.
Read each explanation, even for the ones you got right.

steps.title: How to attempt
steps.body:
- Attempt easy questions first.
- For numericals write the formula, substitute with units, then simplify.
- Mark doubtful ones and return.

steps.title: Coverage
steps.body: This paper mixes every unit of Network Analysis. Scores below 60% mean: re-read the unit whose questions you missed, then retake.

steps.title: Common mistakes in exams
steps.body:
- Skipping units and sign conventions.
- Copying a formula without checking its conditions of validity.
- Not reading 'NOT' / 'incorrect' in the question.

activity.prompt: Before the real exam
items: Formula sheet revised twice
One full mock done under time
Wrong answers re-solved without looking
Derivations listed in the syllabus practised once

quiz.why: Links = b − n + 1 = 12 − 7 + 1 = 6. Twigs are n − 1 = 6, and together they make the 12 branches.

quiz.q: Mock 1: Millman 9 V/3 Ω and 6 V/3 Ω
quiz.why: Millman: V = (9/3 + 6/3)/(1/3 + 1/3) = 5/(2/3) = 7.5 V. With equal resistances, it is the average of 9 and 6.
During charging, the response reaches 1 − e⁻¹ ≈ 63% of the final value after one time constant, t = τ.
Critical damping in a series RLC occurs when α = ω₀, i.e. R/(2L) = 1/√(LC), which gives R = 2√(L/C). Resonance is a different idea (X_L = X_C).

quiz.q: Mock 1: AC max power load for Z_th = 2 − j3
quiz.why: For maximum power transfer, the load is the conjugate of the Thevenin impedance. Z_th = 2 − j3 gives Z_L = 2 + j3, which cancels the reactance.
Referred impedance = n² × Z = 3² × 4 = 36 Ω. The factor is the square of the turns ratio.
z₁₂ = z₂₁ is the condition for a reciprocal network. A symmetric network needs z₁₁ = z₂₂ also.

quiz.q: Mock 1: f_c of RC LPF, R 1 kΩ, C 1 µF

questions.q: Capacitor voltage at t = 0⁺ equals
questions.why: A capacitor voltage cannot change instantly, so v_C(0⁺) = v_C(0⁻). The source voltage does not appear across it immediately.

questions.q: Tellegen's theorem is
questions.why: Tellegen's theorem says Σv·i = 0 over all branches, which means the power delivered by sources equals the power absorbed. It holds for any lumped network.

questions.q: Two-port cascade uses
questions.why: When two-port networks are cascaded, their ABCD (transmission) matrices are multiplied in order. Z and Y matrices apply to series and parallel connections.

questions.q: Neutral current of balanced load
questions.why: In a balanced three-phase load, the three phase currents are equal in size and 120° apart, so they sum to zero. So the neutral current is 0.

questions.q: RC: R = 2 kΩ, C = 10 µF, τ
k for L₁ = 1 H, L₂ = 4 H, M = 1 H
Series RLC R = 2, L = 1, C = 1: damping
questions.why: α = R/(2L) = 2/2 = 1 and ω₀ = 1/√(LC) = 1. Since α = ω₀, it is critically damped.

questions.q: V_oc = 6 V, I_sc = 2 A ⇒ R_th
Twigs and links for n = 5, b = 8
questions.why: Twigs = n − 1 = 4. Links = b − n + 1 = 8 − 5 + 1 = 4. Together they make 8 branches.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Reciprocity theorem does not apply to circuits with dependent sources.  Reason (R): Dependent sources generally make the network non-bilateral.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both are true. Reciprocity needs a linear bilateral network, and dependent sources generally make it non-bilateral, so the theorem does not apply. So R explains A.

questions.q: i(t) for 10 V step into 5 Ω + 1 H (zero IC) at t = 0.2 s
questions.why: The final current is 10/5 = 2 A and τ = L/R = 1/5 = 0.2 s. At t = 0.2 s = τ, i = 2(1 − e⁻¹) = 2 × 0.632 ≈ 1.26 A.

questions.q: Total S: 3 kW at 0.6 lag + 4 kVAR capacitor
questions.why: 3 kW at 0.6 lag has S = 5 kVA and Q = 4 kVAR (inductive). A 4 kVAR capacitor supplies −4 kVAR, so net Q = 4 − 4 = 0. Total S = 3 + j0 kVA, i.e. pf = 1.
A = z₁₁/z₂₁ = 10/5 = 2 and D = z₂₂/z₂₁ = 10/5 = 2. For a symmetric network A = D, as seen here.

questions.q: Parallel RLC R = 1 kΩ, L = 10 mH, C = 1 µF: classify
questions.why: For a parallel RLC, α = 1/(2RC) = 1/(2 × 1000 × 10⁻⁶) = 500, and ω₀ = 1/√(LC) = 1/√(10⁻⁸) = 10⁴. Since α < ω₀, it is underdamped.

questions.q: Case: An 800 Ω amplifier output must drive an 8 Ω speaker for maximum power. Transformer turns ratio N₁:N₂
questions.why: For maximum power, the reflected load must equal the source resistance: n²·8 = 800, so n² = 100 and n = 10. So the turns ratio is 10:1 (step-down), since the 8 Ω speaker is on the low-voltage side.

questions.q: Laplace: series RL R = 4, L = 2, step 8 V, i(0) = 0. I(s)
questions.why: I(s) = V(s)/(R + sL) = (8/s)/(4 + 2s) = 8/(s(2s + 4)) = 4/(s(s + 2)). Dividing the numerator and denominator by 2 gives the simplified form.

questions.q: i(∞) from that I(s)
questions.why: By the final value theorem, i(∞) = lim(s→0) s·I(s) = 4/(0 + 2) = 2 A. This matches V/R = 8/4 = 2 A.

questions.q: Broken neutral case: phases 10∠0, 5∠−120, 10∠120 (A as if neutral present). Sum used in Millman numerator
questions.why: The Millman numerator is the sum of the phase currents as phasors, not their magnitudes. 10∠0° + 5∠−120° + 10∠120° has real part 10 − 2.5 − 5 = 2.5 and imaginary part −4.33 + 8.66 = 4.33, so the result is 5∠60° A.

questions.q: Energy in coupled coils L₁ 1 H, L₂ 1 H, M 0.5 H, i₁ = i₂ = 2 A, opposing
questions.why: Opposing: W = ½L₁i₁² + ½L₂i₂² − Mi₁i₂ = 2 + 2 − 0.5×2×2 = 2 + 2 − 2 = 2 J. In aiding, the term would be added instead.

questions.q: Band-pass centre f for L = 25 mH, C = 0.1 µF

lessons.title: Equivalent circuit and phasor diagram

scenes.text: An 11 kV/415 V transformer feeds a neighbourhood.
Its losses and voltage drop are predicted by a simple equivalent circuit.

steps.title: Equivalent circuit
steps.body:
Primary R₁, X₁; secondary R₂, X₂; magnetising branch R_c ∥ X_m. Referring to primary: R₂′ = a²R₂, X₂′ = a²X₂ (a = N₁/N₂). Approximate circuit moves the shunt branch to the input: R_eq1 = R₁ + a²R₂, X_eq1 = X₁ + a²X₂.
No-load current I₀ = I_c (core loss, in phase with V) + I_m (magnetising, lags 90°); typically 2–5% of rated.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 2200/220 V, R₁ = 2 Ω, R₂ = 0.02 Ω, X₁ = 4 Ω, X₂ = 0.04 Ω: a = 10 ⇒ R_eq1 = 2 + 2 = 4 Ω, X_eq1 = 8 Ω.

**Example 2.** Referred to secondary: R_eq2 = 0.04 Ω, X_eq2 = 0.08 Ω.

**Example 3.** I₀ = 0.5 A at pf 0.2 lag on 230 V: I_c = 0.1 A, I_m = 0.49 A; core loss = 23 W.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Referring with a instead of a².
- Mixing primary and secondary quantities in one equation.
- Forgetting that the magnetising branch is nearly reactive (low pf at no load).

activity.prompt: a = 20, R₂ = 0.01 Ω. Secondary resistance referred to primary (Ω)?

quiz.q: Referring Z from secondary to primary multiplies by
quiz.why: Impedance referred from secondary to primary is multiplied by a² where a = N₁/N₂. Impedance scales as the square of turns ratio since V scales by a and I by 1/a.

quiz.q: No-load pf of a transformer is
quiz.why: At no load the current is mostly the magnetising component, which lags the voltage by nearly 90°, so the power factor is low (about 0.1 to 0.3).
I_c is the core-loss (iron-loss) component of the no-load current. It is in phase with the voltage, while the magnetising component I_m lags it by 90°.

quiz.q: Approximate circuit moves the shunt branch to
quiz.why: In the approximate equivalent circuit, the shunt branch (R_c and X_m) is moved to the input terminals, because the exciting current is small. This makes the series impedance easy to combine.
R_eq1 = R₁ + a²R₂ = 1 + 10² × 0.01 = 1 + 1 = 2 Ω. The secondary resistance is multiplied by a² when referred to the primary.

lessons.title: OC and SC tests, regulation and efficiency

scenes.text: Factories don't load a 500 kVA transformer fully to test it.
Two low-power tests — open and short circuit — give all the losses.

steps.title: Tests
steps.body:
**OC test (LV side, rated V, HV open):** W₀ = core loss; cos φ₀ = W₀/(V I₀); R_c = V/I_c, X_m = V/I_m.
**SC test (HV side, rated I, LV shorted, reduced V):** W_sc = full-load copper loss; Z_eq = V_sc/I_sc, R_eq = W_sc/I_sc², X_eq = √(Z² − R²).

steps.title: Performance
steps.body: Regulation ≈ (I R_eq cos φ ± I X_eq sin φ)/V × 100 (+ lag). η = xS cos φ/(xS cos φ + P_i + x²P_cu). Max η at x = √(P_i/P_cu). All-day η = output kWh/(output + losses kWh) over 24 h — distribution transformers are designed for low core loss.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Doing the SC test at rated voltage (dangerous).
- Taking OC current as rated current.
- Forgetting core loss runs all 24 h in all-day efficiency.

activity.prompt: Parameter extraction
items: OC test on LV side at rated voltage: read V, I₀, W₀
Compute core-loss resistance and magnetising reactance
SC test on HV side at rated current: read V_sc, I_sc, W_sc
Compute Z_eq, R_eq, X_eq
Use them for regulation and efficiency

quiz.why: The open-circuit test is done at rated voltage with the secondary open, so the power read is almost all core loss (iron loss). Copper loss is negligible then.
The short-circuit test is done at rated current with reduced voltage on the primary. This is safe, because full voltage on a shorted winding would cause huge currents.

quiz.q: Max efficiency fraction for P_i = 200 W, P_cu = 800 W
quiz.why: Maximum efficiency occurs when the copper loss equals the iron loss: x²P_cu = P_i. So x = √(200/800) = √(1/4) = 0.5 of full load.
Distribution transformers are energised all day but loaded lightly much of the time. So they are designed with low core loss, to give a high all-day efficiency.
Z_eq = V_sc/I_sc = 60 V/5 A = 12 Ω. It is just the ratio of the voltage to the current in the short-circuit test.

lessons.title: Autotransformers

scenes.text: Long rural lines use autotransformers to boost voltage slightly.
One shared winding saves copper when the ratio is close to 1.

steps.title: Principle
steps.body:
Single winding with a tap; part of the power is transformed, part conducted directly. For ratio a = V₁/V₂ (step-down):
- Copper saving: weight_auto/weight_two-winding = 1 − 1/a (= 1 − V₂/V₁).
- Power conducted = S/a; transformed = S(1 − 1/a).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 230/200 V autotransformer: saving fraction = 200/230 = 87% of copper saved; copper used = 13%.

**Example 2.** 10 kVA two-winding 2400/240 V reconnected as a 2640/2400 V auto: rating = 2640 × (10 000/240) = 110 kVA.

**Example 3.** Step-down 400/320 V, 20 kVA: conducted = 20 × 320/400 = 16 kVA, transformed = 4 kVA.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- No electrical isolation — a fault can put full HV on the LV side (safety concern).
- Using autotransformers for large ratios (savings vanish).
- Mixing formulas for step-up and step-down.

activity.prompt: Autotransformer 400/320 V, 20 kVA. Power transformed inductively (kVA)?

quiz.q: Autotransformer saving is large when ratio is
quiz.why: The saving in copper and size is 1 − 1/a (or 1 − V_low/V_high). It is large when the ratio is close to 1, since most power is conducted directly.
An autotransformer has a common winding, so there is a direct electrical connection between the primary and secondary. It gives no isolation, which is its main disadvantage.
Copper ratio = 1 − V_low/V_high = 1 − 200/230 = 1 − 0.87 ≈ 0.13, i.e. about 13% of that for a two-winding transformer.
Autotransformers suit uses where isolation is not needed and the ratio is near 1: starting induction motors at reduced voltage and boosting or bucking voltage.

quiz.q: Conducted power for step-down S, ratio a
quiz.why: In a step-down autotransformer with ratio a, the part of the power conducted directly is S/a. The remaining S(1 − 1/a) is transformed.

lessons.title: Three-phase transformers and parallel operation

scenes.text: A 132/33 kV substation uses three-phase transformers in parallel.
Wrong phasing between them would cause huge circulating currents.

steps.title: Connections
steps.body: Y–Y (cheap, neutral available, third-harmonic issues), Δ–Δ (no neutral, can run open-delta at 57.7%), Y–Δ (step-down at receiving end, 30° shift), Δ–Y (step-up at generating end / distribution with neutral). Vector groups (e.g. Dyn11) state the phase displacement. Open delta (V–V) capacity = 0.577 of Δ–Δ.

steps.title: Parallel operation conditions
steps.body: Same voltage ratio, same polarity, same phase sequence and vector group (phase displacement), and per-unit impedances nearly equal (with similar X/R) so load shares in proportion to rating: S_A/S_B = Z_B/Z_A (ohmic, referred) or inversely to per-unit impedance on a common base.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 11 kV/415 V Δ–Y: phase ratio = 11 000/(415/√3) = 45.9.

**Example 2.** Two transformers 500 kVA (Z = 5%) and 250 kVA (Z = 5%) share 600 kVA: 400 and 200 kVA (in ratio of ratings).

**Example 3.** Three 50 kVA single-phase units in Δ–Δ give 150 kVA; if one fails (V–V) the bank supplies 86.6 kVA.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Paralleling transformers with different vector groups.
- Forgetting √3 between line and phase voltages for Y windings.
- Assuming open delta gives 2/3 capacity (it gives 57.7%).

activity.prompt: Connection → typical use

quiz.why: An open-delta (V–V) bank carries √3 × the rating of one unit, which is 1/√3 = 57.7% of a three-unit Δ–Δ bank (3 units). The 66.7% figure is wrongly the share of units used.
For parallel operation, transformers must have the same vector group (phase displacement) and voltage ratio. Otherwise there is a circulating current even at no load. Equal kVA is not required.

quiz.q: Load sharing of equal per-unit impedance units is
quiz.why: If the per-unit impedances are equal, each unit takes load in proportion to its kVA rating. If not, the one with the lower per-unit impedance is loaded more.

quiz.q: Phase shift in a Y–Δ bank
quiz.why: A Y–Δ connection introduces a standard 30° phase shift between the primary and secondary line voltages. That is why vector group matters for parallel operation.

quiz.q: Three 100 kVA units in Δ–Δ give
quiz.why: In a Δ–Δ bank, the capacity is the sum of the three units: 3 × 100 = 300 kVA. The 173 kVA applies to an open-delta bank of two units (√3 × 100).

questions.q: Iron loss of a transformer is found by
questions.why: The open-circuit (no-load) test gives the iron loss, because at rated voltage the core is fully excited while the current is small. The SC test gives the copper loss.

questions.q: Autotransformer has
questions.why: An autotransformer has a single winding with a tap, part of which is shared between the primary and secondary. A normal transformer has two separate windings.

questions.q: Referred impedance factor
questions.why: Impedances are referred between sides with the square of the turns ratio, a². Voltage scales by a and current by 1/a, so Z = V/I scales by a².

questions.q: SC test: 100 V, 10 A, 400 W ⇒ R_eq
questions.why: In the SC test, P = I²R_eq, so R_eq = 400/10² = 400/100 = 4 Ω. The watt reading is almost all copper loss.

questions.q: X_eq for that test
Open-delta from three 30 kVA units
questions.why: An open-delta bank of three 30 kVA units' worth (90 kVA total in Δ) carries only 57.7% of this: 0.577 × 90 ≈ 52 kVA. The reduction is because only two transformers are used.

questions.q: Assertion (A): All-day efficiency matters for distribution transformers.  Reason (R): They stay energised 24 h but are often lightly loaded.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both are true. Distribution transformers are energised 24 hours a day, so their core loss runs all day, while the load is often light. Efficiency over the day is therefore what matters, so R explains A.

questions.q: Regulation for I R/V = 1%, I X/V = 4%, pf 0.8 lag
questions.why: Regulation ≈ (IR/V)cosφ + (IX/V)sinφ = 1% × 0.8 + 4% × 0.6 = 0.8 + 2.4 = 3.2%. For a lagging pf, both terms add.

questions.q: η at half load: 20 kVA, pf 1, P_i 200 W, P_cu,FL 400 W
questions.why: At half load, the output is 0.5 × 20 kVA × 1 = 10 kW. Copper loss is 0.5² × 400 = 100 W and iron loss is 200 W. η = 10000/(10000 + 200 + 100) ≈ 97.1%.

questions.q: 2-winding 5 kVA 220/110 V used as 330/220 V auto: rating
questions.why: The two-winding current rating is 5000/110 = 45.45 A on the low-voltage side. As an autotransformer, the output is 330 V × 45.45 A ≈ 15 kVA. It is larger than 5 kVA since most power is conducted directly.

questions.q: Case: Two 1000 kVA transformers with Z = 5% and 6% share 1800 kVA. Load on the 5% unit
questions.why: Parallel transformers share load in inverse proportion to their per-unit impedances. The 5% unit takes 1800 × 6/(5 + 6) = 1800 × 6/11 ≈ 982 kVA, which is less than its 1000 kVA rating. The 6% unit takes the other ≈ 818 kVA.

questions.q: No-load: 0.8 A at pf 0.25, 400 V. Magnetising current
questions.why: The no-load current has a core-loss part I_c = I₀cosφ and a magnetising part I_m = I₀sinφ. With cosφ = 0.25, φ = 75.5°, so I_m = 0.8 × sin 75.5° ≈ 0.775 A. Most of the no-load current is magnetising.

questions.q: Copper saved by 500/400 V autotransformer vs two-winding
questions.why: For an autotransformer, copper saved compared with a two-winding unit equals the ratio k = V₂/V₁ = 400/500 = 0.8, i.e. 80%. A ratio close to 1 saves the most.

questions.q: Load fraction for max efficiency: P_i 1.2 kW, P_cu,FL 3 kW
questions.why: Maximum efficiency occurs when copper loss equals iron loss: x²P_cu,FL = P_i, so x = √(1.2/3) = √0.4 ≈ 0.632 of full load.

questions.q: Regulation at 0.8 leading with %R 2, %X 5
questions.why: Regulation ≈ %R cosφ − %X sinφ for a leading pf = 2 × 0.8 − 5 × 0.6 = 1.6 − 3.0 = −1.4%. The negative value means the terminal voltage rises on load with a leading current.

courses.summary: Construction and windings, EMF and torque equations, armature reaction and commutation, generator types and characteristics, motor characteristics and speed control, starters, losses, efficiency and Swinburne's test.
outcomes: Use EMF and torque equations
Explain armature reaction and commutation remedies
Compare shunt, series and compound characteristics
Control speed, select starters and compute efficiency

lessons.title: Construction, EMF and torque

scenes.text: Many battery forklifts used DC motors for simple speed control.
EMF and torque equations link flux, speed and current.

steps.title: Equations
steps.body:
E = PΦNZ/(60A) (A = P lap, A = 2 wave). Torque T = PΦZI_a/(2πA) = 0.159 PΦZI_a/A N·m. Power: E I_a = Tω.
Motor: V = E_b + I_aR_a; N ∝ E_b/Φ. Generator: V = E − I_aR_a.

steps.title: Construction
steps.body: Yoke, poles with field windings, armature core (laminated) with conductors, commutator (mechanical rectifier) and brushes. Lap windings suit high-current low-voltage; wave windings high-voltage low-current.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 4-pole wave, Z = 600, Φ = 0.02 Wb, N = 1000 rpm: E = 4 × 0.02 × 1000 × 600/(60 × 2) = 400 V.

**Example 2.** Same machine as motor with I_a = 50 A: T = 0.159 × 4 × 0.02 × 600 × 50/2 = 191 N·m (check: E I_a/ω = 400 × 50/104.7 = 191 ✔).

**Example 3.** 220 V shunt motor, R_a = 0.4 Ω, I_a = 30 A: E_b = 208 V.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using A = 2 for lap or A = P for wave.
- rpm vs rad/s in torque from power.
- Forgetting brush drop (~2 V) when the question mentions it.

activity.prompt: 6-pole lap, Z = 480, Φ = 0.025 Wb, N = 1200 rpm. Generated EMF (V)?

quiz.q: Parallel paths in a lap winding
quiz.why: In a lap winding, the number of parallel paths equals the number of poles, A = P. In a wave winding it is always 2.
The commutator reverses the connection of the armature coils every half turn, so the AC induced in the armature coils appears as DC at the brushes. It works as a mechanical rectifier.
By KVL on the armature of a motor: V = E_b + I_aR_a, so back EMF E_b = V − I_aR_a. The back EMF opposes the supply.
From E_b = kΦN, speed N = E_b/(kΦ), so N ∝ E_b/Φ. Weaker flux means higher speed, and a bigger back EMF means higher speed.
Torque T = kΦI_a, so it is proportional to the product of flux and armature current. Speed is not directly part of the torque equation.

lessons.title: Armature reaction and commutation

scenes.text: A DC motor's brushes spark badly under heavy load.
Armature reaction distorts the field and commutation becomes difficult.

steps.title: Armature reaction
steps.body:
Armature mmf distorts and (with saturation) weakens the main field: cross-magnetising effect shifts the magnetic neutral axis (forward for generators, backward for motors); brush shift causes demagnetising and cross-magnetising components.
Remedies: interpoles (commutating poles), compensating windings in pole faces (large machines), high-reluctance pole tips, laminated poles.

steps.title: Commutation
steps.body: Current in a coil must reverse from +I to −I during the short commutation period. Self-induced reactance voltage opposes the reversal ⇒ sparking. Ideal: linear (resistance) commutation. Remedies: interpoles (series with armature, produce opposing EMF), carbon brushes (higher contact resistance — resistance commutation), brush shift (old method).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** For a brush lead of θ mechanical degrees: demagnetising AT per pole = Z I_c θ/360 and cross-magnetising AT per pole = Z I_c (1/(2P) − θ/360), where I_c = I_a/A is the conductor current.

**Example 2.** 4-pole lap, Z = 880, I_a = 120 A ⇒ I_c = 30 A; brush lead 4°: AT_d = (2 × 4/360) × 880 × 30/2 ≈ 293 AT/pole.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Interpole polarity wrong (must oppose reactance voltage).
- Confusing cross-magnetising (distorts) and demagnetising (weakens) components.
- Forgetting that interpoles carry armature current (they must track load).

activity.prompt: Problem → remedy

quiz.why: Interpoles are connected in series with the armature so that their flux is proportional to the load current. The EMF they induce then tracks the reactance voltage at any load.
Armature reaction is the effect of armature current's flux on the main field. It distorts the flux and, due to saturation, weakens it a little. It does not reverse rotation.
Carbon brushes have a high contact resistance. This forces the current in a short-circuited coil to reverse in a controlled way, which helps commutation (resistance commutation).
Compensating windings are placed in slots in the pole faces, in series with the armature, to cancel armature reaction directly under the poles.
In a generator, the cross-magnetising armature flux shifts the magnetic neutral axis (MNA) in the direction of rotation. In a motor, it shifts against rotation.

lessons.title: Generator and motor characteristics

scenes.text: A crane needs huge torque at start; a lathe needs near-constant speed.
Series motors suit the first; shunt motors the second.

steps.title: Generators
steps.body: Separately excited (stable, wide range), shunt (self-excited: needs residual flux, field resistance < critical resistance, speed > critical speed; voltage drops with load), series (voltage rises with load — boosters), compound (cumulative flat/over-compound).

steps.title: Motors
steps.body:
- **Shunt:** N nearly constant (drops 5–10% from no load to full load); T ∝ I_a.
- **Series:** T ∝ I_a² (unsaturated), N ∝ 1/I_a — very high starting torque; never start/run unloaded (runaway).
- **Compound (cumulative):** high starting torque with a safe no-load speed.
Speed regulation = (N₀ − N_FL)/N_FL × 100.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Shunt motor 230 V, R_a = 0.5 Ω, 1000 rpm at I_a = 20 A; at I_a = 40 A (same Φ): E_b 220 → 210 ⇒ N = 1000 × 210/220 = 955 rpm.

**Example 2.** Series motor at I = 20 A runs 1000 rpm; at 40 A (linear magnetics, R negligible): N ≈ 500 rpm, T ×4.

**Example 3.** Shunt generator OCC with field resistance line slope 50 Ω — if field circuit R exceeds the critical resistance (slope of the OCC air-gap line), voltage won't build up.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Belt-driving a series motor (belt slip ⇒ no load ⇒ runaway).
- Forgetting residual magnetism for self-excitation.
- Assuming T ∝ I_a² for a saturated series motor at high load (closer to ∝ I_a).

activity.prompt: Choose the DC motor

quiz.q: Series motor torque at low saturation
quiz.why: In a series motor, the armature current also makes the field. At low saturation, Φ ∝ I_a, so T ∝ ΦI_a ∝ I_a². At high saturation, T is closer to ∝ I_a.
A self-excited generator starts from the small residual flux in the poles. This produces a small EMF, which drives field current and builds up the flux and voltage.
With no load, a series motor's armature current and flux become very small, so N ∝ 1/Φ becomes extremely large (runaway). So it must never be run without load.
In a shunt motor, the field is connected across a constant supply, so Φ is nearly constant. Back EMF changes little with load, so speed is nearly constant.
Speed regulation = (no-load speed − full-load speed)/full-load speed = (N₀ − N_FL)/N_FL. The denominator is the full-load speed.

lessons.title: Speed control, starters, losses and efficiency

scenes.text: Older lifts used DC motors with Ward-Leonard control for smooth speed.
Speed can be varied by flux, armature voltage or resistance.

steps.title: Speed control (shunt)
steps.body:
N ∝ (V − I_aR_a)/Φ.
- **Field (flux) control:** weaken Φ ⇒ speed above base; constant power.
- **Armature resistance control:** speed below base; wasteful.
- **Armature voltage control (Ward-Leonard, power electronics):** smooth, wide range; constant torque below base.
Series motors: field diverter, tapped field, series–parallel (traction).

steps.title: Starters, losses and efficiency
steps.body:
At start E_b = 0 ⇒ I = V/R_a (dangerous). Starters (3-point, 4-point) add resistance and include no-volt and overload releases.
Losses: copper (armature, field), iron (hysteresis, eddy), mechanical (friction, windage), brush contact. Max efficiency when variable (copper) loss = constant losses.
**Swinburne's test:** no-load run as motor gives constant losses ⇒ efficiency predicted at any load (no load test needed, but ignores load-dependent iron changes).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 220 V motor, R_a = 0.5 Ω, full-load I_a = 40 A: without starter I = 440 A; to limit to 2 × FL (80 A): R_total = 2.75 Ω ⇒ starter 2.25 Ω.

**Example 2.** Field weakening: 1000 rpm, reduce Φ by 20% (E_b ≈ constant) ⇒ N ≈ 1250 rpm.

**Example 3 (Swinburne).** 220 V shunt motor no-load I = 3 A, R_sh = 220 Ω (I_sh = 1 A), R_a = 0.3 Ω: constant losses = 660 − (2² × 0.3) = 658.8 W. At I_L = 40 A: I_a = 39 A, Cu = 456 W ⇒ input 8800 W, output 8800 − 658.8 − 456 = 7685 W ⇒ η = 87.3%.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Opening the field of a running shunt motor (overspeed).
- Forgetting the field current in Swinburne's input.
- Using armature resistance control for long-term efficient operation.

activity.prompt: Starter: 230 V, R_a = 0.25 Ω, limit starting current to 50 A. Total resistance needed (Ω)?

quiz.why: Since N ∝ 1/Φ, weakening the field raises the speed above the base speed. Armature voltage control is used for speeds below base.
In a 4-point starter, the no-volt release coil is connected directly across the supply, separate from the field circuit. Field-weakening to high speed then does not drop the arm out.
The efficiency of a DC machine is maximum when the variable (copper) loss equals the constant loss.
Swinburne's test is a no-load test run on a shunt machine, from which the constant losses are found. Efficiency is then calculated indirectly at any load.
The Ward-Leonard system controls the speed of a DC motor smoothly by varying the armature voltage from a motor-generator set, with the field of the generator varied.

questions.q: Commutator converts
questions.why: The armature coils carry alternating EMF. The commutator and brushes rectify this, so that DC appears at the terminals.
options: AC in armature to DC at terminals

questions.q: Wave winding parallel paths
questions.why: A wave winding always has 2 parallel paths, whatever the number of poles. A lap winding has as many paths as poles.

questions.q: DC motor with highest starting torque
questions.why: A series motor has T ∝ I_a² (before saturation), so it gives the highest torque at start when the current is high. That is why it is used for traction.

questions.q: E for 4-pole lap, Z = 400, Φ = 0.03, N = 1500
Back EMF: 440 V, R_a 0.2 Ω, I_a 50 A
Starting current without starter: 220 V, R_a 0.2 Ω
questions.why: At start, back EMF is zero, so I_st = V/R_a = 220/0.2 = 1100 A. This is why a starter resistance is needed.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Interpoles improve commutation.  Reason (R): They induce an EMF opposing the reactance voltage in commutating coils.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both are true. During commutation, the reversing coil has a reactance voltage opposing the current reversal. Interpoles induce an EMF against it, so the current reverses without sparking. R explains A.

questions.q: Shunt motor 250 V, R_a 0.5 Ω: 1000 rpm at 20 A. Speed at 40 A (same Φ)
questions.why: E_b1 = 250 − 20 × 0.5 = 240 V; E_b2 = 250 − 40 × 0.5 = 230 V. With the same flux, N₂ = 1000 × 230/240 ≈ 958 rpm. More load slows the motor slightly.

questions.q: Series motor (linear): 1200 rpm at 30 A; speed at 60 A (neglect R)
questions.why: Neglecting R, E_b ≈ V is constant and Φ ∝ I_a. So N ∝ 1/Φ ∝ 1/I_a: doubling the current halves the speed, 1200 → 600 rpm.

questions.q: Torque of motor: E_b = 200 V, I_a = 50 A, N = 1000 rpm
questions.why: Electromagnetic power = E_bI_a = 200 × 50 = 10 kW. ω = 2π × 1000/60 = 104.7 rad/s. T = 10000/104.7 ≈ 95.5 N·m.

questions.q: Case: A 220 V shunt motor at 1500 rpm needs 1800 rpm for a fan upgrade at the same load torque. Method
questions.why: Speed above base needs a weaker field since N ∝ 1/Φ. For 1800 rpm, Φ must be 1500/1800 ≈ 0.83 of the original, a reduction of about 17%. Resistance in the armature only lowers speed.

questions.q: Swinburne: no-load 230 V, 4 A, I_sh 1 A, R_a 0.5 Ω: constant losses
questions.why: Input at no load = 230 × 4 = 920 W. Armature copper loss = (4 − 1)² × 0.5 = 4.5 W. Constant losses = 920 − 4.5 = 915.5 W. Subtract the shunt current from the line current for I_a.

questions.q: Efficiency of that motor at I_L = 31 A
Demagnetising AT/pole: Z = 600, I_c = 25 A, brush lead 6° (mech)
questions.why: Demagnetising ampere-turns per pole = (2θ/360) × Z × I_c/2 with θ = 6° brush lead: (12/360) × 600 × 25/2 = 250 AT. The factor I_c is the conductor current.

questions.q: Wave-wound 6-pole generator, Z = 300, Φ = 0.05 Wb, N = 800 rpm: E

courses.summary: Rotating magnetic field, construction (squirrel cage and wound rotor), slip, rotor EMF and frequency, equivalent circuit, power flow, torque–slip characteristic, starting methods, speed control, induction generator and single-phase induction motors.
outcomes: Compute synchronous speed, slip and rotor frequency
Use the equivalent circuit and power-flow relations
Analyse torque–slip, starting and maximum torque

lessons.title: Rotating field, slip and rotor quantities

scenes.text: Over two-thirds of industrial electrical energy drives induction motors.
A rotating field 'drags' the rotor along — it can never quite catch up.

steps.title: Basics
steps.body:
N_s = 120f/P. Slip s = (N_s − N)/N_s. Rotor frequency f_r = sf. Rotor EMF E₂ₛ = sE₂ (E₂ at standstill). Rotor reactance X₂ₛ = sX₂. Rotor current I₂ = sE₂/√(R₂² + (sX₂)²).
A three-phase winding fed with balanced currents produces a constant-magnitude field (1.5 × Φ_max per phase) rotating at N_s.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 6-pole, 50 Hz at 960 rpm: N_s = 1000, s = 0.04, f_r = 2 Hz.

**Example 2.** Rotor standstill EMF 100 V/phase, R₂ = 0.05 Ω, X₂ = 0.5 Ω, s = 0.04: E₂ₛ = 4 V, X₂ₛ = 0.02 Ω ⇒ I₂ = 4/√(0.0025 + 0.0004) = 74.3 A.

**Example 3.** Reversing two supply leads reverses the field and the motor.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using rotor speed instead of N_s in f_r.
- Forgetting reactance scales with s.
- Thinking the motor can run at s = 0 under load.

activity.prompt: 4-pole, 50 Hz induction motor at 1455 rpm. Slip in percent?

quiz.why: Rotor frequency f_r = sf = 0.05 × 50 = 2.5 Hz. The slip tells how fast the rotor lags the field.
Rotor EMF is proportional to the relative speed between the field and the rotor, so at slip s it is sE₂, where E₂ is the EMF at standstill.
Swapping any two of the three supply phases reverses the direction of the rotating field, and so the motor reverses.
Induction motors run with a small slip at full load, typically 2–6%. A slip of 0 would give no torque.

lessons.title: Equivalent circuit and power flow

scenes.text: A 15 kW motor draws 17 kW — the difference is lost as heat and friction.
The equivalent circuit splits rotor input into copper loss and mechanical power.

steps.title: Power flow
steps.body:
Input → stator Cu and core loss → air-gap power P_ag (rotor input).
Rotor Cu loss = sP_ag; gross mechanical power P_m = (1 − s)P_ag; P_ag : P_cu2 : P_m = 1 : s : (1 − s).
Shaft output = P_m − friction & windage. Torque T = P_ag/ω_s = P_m/ω_r.
Equivalent circuit (per phase, referred to stator): R₁ + jX₁, magnetising branch, then jX₂′ and R₂′/s = R₂′ + R₂′(1 − s)/s (load resistance).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** P_ag = 20 kW at s = 0.04: rotor Cu = 800 W; P_m = 19.2 kW. Torque at 1500 rpm sync: T = 20 000/157.08 = 127.3 N·m.

**Example 2.** Motor input 50 kW, stator losses 2 kW, s = 0.03, friction 1 kW: P_ag = 48 kW; rotor Cu = 1.44 kW; P_m = 46.56 kW; output 45.56 kW; η = 91.1%.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Computing torque with rotor speed from air-gap power (use ω_s with P_ag).
- Forgetting that rotor copper loss = s × air-gap power.
- Missing mechanical losses in output.

activity.prompt: Power flow of an induction motor
items: Electrical input to stator
Subtract stator copper and core losses ⇒ air-gap power
Subtract rotor copper loss (s × P_ag) ⇒ gross mechanical power
Subtract friction and windage ⇒ shaft output

quiz.why: Air-gap power splits as rotor copper loss = sP_ag and mechanical power = (1 − s)P_ag. So rotor copper loss = s × P_ag.
Gross mechanical power is the part of air-gap power that is not lost in the rotor: P_m = (1 − s)P_ag.
The torque is T = P_ag/ω_s, where ω_s is the synchronous angular speed. The air-gap power is transferred at synchronous speed.
In the equivalent circuit, the mechanical power is shown as power in a load resistor R₂′(1 − s)/s, since R₂′/s = R₂′ + R₂′(1 − s)/s.
At standstill s = 1, so (1 − s) = 0 and the mechanical power is zero, though there is torque. All air-gap power is lost as rotor heat.

lessons.title: Torque–slip characteristic and maximum torque

scenes.text: A crusher motor stalls if the load exceeds its pull-out torque.
The torque–slip curve shows starting, maximum and full-load torques.

steps.title: Torque expressions
steps.body:
T = (3/ω_s) × V²(R₂′/s)/[(R₁ + R₂′/s)² + (X₁ + X₂′)²] (per-phase V).
Neglecting stator impedance: T ∝ sR₂/(R₂² + s²X₂²).
Maximum torque at s_m = R₂/X₂ (independent of R₂ in magnitude): T_max ∝ E₂²/(2X₂).
Low slip region: T ∝ s (linear, stable); high slip: T ∝ 1/s.
T/T_max = 2s s_m/(s² + s_m²). Starting torque maximum when R₂ = X₂.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** R₂ = 0.02 Ω, X₂ = 0.1 Ω: s_m = 0.2 ⇒ at N_s = 1500, speed at max torque = 1200 rpm.

**Example 2.** T_st/T_max = 2(1)(0.2)/(1 + 0.04) = 0.385.

**Example 3.** Full-load slip 0.04: T_FL/T_max = 2(0.04)(0.2)/(0.0016 + 0.04) = 0.385. To get T_st = T_max, add external rotor resistance so R₂ = X₂ = 0.1 Ω (slip-ring motor).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking adding rotor resistance changes T_max (it changes only where it occurs).
- Using line voltage in per-phase torque formula.
- Forgetting T ∝ V² (a 10% voltage dip reduces torque by ~19%).

activity.label: Slip (as fraction) for a motor with s_m = 0.2

bands.text: Low slip: torque rises almost linearly — stable running region.
High slip up to standstill (s = 1): torque falls; s = 1 gives starting torque.

quiz.why: Maximum torque occurs at slip s_m = R₂/X₂, where the rotor resistance equals the standstill rotor reactance.
Adding rotor resistance moves the slip of maximum torque to a higher value (s_m = R₂/X₂), but T_max itself is unchanged. This also improves starting torque.

quiz.q: Torque varies with supply voltage as
quiz.why: Torque is proportional to the square of the supply voltage, T ∝ V², since the rotor EMF and the current are both proportional to V.
Starting torque is maximum when s_m = 1, i.e. R₂ = X₂. Then the maximum torque of the motor occurs right at standstill.
The stable region is where torque rises with slip, from 0 up to s_m, so a small slowdown raises torque and restores the speed. Beyond s_m, the slope is negative and the motor stalls.

lessons.title: Starting, speed control, induction generator and single-phase motors

scenes.text: A 30 kW borewell pump motor would draw 6–7× rated current direct-on-line.
A star–delta starter cuts starting current to one third.

steps.title: Starting methods
steps.body:
- DOL: I_st ≈ 5–7 I_FL; small motors.
- Star–delta: starting phase voltage 1/√3 ⇒ line current and torque 1/3 of DOL.
- Autotransformer (tap x): current and torque × x².
- Rotor resistance (slip-ring): high torque, low current.
- Soft starters/VFDs: smooth, controllable.

steps.title: Speed control and others
steps.body:
Speed control: V/f control with VFDs (constant flux, most common today), pole changing, rotor resistance (slip-ring), slip-power recovery.
**Induction generator:** driven above N_s (negative slip); needs reactive power (grid or capacitors) — wind turbines.
**Single-phase induction motors:** pulsating field = two counter-rotating fields (double revolving field theory) ⇒ no starting torque; use split-phase, capacitor-start, capacitor-run, shaded-pole designs (fans, pumps, compressors).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** DOL starting current 6 I_FL, T_st = 1.8 T_FL ⇒ star–delta: 2 I_FL and 0.6 T_FL.

**Example 2.** Autotransformer 70% tap: current from line = 0.49 × 6 = 2.94 I_FL; torque 0.88 T_FL.

**Example 3.** V/f: 400 V 50 Hz motor run at 25 Hz ⇒ apply ~200 V to keep flux constant.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Star–delta on a motor not designed for delta running.
- Reducing frequency without reducing voltage (saturation, overheating).
- Thinking a single-phase motor self-starts without auxiliary winding.

activity.prompt: Starter → starting current (relative to DOL)

quiz.why: In star, the phase voltage is 1/√3 of the delta value, so torque (∝ V²) falls to 1/3 of that for direct-on-line (DOL) starting. Line current also falls to 1/3.
Most modern drives use variable-frequency drives (VFDs) with V/f control, since they are efficient and give smooth control over a wide range of speeds.
If the rotor is driven above synchronous speed, the slip becomes negative and the machine delivers power to the supply, i.e. it acts as an induction generator.

quiz.q: Single-phase IM has no starting torque because
quiz.why: A single-phase winding produces a pulsating field, which can be seen as two equal fields rotating in opposite directions. They cancel at standstill, so there is no starting torque.
Ceiling fans use single-phase capacitor-run motors. The capacitor produces a phase-shifted auxiliary winding current, giving a rotating field and starting torque.

questions.q: Synchronous speed formula
questions.why: N_s = 120f/P, where f is the frequency in Hz and P the number of poles. For example, 120 × 50/4 = 1500 rpm.

questions.q: Squirrel-cage rotor bars are
questions.why: In a squirrel-cage rotor, the bars are permanently short-circuited at both ends by end rings, so there are no slip rings or external connections.
options: insulated from each other at ends

questions.q: Induction motor speed is
questions.why: The rotor must run slower than the field to cut the flux and have an induced current. So the speed is slightly less than synchronous speed.

questions.q: Rotor Cu loss at s = 0.05, P_ag = 10 kW
questions.why: Rotor copper loss = sP_ag = 0.05 × 10 kW = 0.5 kW = 500 W. The rest, 9.5 kW, is the mechanical power.

questions.q: Speed of 4-pole 50 Hz motor at 4% slip
Star–delta starter line current relative to DOL
questions.why: In star, the phase voltage is reduced by 1/√3, so the phase current also falls by 1/√3. Since line current in delta is √3 × phase current, the line current drops to 1/3 of the DOL value.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Maximum torque of an induction motor is independent of rotor resistance.  Reason (R): Rotor resistance only shifts the slip at which maximum torque occurs.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both are true. T_max depends on the rotor reactance and the voltage (T_max ∝ E²/2X₂), not on R₂. Changing R₂ only shifts the slip at which T_max occurs (s_m = R₂/X₂), so R explains A.

questions.q: s_m for R₂ = 0.04, X₂ = 0.2 Ω
questions.why: s_m = R₂/X₂ = 0.04/0.2 = 0.2. The maximum torque occurs at 20% slip.

questions.q: Torque if voltage falls to 90%
questions.why: Torque ∝ V², so at 90% voltage the torque is 0.9² = 0.81 of its normal value, i.e. 81%. A small voltage drop causes a bigger torque drop.

questions.q: T at P_ag = 30 kW, N_s = 1000 rpm
Case: A 22 kW pump motor on a weak supply trips on DOL start. Cheapest effective fix for a delta-rated motor
questions.why: A star–delta starter reduces the starting current to 1/3 of DOL and is cheap, but needs a motor rated for delta running. So it is the cheapest effective fix. A larger fuse or bigger motor would not reduce the supply dip.

questions.q: T_st/T_max for s_m = 0.25
questions.why: T/T_max = 2s s_m/(s² + s_m²); at starting s = 1 this gives 2s_m/(1 + s_m²) = 0.5/1.0625 ≈ 0.47.

questions.q: Input 40 kW, stator loss 1.5 kW, s = 0.04, F&W 0.6 kW: output
questions.why: P_ag = 40 − 1.5 = 38.5 kW. P_m = (1 − 0.04) × 38.5 = 36.96 kW. Output = 36.96 − 0.6 = 36.36 ≈ 36.4 kW after friction and windage.

questions.q: External rotor resistance per phase to get T_st = T_max with R₂ = 0.05, X₂ = 0.4
questions.why: Starting torque is maximum when s_m = 1, i.e. total rotor resistance = X₂ = 0.4 Ω. So R_ext = 0.4 − 0.05 = 0.35 Ω per phase.

questions.q: Autotransformer starter tap for starting current 2× FL when DOL is 6× FL
questions.why: Starting current ∝ x² times DOL current (x = tap fraction). We want 2/6 = 1/3, so x² = 1/3 and x = 0.577, i.e. about 57.7% tap.

outcomes: Compute EMF with pitch and distribution factors
Find regulation by the synchronous impedance method
Explain synchronisation conditions and power–angle relation
Interpret V-curves and power-factor correction by synchronous motors

lessons.title: Construction and EMF equation

scenes.text: A 500 MW turbo-alternator spins at 3000 rpm with a 2-pole cylindrical rotor.
Hydro alternators turn slowly with many salient poles.

steps.title: Construction
steps.body: Stationary armature (stator) and rotating DC field (rotor) via slip rings or brushless exciter. Cylindrical (non-salient) rotors: high speed (steam/gas turbines, 2 or 4 poles). Salient poles: low speed (hydro, diesel), many poles. N_s = 120f/P.

steps.title: EMF equation and winding factors
steps.body:
E_ph = 4.44 f Φ T_ph K_p K_d (T_ph = turns per phase).
Pitch (coil-span) factor K_p = cos(α/2), α = chording angle (electrical).
Distribution factor K_d = sin(mβ/2)/(m sin(β/2)), m = slots per pole per phase, β = slot angle (electrical) = 180°P/S (S slots).
Short pitching (e.g. 5/6) reduces harmonics (5th, 7th).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 3-phase, 4-pole, 36 slots: m = 3, β = 20°. K_d = sin 30°/(3 sin 10°) = 0.5/0.521 = 0.960. Coil span 8 slots (full pitch 9) ⇒ α = 20° ⇒ K_p = cos 10° = 0.985.

**Example 2.** f = 50 Hz, Φ = 0.05 Wb, T_ph = 120: E = 4.44 × 50 × 0.05 × 120 × 0.985 × 0.960 = 1260 V/phase (≈ 2182 V line in star).

**Example 3.** Hydro alternator 50 Hz at 150 rpm ⇒ P = 40 poles.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using mechanical instead of electrical angles in K_d and K_p.
- Forgetting that line voltage = √3 × phase in star.
- Counting conductors instead of turns.

activity.prompt: 50 Hz alternator at 300 rpm. Number of poles?

quiz.why: Turbo-alternators run at high speed (1500–3000 rpm) with few poles, and their long, slim rotors are cylindrical (non-salient) for mechanical strength.
Pitch factor K_p = cos(α/2), where α is the angle by which the coil is short of full pitch (in electrical degrees). For full pitch α = 0 and K_p = 1.
The slot angle in electrical degrees is β = 180° × P/slots. Here: 180 × 4/48 = 15°.
Short-pitch coils cut out some harmonics (such as the 3rd, 5th, 7th) from the EMF waveform, with only a small loss of the fundamental.

quiz.q: Field winding of an alternator is on
quiz.why: In most alternators, the DC field winding is on the rotor, fed through slip rings, and the AC armature winding is on the stator. This avoids taking high power through slip rings.

lessons.title: Armature reaction, synchronous reactance and regulation

scenes.text: An isolated diesel generator's voltage drops when a large motor starts.
Synchronous reactance models armature reaction plus leakage.

steps.title: Armature reaction by pf
steps.body:
Unity pf: cross-magnetising. Zero lagging: demagnetising (needs more field). Zero leading: magnetising. Synchronous reactance X_s = X_l + X_ar; Z_s = R_a + jX_s.
Per phase: E = V + I(R_a + jX_s).

steps.title: Regulation (EMF / synchronous impedance method)
steps.body:
Z_s from OC and SC tests at the same field current: Z_s = E_oc/I_sc. Regulation = (E − V)/V × 100. Pessimistic method (overestimates) because it assumes linear magnetics; MMF (optimistic) and ZPF/Potier (accurate) methods also used.
Lagging pf ⇒ positive regulation; leading pf may give negative regulation.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using line voltage in per-phase equations.
- Sign of the current angle for leading vs lagging.
- Taking Z_s from OC and SC values at different field currents.

activity.prompt: OC voltage 500 V/phase and SC current 100 A at the same field current. Z_s (Ω)?

quiz.why: At zero-pf lagging load, the armature current lags the EMF by 90°, and its flux directly opposes the main field. This is demagnetising armature reaction.
Synchronous impedance is Z_s = E_oc/I_sc, taken at the same field current in the open- and short-circuit tests.
The EMF method ignores saturation and treats Z_s as constant. It overestimates the voltage rise needed, so it gives a higher regulation, i.e. a pessimistic result.
At a leading power factor, armature reaction is magnetising, and the terminal voltage can exceed the no-load EMF, making regulation negative.
The synchronous reactance X_s is the sum of the leakage reactance and the reactance that represents armature reaction. R_a is separate.

lessons.title: Synchronisation, parallel operation and power–angle

scenes.text: Before closing the breaker, operators watch a synchroscope.
Closing out of phase can damage the machine with huge currents.

steps.title: Synchronising conditions
steps.body:
Equal voltage, equal frequency, same phase sequence, and zero phase angle at closing. Methods: lamps (dark/bright lamp), synchroscope, automatic synchronisers.
Once on an infinite bus: real power controlled by prime-mover input (governor); reactive power and pf controlled by field excitation.

steps.title: Power–angle relation
steps.body:
Cylindrical rotor (R_a neglected): P = (3EV/X_s) sin δ (three-phase, per-phase E, V). Maximum (steady-state limit) at δ = 90°: P_max = 3EV/X_s. Salient pole adds a reluctance term (V²/2)(1/X_q − 1/X_d) sin 2δ.
Synchronising power coefficient P_s = dP/dδ = (3EV/X_s) cos δ.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** E = 1.2 pu, V = 1.0 pu, X_s = 1.0 pu, P = 0.6 pu: sin δ = 0.5 ⇒ δ = 30°. P_max = 1.2 pu.

**Example 2.** Increasing excitation with the same P: E rises ⇒ δ falls; machine supplies more lagging reactive power (over-excited).

**Example 3.** Per-phase E = 2500 V, V = 2400 V, X_s = 10 Ω, δ = 20°: P = 3 × 2500 × 2400 × 0.342/10 = 615.6 kW.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking excitation changes real power (governor does).
- Using single-phase formula for three-phase power.
- Operating near δ = 90° (no margin — loss of synchronism).

activity.prompt: Synchronising an alternator to the bus
items: Bring the machine to near-synchronous speed with the prime mover
Adjust excitation so terminal voltage equals bus voltage
Check phase sequence matches
Adjust speed until the synchroscope pointer turns very slowly
Close the breaker at the in-phase position

quiz.q: Real power output is controlled by
quiz.why: For a grid-connected alternator, real power is set by the mechanical power from the prime mover (governor). Excitation only affects the reactive power.
Reactive power output is controlled by the field excitation. Over-excitation makes the alternator supply lagging VARs, under-excitation makes it absorb.
Power P = (EV/X)sinδ is maximum at δ = 90°. Beyond that, a larger δ gives less power, so the machine goes unstable. That is the steady-state limit.

quiz.q: P for E = V = 1 pu, X = 0.5 pu, δ = 30°

quiz.why: Synchronising needs equal voltage, frequency and phase sequence (and phase angle). The two machines can have different kVA ratings.

lessons.title: Synchronous motors and V-curves

scenes.text: A cement plant runs a large over-excited synchronous motor on its mill.
It drives the load AND supplies reactive power, improving the plant's pf.

steps.title: Operation
steps.body:
Runs only at N_s; not self-starting (rotor can't follow the field from rest). Starting: damper (amortisseur) windings as induction motor, pony motor, or VFD.
V-curves: armature current vs field current at constant load — minimum at unity pf; under-excited ⇒ lagging pf, over-excited ⇒ leading pf. Inverted-V curves: pf vs field current.
Synchronous condenser: over-excited motor at no load — variable reactive power source.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Plant: 800 kW at 0.7 lag (Q = 816 kVAR). Add a 300 kW synchronous motor at 0.8 lead (Q = −225 kVAR): total P = 1100 kW, Q = 591 kVAR ⇒ pf = 0.88 lag.

**Example 2.** To reach unity overall, the motor must supply 816 kVAR ⇒ its kVA = √(300² + 816²) = 869 kVA.

**Example 3.** 6-pole 50 Hz synchronous motor speed = 1000 rpm at any load (within pull-out).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Expecting slip in a synchronous motor.
- Confusing under-excited (lagging) with over-excited (leading).
- Forgetting damper windings also damp hunting.

activity.prompt: Excitation state of a synchronous motor

items.text: Minimum armature current for given load
Supplies reactive power to the system

quiz.why: A synchronous motor locks to the rotating field, so its speed is exactly the synchronous speed N_s at any load, as long as it stays in synchronism.

quiz.q: Bottom of a V-curve corresponds to
quiz.why: On a V-curve (armature current vs field current), the lowest current is at unity power factor. Either side, the current rises with a lagging or leading pf.
A synchronous condenser is a synchronous motor run at no load, with over-excitation, so that it supplies reactive power to the grid like a capacitor.
options: an over-excited motor at no load

quiz.why: A synchronous motor has no starting torque by itself. It is started with damper (amortisseur) windings, as an induction motor, or by a VFD, and then synchronised.
An over-excited synchronous motor draws a leading current, i.e. it supplies reactive power, so its power factor is leading.

questions.q: Hydro alternators typically have
questions.why: Hydro turbines run slowly, so the alternators need many poles to give 50 Hz. These have large-diameter rotors with salient poles.

questions.q: EMF equation constant
questions.why: The EMF equation for an alternator is E = 4.44 f Φ T K_p K_d, the same form as the transformer EMF equation.

questions.q: Synchronous motors are self-starting?
questions.why: Synchronous motors have no starting torque, since the rotor cannot lock on to a fast-rotating field from rest. They need damper windings or a drive.

questions.q: Speed of 4-pole 60 Hz alternator
Pitch factor for 150° coil span
questions.why: A 150° span is 30° short of full pitch (180°), so α = 30° and K_p = cos(α/2) = cos 15° ≈ 0.966.

questions.q: Regulation if E = 260 V, V = 230 V
Assertion (A): Increasing excitation of a grid-connected alternator mainly changes reactive power.  Reason (R): Real power is set by the prime mover; excitation changes E and the reactive output.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both are true. Real power is fixed by the prime mover, so excitation changes E and the reactive power only. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: K_d for m = 2, β = 30°
E for V = 1 pu, I = 1 pu at unity pf, X_s = 0.8 pu
questions.why: At unity pf, E = √(V² + (IX_s)²) = √(1 + 0.64) ≈ 1.28 pu. The IX_s drop is at 90° to V, so it adds in quadrature.

questions.q: δ for P = 0.8 pu, E = 1.6, V = 1, X_s = 1
questions.why: P = (EV/X_s)sinδ gives 0.8 = 1.6 × 1/1 × sinδ, so sinδ = 0.5 and δ = 30°.

questions.q: Case: A plant runs 600 kW at 0.6 lag. A synchronous motor taking 200 kW is added to make the overall pf 1. Motor kVAR (leading)
questions.why: At 0.6 pf, the plant has P = 600 kW and Q = 600 × tan(53.13°) = 800 kVAR lagging. For unity pf overall, the motor must supply 800 kVAR leading.

questions.q: Motor kVA for that case
questions.why: The motor kVA = √(P² + Q²) = √(200² + 800²) = √680000 ≈ 825 kVA. The kVA is bigger than the real power because of the large reactive part.

questions.q: Regulation with V = 1, I = 1 pu at 0.8 lag, X_s = 1 pu, R = 0
Synchronising power coefficient at δ = 30° (P_max = 1.2 pu)
questions.why: The synchronising power coefficient is dP/dδ = P_max cosδ = 1.2 × cos 30° = 1.2 × 0.866 ≈ 1.04 pu per rad. It measures the restoring effect.

questions.q: Distribution factor for 3-phase, 6-pole, 54 slots
questions.why: Slots per pole per phase m = 54/(6 × 3) = 3. Slot angle β = 180 × 6/54 = 20°. K_d = sin(60°/... ) = sin(mβ/2)/(m sin(β/2)) = sin 30°/(3 sin 10°) = 0.5/0.521 ≈ 0.960.

lessons.title: Formula sheet: transformers and DC machines

scenes.text: Ananya has one evening to revise Electrical Machines.
She works through a one-page sheet, then tests herself.

steps.title: Transformers
steps.body:
- E = 4.44fNΦ; Z′ = a²Z
- OC → P_i, R_c, X_m; SC → P_cu, R_eq, X_eq
- Reg ≈ (IR cos φ ± IX sin φ)/V; η max at x = √(P_i/P_cu)
- Auto saving V₂/V₁ (step-down); open delta 57.7%

steps.title: DC machines
steps.body:
- E = PΦNZ/60A (A = P lap, 2 wave); T = PΦZI_a/2πA
- Motor E_b = V − I_aR_a; N ∝ E_b/Φ
- Series T ∝ I² (unsat.); never unloaded
- Starter R = V/I_st − R_a; Swinburne constant losses

steps.title: How to use this sheet
steps.body:
- Cover the right-hand side of each formula and try to recall it.
- For every formula, say its conditions of validity aloud (units, assumptions, ranges).
- Re-solve one worked example from the matching unit without looking.

steps.title: Common slips to avoid
steps.body:
- Mixing units (kN vs N, mm vs m, km/h vs m/s, degrees vs radians).
- Using a formula outside its assumptions.
- Dropping signs or factors such as 2, ½, π or √3.

quiz.q: R_eq from SC: 50 V, 10 A, 300 W
quiz.why: In the short-circuit test the wattmeter reads full-load copper loss, so R_eq = P/I² = 300/10² = 3 Ω (while Z_eq = 50/10 = 5 Ω).

quiz.q: Back EMF 230 V, R_a 0.4, I_a 25 A

lessons.title: Formula sheet: induction and synchronous machines

scenes.text: Ananya has one evening to revise Electrical Machines.
She works through a one-page sheet, then tests herself.

steps.title: Induction
steps.body:
- N_s = 120f/P; s = (N_s − N)/N_s; f_r = sf
- P_ag : P_cu2 : P_m = 1 : s : 1 − s; T = P_ag/ω_s
- s_m = R₂/X₂; T ∝ V²; Y–Δ start 1/3; auto x²

steps.title: Synchronous
steps.body:
- E = 4.44fΦT K_pK_d; K_p = cos(α/2); K_d = sin(mβ/2)/(m sin(β/2))
- E = V + IZ_s; Z_s = E_oc/I_sc
- P = 3EV sin δ/X_s; excitation → Q; governor → P
- V-curves: minimum I at unity pf

steps.title: How to use this sheet
steps.body:
- Cover the right-hand side of each formula and try to recall it.
- For every formula, say its conditions of validity aloud (units, assumptions, ranges).
- Re-solve one worked example from the matching unit without looking.

steps.title: Common slips to avoid
steps.body:
- Mixing units (kN vs N, mm vs m, km/h vs m/s, degrees vs radians).
- Using a formula outside its assumptions.
- Dropping signs or factors such as 2, ½, π or √3.

statements.s: Induction motors can run at synchronous speed under load.
Synchronous motors can improve plant pf.
Adding rotor resistance changes T_max.

quiz.q: P_max for E = 1.5, V = 1, X = 1.25 pu
quiz.why: P_max = EV/X = 1.5 × 1/1.25 = 1.2 pu, which occurs at δ = 90°.
A 5/6 pitch coil is 1/6 short of full pitch, i.e. 30° short. So K_p = cos(30°/2) = cos 15° ≈ 0.966.

lessons.title: Mock paper 1 (timed practice)

scenes.text: Set a 30-minute timer and attempt every question before checking.
Read each explanation, even for the ones you got right.

steps.title: How to attempt
steps.body:
- Attempt easy questions first.
- For numericals write the formula, substitute with units, then simplify.
- Mark doubtful ones and return.

steps.title: Coverage
steps.body: This paper mixes every unit of Electrical Machines. Scores below 60% mean: re-read the unit whose questions you missed, then retake.

steps.title: Common mistakes in exams
steps.body:
- Skipping units and sign conventions.
- Copying a formula without checking its conditions of validity.
- Not reading 'NOT' / 'incorrect' in the question.

activity.prompt: Before the real exam
items: Formula sheet revised twice
One full mock done under time
Wrong answers re-solved without looking
Derivations listed in the syllabus practised once

quiz.why: The short-circuit test is done at rated current, so the input power is almost entirely copper loss. The iron loss is negligible because the voltage is low.
A wave winding always has 2 parallel paths, independent of the number of poles.

quiz.q: Mock 1: Rotor Cu loss 5% slip, P_ag 20 kW
quiz.why: Rotor copper loss = sP_ag = 0.05 × 20 kW = 1 kW.

quiz.q: Mock 1: Alternator real power is set by
quiz.why: Real power from an alternator on the grid is controlled by the mechanical input from the prime mover (governor). Excitation controls reactive power.
An under-excited synchronous motor draws a lagging current, like an inductor, so its pf is lagging. Over-excitation gives leading pf.
A star–delta starter applies the reduced voltage in star, so the line current is 1/3 of the direct-on-line current.

questions.q: Core of a transformer is laminated to reduce
questions.why: The core is made from thin insulated laminations to break the paths of eddy currents. This reduces eddy-current loss, a part of iron loss.

questions.q: DC motor for traction
questions.why: A DC series motor gives very high torque at low speed (T ∝ I_a²), which suits traction loads like trains and trams.

questions.q: N_s for 2-pole 50 Hz
Synchronous condenser supplies
questions.why: An over-excited synchronous machine running at no load supplies reactive power to the grid, which helps with voltage control and power factor.

questions.q: η of 25 kVA transformer at FL, pf 0.8, P_i 250 W, P_cu 500 W
Rotor EMF at s = 0.03 if standstill E₂ = 120 V
questions.why: Rotor EMF = sE₂ = 0.03 × 120 = 3.6 V. At low slip the rotor EMF is small.

questions.q: Shunt motor speed if Φ reduced 10% (E_b ~ const)
questions.why: N ∝ E_b/Φ. If Φ falls by 10% and E_b stays about the same, N becomes 1/0.9 ≈ 1.11 times. Weaker field means higher speed.

questions.q: Torque at P_ag 15 kW, 1500 rpm sync
Assertion (A): A DC series motor's speed rises sharply at light load.  Reason (R): Flux falls with armature current and N ∝ E_b/Φ.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both are true. In a series motor, the flux falls as armature current falls, and N ∝ E_b/Φ, so at light load the speed rises sharply. R explains A.

questions.q: Autotransformer 240/200 V, 12 kVA: transformed kVA
questions.why: The power transformed (by induction) in an autotransformer is S(1 − V_low/V_high) = 12 × (1 − 200/240) = 12 × 0.1667 = 2 kVA. The rest is conducted directly.

questions.q: E per phase: f 50, Φ 0.04, T 100, K_p 0.96, K_d 0.96
T_FL/T_max for s = 0.05, s_m = 0.25
Case: Two transformers 600 kVA (4%) and 400 kVA (6%) share 900 kVA. 400 kVA unit carries
Regulation: V 1 pu, I 1 pu unity pf, R 0.05, X_s 1.2 pu
Swinburne: 250 V, no-load 5 A, I_sh 1 A, R_a 0.2 Ω — constant losses
questions.why: Input at no load = 250 × 5 = 1250 W. Armature copper loss = (5 − 1)² × 0.2 = 3.2 W. Constant losses = 1250 − 3.2 = 1246.8 W.

questions.q: Speed of a 4-pole induction motor whose rotor current frequency is 1.5 Hz on 50 Hz
questions.why: Rotor current frequency = sf, so s = 1.5/50 = 0.03. N_s = 1500 rpm, so N = 1500 × 0.97 = 1455 rpm.

questions.q: Starting torque with autotransformer at 60% tap if DOL T_st = 2 T_FL
questions.why: Starting torque scales with the square of the tap fraction: 0.6² = 0.36. So T_st = 0.36 × 2 T_FL = 0.72 T_FL.

questions.q: Power at δ = 25°: E 11 kV line, V 11 kV line, X_s 8 Ω per phase (3-phase)
questions.why: Phase voltage = 11 kV/√3. 3-phase power = V_L E_L sinδ/X_s = (11000 × 11000 × sin 25°)/8 = 121×10⁶ × 0.4226/8 ≈ 6.39 MW.

questions.q: Pull-out torque ratio if supply voltage falls 20%
questions.why: Pull-out (maximum) torque is proportional to V². At 80% voltage, the ratio is 0.8² = 0.64.

Convert quantities to per-unit and change base
Compute line inductance and capacitance using GMD and GMR
