lessons.title: Lab: PMSM and BLDC motor drives — torque, back-emf and speed

scenes.text: A hub motor has permanent magnets and three phases switched electronically by Hall sensors.
Torque is proportional to current; speed is set by voltage.

steps.title: BLDC vs PMSM
steps.body: **BLDC**: trapezoidal back-emf, **120° conduction** (two phases on at a time), position from three Hall sensors (6 commutation states per electrical cycle), simple, higher torque ripple. **PMSM**: sinusoidal back-emf, sinusoidal currents, needs encoder/resolver, smooth torque, field-oriented control. Equations (SI): **E = K_e ω**, **T = K_t I** (K_t = K_e in consistent SI units), **V = E + I R**. PMSM torque: **T = (3/2) p λ_pm i_q** (p = pole pairs). Advantages of PM machines: high efficiency, power density, no rotor copper loss. Demerits: magnet cost, demagnetisation, field-weakening needs negative i_d.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Hub motor: V = 48 V, K_e = K_t = 0.05 V·s/rad, R = 0.5 Ω (equivalent), I = 10 A: E = 48 − 5 = 43 V ⇒ ω = 860 rad/s = **8212 rpm**; T = 0.05 × 10 = **0.5 N·m**.

**Example 2.** PMSM, p = 3, λ_pm = 0.1 Wb, i_q = 10 A: T = 1.5 × 3 × 0.1 × 10 = **4.5 N·m**.

**Example 3.** Three Hall sensors give 6 valid states ⇒ commutation every 60° electrical; a 4-pole-pair motor commutates 6 × 4 = 24 times per mechanical revolution.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing mechanical and electrical speed (ω_e = p ω_m).
- Using BLDC 6-step commutation for smooth low-speed servo work.
- Over-driving current beyond demagnetisation limits.

activity.prompt: PMSM with 3 pole pairs, flux linkage 0.1 Wb, i_q = 10 A. Torque T = 1.5 p λ i_q?

lessons.title: Lab: Vector (field-oriented) control — Clarke and Park transforms

story.title: Making an AC motor behave like a DC motor

scenes.text: Field-oriented control splits stator current into a flux part and a torque part.
The Clarke and Park transforms do the splitting.

steps.title: Transforms and idea
steps.body: **Clarke (abc → αβ), amplitude-invariant**: i_α = i_a; i_β = (i_a + 2 i_b)/√3. **Park (αβ → dq) at rotor-flux angle θ**: i_d = i_α cos θ + i_β sin θ; i_q = −i_α sin θ + i_β cos θ. In the rotating frame aligned with rotor flux: **i_d controls flux, i_q controls torque**: T = (3/2) p (L_m/L_r) ψ_r i_q for an induction motor. **Indirect FOC**: the flux angle is obtained as θ = ∫(ω_r + ω_sl) dt with **slip frequency ω_sl = i_q/(T_r i_d)**, T_r = L_r/R_r. Cascade: speed PI → i_q*; flux (or i_d*) → current PI loops in dq → inverse Park → SVPWM.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing amplitude-invariant and power-invariant transforms (factor √(2/3)).
- Using the wrong flux angle (stator vs rotor).
- Not decoupling d and q cross-terms in current loops.

lessons.title: Lab: Stepper, switched-reluctance and servo drives

scenes.text: A stepper motor moves a print head in exact increments, until it is overloaded and skips.
Closed-loop servo or microstepping removes the problem.

steps.title: Stepper and SRM
steps.body: **Stepper motor**: step angle (VR) = 360/(m × N_r) for m phases and N_r rotor teeth; hybrid motors 1.8° (200 steps/rev) or 0.9°; speed **N (rpm) = (step angle × pulse rate)/6** (step angle in degrees × pps/360 × 60). Half-stepping halves the step angle; **microstepping** gives smooth motion. Holding torque, detent torque, pull-in and pull-out curves; resonance. **Switched reluctance motor (SRM)**: doubly salient, no magnets or rotor winding; torque **T = ½ i² dL/dθ**, independent of current direction ⇒ unipolar converter (asymmetric half-bridge); rugged, high speed, cheap; torque ripple and acoustic noise. **Servo drive**: PMSM/BLDC with encoder, three nested loops (current, speed, position).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 3-phase VR stepper with 8 rotor teeth: step = 360/(3 × 8) = **15°**; for 1000 pulses/s speed = 15 × 1000/6 = **2500 rpm**. A hybrid motor with 1.8° step at 1000 pps: speed = 1.8 × 1000/6 = **300 rpm**.

**Example 2.** SRM: i = 10 A, dL/dθ = 0.05 H/rad ⇒ T = 0.5 × 100 × 0.05 = **2.5 N·m**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting that stepper torque falls steeply with speed.
- Running resonance without damping.
- Believing SRM needs bipolar current (it does not).

activity.prompt: A hybrid stepper has 1.8° step. It is driven at 2000 pulses/s. Speed in rpm?

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone — choose between FOC and DTC and size a PMSM servo

scenes.text: A factory is upgrading CNC spindles and must choose control and motor sizing.
Torque response, ripple and switching frequency drive the choice.

steps.title: FOC vs DTC
steps.body:
**FOC (vector)**: PI current loops, SVPWM, fixed switching frequency, low torque ripple, needs coordinate transforms, tuning sensitive to parameters. **DTC (direct torque control)**: hysteresis controllers for flux and torque, switching table, very fast torque response, no current loops or PWM, but variable switching frequency and higher torque ripple unless using SVM-DTC. Choice: servo/smooth low-speed → FOC; fast torque (traction, cranes) → DTC.
**Sizing**: i_q* = T/(1.5 p λ). Check current ≤ drive peak; thermal limit with rms torque over the cycle.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: Required peak torque 20 N·m, p = 4, λ = 0.1 Wb ⇒ i_q = 20/(1.5 × 4 × 0.1) = **33.3 A (peak)** ⇒ rms = 23.6 A; choose a drive with ≥ 25 A rms continuous and ≥ 35 A peak. Check: base speed 3000 rpm ⇒ ω_e = 4 × 314.16 = 1256.6 rad/s; E_peak (phase) = ω_e λ = **125.7 V**; line-line peak = 218 V ⇒ DC bus ≥ about 300 V; use a 3-phase 400 V supply (V_dc ≈ 565 V) for margin.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Selecting only on torque and forgetting back-emf at top speed.
- Not providing field-weakening current margin.
- Ignoring encoder resolution for position accuracy.

steps.title: Dynamics and rating
steps.body:
- T − T_L = J dω/dt; ω = 2πN/60.
- J_eq = J_m + J_L/a²; T_L' = T_L/(aη) motoring, T_L η/a regenerating; linear: J = m(v/ω)².
- Loads: constant torque; ∝ω (calender); ∝ω² (fan, pump, P ∝ ω³); ∝1/ω (constant power).
- Stability: dT/dω < dT_L/dω.
- Heating: θ = θ_f(1 − e^(−t/τ)); I_eq = √(ΣI²t/Σt). Insulation A105, E120, B130, F155, H180 °C.

steps.title: DC and converter drives
steps.body:
- N = (V − I_aR_a)/kφ; R_start = V/I_max − R_a; dynamic braking I = E_b/(R_a + R_b); plugging I = (V + E_b)/(R_a + R).
- 1-ph full: V_o = (2V_m/π)cos α; semi: (V_m/π)(1 + cos α); 3-ph full: 1.35 V_LL cos α; semi: 0.675 V_LL(1 + cos α).
- Dual converter: α₁ + α₂ = 180°.
- Chopper: V_o = D V_s; ΔI = V D(1 − D)/(fL); rheostatic R_eff = R_b(1 − D); class B: (1 − D)V_s.
- Closed loop ΔN = ΔN_ol/(1 + K); PI: T_i = T_a, K_p = ω_c R_a T_a/K_c.

steps.title: AC, PM and vector drives
steps.body:
- N_s = 120f/P; s = (N_s − N)/N_s; P_cu2 = sP_ag; P_m = (1 − s)P_ag.
- V/f const: flux const; above base: T_max ∝ 1/f².
- Same torque: s ∝ R₂.
- VSI: six-step 0.78 V_dc; SPWM 0.612 m V_dc; SVPWM 0.707 V_dc.
- Affinity: Q ∝ N, H ∝ N², P ∝ N³.
- PMSM T = 1.5pλi_q; BLDC E = K_eω, T = K_tI.
- Clarke i_β = (i_a + 2i_b)/√3; Park i_d = i_α cos θ + i_β sin θ; i_q = −i_α sin θ + i_β cos θ; ω_sl = i_q/(T_r i_d).
- Stepper: N(rpm) = step(°) × pps/6; SRM T = ½i²dL/dθ.

lessons.title: Lab: Speed control of a DC shunt motor (armature-voltage and field control)

scenes.text: A 220 V DC shunt motor is coupled to a tachometer on the lab bench.
You will plot speed against armature voltage and field current.

steps.title: Aim, apparatus, theory
steps.body:
**Aim**: to control the speed of a DC shunt motor by (a) varying armature voltage with field constant, (b) varying field current with armature voltage constant, and plot N vs V_a and N vs I_f.
**Apparatus**: DC shunt motor (220 V, 5 HP typical), variable DC source or Ward–Leonard, rheostats, voltmeter, ammeters, digital tachometer, 3-point starter, loading arrangement.
**Theory**: N ∝ (V_a − I_a R_a)/φ; N rises with V_a (linear) and with decreasing I_f (approximately inversely).

| V_a (V) | I_a (A) | E_b = V_a − I_aR_a (R_a = 0.5 Ω) | N (rpm) predicted |

| 220 | 10 | 215 | 1000 |
| 165 | 10 | 160 | 744 |
| 110 | 10 | 105 | 488 |
N predicted = 1000 × E_b/215. For V_a = 165: 1000 × 160/215 = **744 rpm**. Plot N vs V_a: straight line (constant flux, constant torque region).

steps.title: Precautions
steps.body:
- Start with maximum field current (rheostat cut out) and minimum armature voltage.
- Never open the field circuit when running (runaway).
- Do not exceed rated armature current or speed.

steps.body:
**Aim**: to study the single-phase full-converter fed separately excited DC motor and verify V_o = (2V_m/π) cos α. **Apparatus**: 230 V single-phase supply, isolation transformer, thyristor bridge trainer with firing circuit (potentiometer for α), DC motor with tacho, CRO, voltmeters.
**Procedure**: set α = 0°, record output voltage and speed; increase α to 30°, 60°, 90° and record; observe waveforms on CRO (isolated probes, safe supply).

In practice, with load the output differs slightly because of discontinuous conduction and overlap.

items.a: The converter then enters inversion mode (negative average voltage) and can feed energy back to the supply if the machine acts as a generator.

items.q: What is the effect of α on input PF?
items.a: Displacement factor = cos α, so the PF falls as the speed is reduced.

items.q: Why use a freewheeling diode with half-controlled bridge?
items.a: It prevents negative voltage and the 'freewheeling' of load current, improving PF and preventing loss of control.

items.q: Why is a smoothing inductor required?
items.a: The output ripple is large at 100 Hz and the current may become discontinuous at light load, degrading speed regulation.

items.q: What is meant by cascade control?
items.a: An inner current loop and an outer speed loop; the inner loop protects against over-current and gives fast torque response.

lessons.title: Why high voltage? Ionisation, electron avalanche and Townsend's first mechanism

story.title: The gap that glows before it fails

scenes.text: On a dry day a 1 cm air gap at 30 kV peak suddenly flashes over.
Before the flash, a tiny current grows exponentially as electrons multiply in an avalanche.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
**Ionisation** by collision: a free electron accelerated by field E gains energy; if it exceeds the ionisation energy of the gas atom (≈ 15.6 eV for N₂, 12.1 eV for O₂) a new electron–ion pair forms. **Townsend's first ionisation coefficient α** = number of ionising collisions per electron per cm of drift in field direction (α/p = f(E/p)). **Secondary coefficient γ** = electrons liberated at the cathode per positive ion (or photon) arriving. Other processes: attachment (electronegative gases like SF₆, O₂), recombination, photo-ionisation, thermal ionisation.
**Townsend equation** (current growth): **I = I₀ e^(αd)/[1 − γ(e^(αd) − 1)]**. **Breakdown (spark) criterion**: **γ(e^(αd) − 1) = 1**, denominator → 0, current self-sustaining.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing α (per-electron per-cm) with γ (per ion at cathode).
- Applying Townsend's mechanism to long gaps (pd > ~1000 torr·cm), where streamers dominate.
- Forgetting that the current before breakdown is non-self-sustaining (needs external source).

activity.prompt: α = 5 cm⁻¹, d = 1 cm, γ = 0, I₀ = 10⁻⁸ A. Current at the anode in µA (3 decimals)?

options: Ionising collisions per electron per cm

quiz.why: The denominator of the current equation vanishes.

lessons.title: Paschen's law and its limits

story.title: Why a vacuum gap and a pressurised gap both resist

scenes.text: Breakdown voltage depends on the product pressure × gap, not on either alone.
A minimum exists: about 300 V in air.

steps.title: Paschen's law
steps.body: Because α/p = f(E/p), the breakdown voltage in a uniform field depends only on the product **p·d**: **V_b = B p d / [ln(A p d) − ln(ln(1 + 1/γ))]** (A, B are gas constants; for air A ≈ 15 cm⁻¹torr⁻¹, B ≈ 365 V cm⁻¹torr⁻¹). There is a **minimum** (~ 300–330 V for air at pd ≈ 0.5–0.9 torr·cm): below it electrons cross the gap without enough collisions (vacuum insulation), above it the gas is denser so energy gain per mean free path is smaller. At normal pressure, uniform-field breakdown of air is about **30 kV/cm peak** (≈ 3 MV/m); SF₆ is about 2.5 times higher; it also rises with pressure (compressed-gas insulation). Failures of the law: very short gaps (pd < 0.01), very long gaps, non-uniform fields, high frequency, and strongly attaching gases.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Air with A = 15, B = 365, γ = 0.01: ln(1 + 1/γ) = ln 101 = 4.615; ln of that = 1.529. For pd = 5 torr·cm: V_b = 365 × 5/[ln 75 − 1.529] = 1825/[4.317 − 1.529] = **654.6 V**.

**Example 2.** Same gap with the pressure doubled but the spacing halved (pd unchanged) ⇒ V_b unchanged (**654.6 V**).

**Example 3.** Air at 30 kV/cm peak: a 2 cm uniform gap breaks down at about 60 kV peak.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying breakdown voltage rises linearly with pressure at fixed gap in every range.
- Using the law for corona (non-uniform fields) and long gaps.
- Forgetting that the minimum voltage exists.

lessons.title: Streamer (Raether–Meek) mechanism, time lags and non-uniform fields

story.title: The long spark in a lightning-rod test

scenes.text: A 2 m rod–plane gap breaks down faster than Townsend's theory predicts.
Space charge in the avalanche head launches a streamer.

steps.title: Streamer mechanism
steps.body:
When the avalanche reaches a critical size (**αx ≈ 18–20, i.e. e^(αx) ≈ 10⁸ electrons**) the space-charge field equals the applied field at the head: **Raether–Meek criterion**. Photo-ionisation ahead of the head creates secondary avalanches, forming a conducting streamer that crosses the gap in ~ 10⁻⁷ s (much faster than Townsend, which needs ion transit ≈ 10⁻⁵ s). It applies at high pd (> 1000 torr·cm), overvoltages and large gaps.
**Time lags**: statistical time lag (waiting for an initiatory electron) + formative time lag (growth of discharge). **Impulse ratio** = impulse breakdown voltage/AC (peak) breakdown voltage (≈ 1.0 for uniform gaps; > 1 for non-uniform). **Non-uniform field**: partial discharge (corona) at the high-stress electrode; **polarity effect**: in a point–plane gap, positive point breaks down at lower voltage than negative (~ 5–8 kV/cm vs ~ 10 kV/cm) because positive space charge in front of the point intensifies the field (needle-plane, pol. effect). Long-air-gap leader mechanism applies above ~ 1 m.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Critical avalanche length: α = 20 cm⁻¹ ⇒ αx = 18.4 ⇒ x = 0.92 cm (streamer starts when the avalanche head covers 0.92 cm of gap).

**Example 2.** Impulse ratio: impulse breakdown 180 kV peak, AC breakdown 120 kV peak ⇒ ratio = **1.5**.

**Example 3.** Streamer crossing a 5 cm gap at 10⁶ m/s ⇒ t = 0.05/10⁶ = 5 × 10⁻⁸ s = **50 ns**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using Townsend for lightning-length gaps.
- Mixing polarity: positive rod breaks down at lower voltage than negative rod.
- Treating statistical lag as zero for short impulses.

lessons.title: Lab: Corona — critical voltage and power loss

story.title: The 220 kV line that hisses in the fog

scenes.text: On a foggy night a 220 kV line hisses and glows.
Corona loss wastes power and generates radio noise.

steps.title: Corona
steps.body: Corona is a partial discharge in the region of high stress near conductors in non-uniform fields. **Peek's law**: critical disruptive voltage (rms, phase to neutral) **V_c = g₀ m_o δ r ln(D/r)** kV, with g₀ = 21.1 kV/cm (rms), r = conductor radius (cm), D = spacing (cm), m_o = surface factor (0.85–0.95 for stranded), δ = air density factor = 0.386 p/(273 + t) (p in mmHg, t in °C; δ ≈ 0.98 at 760 mmHg, 25 °C). **Visual critical voltage** V_v = g₀ m_v δ r (1 + 0.3/√(δ r)) ln(D/r) (m_v = 0.72 – 0.82). **Peek corona loss**: **P = (241/δ)(f + 25)√(r/D)(V − V_c)² × 10⁻⁵ kW/km/phase** (V, V_c rms phase kV). Effects: power loss, radio/TV interference, audible noise, ozone/nitrous oxide, corrosion, harmonic currents. Reduction: bundled conductors, larger diameter, hollow conductors, grading rings.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** r = 1 cm, D = 300 cm, m_o = 0.85, δ = 1: V_c = 21.1 × 0.85 × 1 × ln 300 = 21.1 × 0.85 × 5.704 = **102.3 kV** (phase), ⇒ line-line 177.2 kV.

**Example 2.** On a 220 kV line (V = 127.0 kV phase, f = 50, same conductor): P = (241)(75)√(1/300)(127.0 − 102.3)² × 10⁻⁵ = 241 × 75 × 0.05774 × 610 × 10⁻⁵ = **6.38 kW/km/phase**.

**Example 3.** Bundling two conductors per phase reduces surface gradient by ~ 20–30 %, raising V_c above the operating voltage.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using line voltage in Peek's formula (it needs phase voltage, rms).
- Using conductor diameter instead of radius.
- Forgetting that fog and rain lower V_c and raise loss.

story.title: Selecting the clearance in a 33 kV indoor switchgear room

scenes.text: A designer must choose the phase-to-earth clearance for indoor 33 kV equipment.
Gap breakdown values, altitude and a safety factor decide the dimension.

steps.title: Method
steps.body: 1. Required withstand: lightning impulse level (e.g. 170 kV for 36 kV class) and power-frequency 70 kV rms. 2. Convert to peak: 70 × √2 = 99 kV. 3. Air breakdown ≈ 30 kV/cm peak for uniform fields but only ~ 5–10 kV/cm for sharp edges and long gaps; use a utilisation factor η = E_mean/E_max (0.3–0.5 for rod/bus corners). 4. Apply altitude factor (δ) and safety factor (≥ 1.2). 5. Add margin for pollution/humidity.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: Withstand 99 kV peak, η = 0.4 (non-uniform), E_b = 30 kV/cm × 0.4 = 12 kV/cm effective; gap = 99/12 = 8.25 cm; × 1.2 safety = **9.9 cm**; at 2000 m altitude δ ≈ 0.80 ⇒ gap = 9.9/0.8 = **12.4 cm** (altitude correction approximates the breakdown ∝ δ). Typical indoor 33 kV clearance is 320 mm because of impulse and creepage; this pure-AC calculation is a lower bound.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using rms voltage with a peak breakdown field.
- Ignoring altitude and humidity.
- Using uniform-field strength for edges.

lessons.title: Breakdown of liquid dielectrics

story.title: The transformer that failed the oil test

scenes.text: A sample from a 132 kV transformer breaks down at 22 kV in the oil test cup.
A few tens of ppm of moisture and fibres have destroyed its strength.

steps.title: Mechanisms
steps.body:
**Pure liquids**: electronic breakdown (field emission/ionisation, ≈ 1 MV/cm for hydrocarbons) and **cavitation/bubble** theory (bubbles formed by electrostatic forces, heating or field-emission current vaporise the liquid; breakdown when the bubble reaches critical size).
**Commercial liquids**: **suspended particle theory** — solid particles (fibres, carbon, metal) and water droplets with higher permittivity are drawn into the high-field region and form a conducting bridge; thus breakdown is controlled by contamination, not by the molecular process. Also: **thermal** and **electromechanical** processes.
**Factors**: moisture (dissolved + free), dissolved gases, particles, electrode shape/area, gap spacing, temperature, pressure, oil ageing, voltage waveform. **Oil test**: IEC-type cup with 2.5 mm gap and spherical/VDE electrodes, 6 tests, ramp 2 kV/s; in-service oil typically needs ≥ 30 kV (limits depend on voltage class and standard); new processed oil typically 50–70 kV or more.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Six breakdown readings (kV): 42, 45, 40, 44, 43, 46. Mean = 260/6 = **43.3 kV**; standard deviation ≈ 2.2 kV. Acceptable for 33 kV-class transformers (limit ≥ 30 kV).

**Example 2.** A water droplet (ε_r = 80) in oil (ε_r = 2.2) is polarised more strongly than the oil, so the force F ∝ ∇E² pulls it toward the high-field region between the electrodes, where droplets align into a bridge.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Believing pure oil is the usual case: service oil always has particles.
- Testing without stirring/resting time between breakdowns.
- Using a different gap or electrode shape from the standard.

steps.title: Practice
steps.body: Degassing and filtering (vacuum dehydration) restore strength; silica-gel breathers keep new moisture out.

activity.prompt: Six oil breakdown readings: 42, 45, 40, 44, 43, 46 kV. Mean BDV?

lessons.title: Breakdown of solid dielectrics: intrinsic, thermal, electromechanical, treeing

story.title: A cable that failed after 11 years

scenes.text: An XLPE cable failed with a tiny tree-shaped channel.
Electrical treeing grew from a void over years under normal stress.

steps.title: Mechanisms
steps.body:
- **Intrinsic (electronic)**: electron avalanche in the solid at very high stress (≈ 10⁷–10⁹ V/m), time ~ 10⁻⁸ s; relevant only for pure materials in short impulses.
- **Electromechanical**: Maxwell stress compresses the specimen; breakdown when E = 0.6√(Y/ε₀ε_r) (Y = Young's modulus) (Stark–Garton).
- **Thermal**: dielectric loss heat exceeds heat dissipated; **W = ω ε₀ ε_r tan δ E²** (W/m³, E rms). Breakdown field falls with temperature.
- **Partial discharge/erosion** in internal voids, **treeing** (electrical, water, electro-chemical), surface tracking and flashover.
Breakdown strength depends on thickness (thin films stronger), time of stressing (V–t life curve: **V^n t = const**, n ≈ 9–12 for polymers), temperature, frequency and ageing.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Heat generation: ε_r = 4, tan δ = 0.02, f = 50 Hz, E = 5 MV/m (rms): W = 2π × 50 × 8.854 × 10⁻¹² × 4 × 0.02 × (5 × 10⁶)² = **5563 W/m³**. This is small, so thermal breakdown is unlikely unless tan δ rises with temperature.

**Example 2.** Life law V^n t = const, n = 10: if the stress is raised 10 % (× 1.1), life falls by factor 1.1¹⁰ = **2.59**; the cable would last only 39 % as long.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using breakdown strength of thin lab film for thick insulation.
- Ignoring V–t characteristics.
- Treating treeing as only a high-voltage phenomenon: water trees occur at normal stress in wet conditions.

lessons.title: Lab: Composite dielectrics, cavity breakdown and partial discharge inception

scenes.text: A 0.5 mm gas gap sits in the epoxy of a bushing.
Most of the voltage drops across the air layer, which is the weakest part.

steps.title: Composite dielectrics
steps.body: For layers in series with permittivities ε₁, ε₂ and thicknesses d₁, d₂: **E₁/E₂ = ε₂/ε₁** and **E₁ = V ε₂/(ε₂ d₁ + ε₁ d₂)** (field in layer 1). A gas void (ε_r ≈ 1) in solid (ε_r = 4) therefore carries a field 4 times higher (for a flat void normal to the field); since air breakdown (≈ 3 kV/mm) is lower than the solid's, the void discharges first = **partial discharge (PD)**, which erodes the solid and drives treeing. The PD inception voltage ≈ V_b,void/ε_r (approx.).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Series: air film 0.5 mm (ε_r = 1) + solid 5 mm (ε_r = 4); V = 10 kV peak: E_air = 10 × 4/(4 × 0.5 + 1 × 5) = 40/7 = **5.71 kV/mm** (> 3 kV/mm ⇒ discharge); E_solid = 10 × 1/7 = **1.43 kV/mm**. Check: 5.71 × 0.5 + 1.43 × 5 = 10 ✔.

**Example 2.** Void in solid with ε_r = 4: PD starts when the field in the void reaches 3 kV/mm ⇒ the stress in the solid is about 3/4 = **0.75 kV/mm** — far below the solid's strength, yet harmful over time.

**Example 3.** Remedy: impregnation with oil/resin under vacuum removes voids; semiconducting layers grade the field.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying E₁/E₂ = ε₁/ε₂ (inverted).
- Forgetting that the void's breakdown depends on its size (Paschen).
- Believing PD is harmless below the solid's strength.

lessons.title: Lab: Cable stress and capacitance/intersheath grading

story.title: Why a single-core cable has a 'graded' insulation

scenes.text: The field in a cable is highest at the core, so the core limits the voltage rating.
Grading spreads the stress more evenly.

steps.title: Stress distribution
steps.body: Single-core cable (core radius r, sheath radius R): field at radius x: **E(x) = V/(x ln(R/r))**; maximum at the core: **E_max = V/(r ln(R/r))**; minimum at sheath. For a given R, E_max is minimum when **R/r = e = 2.718**. **Capacitance grading** uses layers of different permittivity (high ε near the core) to equalise E_max in each; **intersheath grading** inserts concentric metallic sheaths at intermediate potentials (with leakage current and loss concerns). With **two layers**: E_max1 = E_max2 gives ε₁ r₁ = ε₂ r₂.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** V = 100 kV (peak), r = 1 cm, R = 4 cm: E_max = 100/(1 × ln 4) = 100/1.386 = **72.1 kV/cm**. For R = 2.718 cm: E_max = 100/1 = 100 kV/cm. Larger R reduces stress but costs more material.

**Example 2.** With the permitted E_max = 50 kV/cm and V = 100 kV peak, need r ln(R/r) = 2 cm; if r = 1.5 cm ⇒ ln(R/r) = 1.333 ⇒ R/r = 3.79 ⇒ R = **5.69 cm**.

**Example 3.** Two-layer grading: inner layer ε₁ = 4, outer ε₂ = 2 and r₁ = 1 cm: equal E_max requires ε₁ r₁ = ε₂ r₂ ⇒ r₂ = 2 cm (boundary radius).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using rms for the stress limit (use peak with peak strength).
- Using diameters in place of radii.
- Forgetting that the 'optimum' R/r = e minimises E_max for a given R only.

steps.title: Method
steps.body: Collect clues: location (joint or run), age, environment, loading, test history. **Water trees** (wet, moderate E, long life) vs **electrical trees** (voids, impurities, higher stress, PD) vs **thermal** (high loading, high ambient) vs **mechanical** (damage). Tests: PD, tan δ, IR/polarisation index, VLF withstand.

steps.title: Case
steps.body:
Failure at a joint with moisture ingress; tan δ trend over 2 years climbed from 0.001 to 0.01; PD at 1.5 U₀ of 800 pC. Diagnosis: poorly sealed joint ⇒ water treeing/PD ⇒ breakdown. Corrective: replace joint, improve sealing and drainage, test neighbouring cables by VLF tan δ.
**Numbers**: U₀ = 11/√3 = 6.35 kV; test at 1.5 U₀ = 9.5 kV rms.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Replacing only the failed section and ignoring the cause.
- Ignoring trending of tan δ.

lessons.title: Power-frequency high voltage: testing transformer, cascade and resonant circuits

scenes.text: A 400 kV bushing must withstand about 630 kV rms in the factory test.
One transformer cannot insulate that — engineers stack them in cascade.

steps.title: Test transformers
steps.body:
**Single transformer**: HV winding insulated in a column; output limited to ~ 300–400 kV by insulation and size. **Cascade**: stages with the low-voltage primary of stage 2 fed from a tertiary winding of stage 1; stage 2 tank is raised to the stage-1 HV potential; **output ≈ n × V₁**; the first stage carries the most load (for a 3-stage set the stage ratings are in the ratio 3 : 2 : 1 of the unit kVA). Short-circuit voltage is high (~ 5–10 %) so a capacitive load causes a Ferranti-type voltage rise.
**Resonant test sets**: series resonance with a variable reactor L and a capacitive load C (cable, GIS): f = 1/(2π√(LC)); the **Q-factor** amplifies: V_out = Q V_in; the source supplies only losses (kVA_source = kVA_test/Q). Ideal for GIS and cables (frequency-tuned 20–300 Hz); **Tesla coil** for high-frequency high voltage.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Series resonance: capacitive load 0.5 µF at 50 Hz: L = 1/(ω²C) = 1/(314.16² × 0.5 × 10⁻⁶) = **20.26 H**.

**Example 2.** Q = 50, input 10 kV ⇒ output **500 kV**. Test current I = ωCV = 314.16 × 0.5 × 10⁻⁶ × 500 × 10³ = **78.5 A**; test kVA = 500 × 78.5 = 39 270 kVA; source kVA = 39 270/50 = **785 kVA**.

**Example 3.** 3-stage cascade of 100 kV units: output 300 kV (rms); the first stage carries three times the stage-3 kVA.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting that cascade stages carry unequal kVA.
- Using resonance with a load that has stray inductance without checking Q.
- Ignoring the harmonic content of the source (the test wave should be sinusoidal, crest factor √2 ± 5 %).

lessons.title: Lab: DC high voltage — rectifier and Cockcroft–Walton multiplier

story.title: Making 500 kV from a 50 kV transformer

scenes.text: A table-top voltage multiplier builds up hundreds of kV from a modest transformer.
Each stage is a diode pair and two capacitors.

steps.title: Cockcroft–Walton
steps.body: An n-stage voltage multiplier gives ideal no-load output **V₀ = 2 n V_m** (V_m = peak of transformer secondary). With load current I at frequency f and stage capacitance C: **voltage drop ΔV = (I/fC)(2n³/3 + n²/2 − n/6)** and **ripple (p–p) δV = (I/fC)·n(n + 1)/2**. Hence, for good regulation, use large C, high f, few stages. Optimum number of stages for maximum output: n_opt = √(V_m f C/I). Other DC sources: half-wave/full-wave rectifier (ripple factor = I/(2fCV)), Van de Graaff generators, electrostatic generators. Applications: X-ray, electrostatic precipitators, HVDC testing, particle accelerators, cable DC tests.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** n = 5, V_m = 50 kV: V₀ = 2 × 5 × 50 = **500 kV**. I = 5 mA, f = 50 Hz, C = 0.1 µF ⇒ I/(fC) = 5×10⁻³/(50 × 10⁻⁷) = 1000 V. ΔV = 1000 × (2 × 125/3 + 25/2 − 5/6) = 1000 × (83.33 + 12.5 − 0.83) = **95 kV**; ripple = 1000 × 15 = **15 kV p–p**. Output at load ≈ 500 − 95 = **405 kV**.

**Example 2.** Raising f to 500 Hz reduces ΔV and ripple ten times: ΔV = 9.5 kV, ripple 1.5 kV.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Taking the first-stage ripple formula for all n.
- Using rms instead of peak V_m.
- Ignoring that the regulation worsens as n³.

lessons.title: Lab: Impulse voltage — standard waves and Marx generator

scenes.text: A 10-stage Marx generator charges capacitors in parallel and discharges them in series.
The standard lightning wave rises in 1.2 µs and decays to half in 50 µs.

steps.title: Impulse generation
steps.body: **Standard lightning impulse 1.2/50 µs** (front time T₁ = 1.2 µs ± 30 %, time to half-value T₂ = 50 µs ± 20 %); **switching impulse 250/2500 µs**. Waveform: v(t) = V₀(e^(−αt) − e^(−βt)). **Marx generator**: n capacitors C charged in parallel to V through resistors, then spark gaps fire in series ⇒ erected voltage n V; generator capacitance C_s = C/n. Energy W = ½ C_s (nV)² = ½ n C V². **Wave shaping** (simple circuit): front resistance R₁ with C₁ (generator) and C₂ (load) ⇒ **T_f ≈ 3 R₁ C₁C₂/(C₁ + C₂)**, **T_t ≈ 0.7 (R₁ + R₂)(C₁ + C₂)**. Utilisation efficiency η = V_peak/(nV) ≈ 0.85–0.95. Tail-chopped waves are used for transformer tests.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 10 stages, 100 kV per stage, C = 0.5 µF per stage: erected 1000 kV; C_s = 0.05 µF; energy = ½ × 5 × 10⁻⁸ × (10⁶)² = **25 kJ**.

**Example 2.** Design: C₁ = 25 nF, C₂ = 1 nF ⇒ series C = 0.9615 nF; R₁ = T_f/(3 × 0.9615 nF) = 1.2 µs/(2.885 nF) = **416 Ω**; R₁ + R₂ = 50 µs/(0.7 × 26 nF) = 2747 Ω ⇒ **R₂ = 2331 Ω**.

**Example 3.** Peak voltage with η = 0.9: 1000 kV × 0.9 = 900 kV.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing charging voltage with the output (n V).
- Neglecting the lead inductance in the front-time estimate.
- Using the simplified tail formula for high-capacitance loads without checking.

activity.prompt: Marx generator: 10 stages, C = 0.5 µF per stage, 100 kV per stage. Stored energy in kJ?

steps.title: Impulse current and others
steps.body: **Impulse current generator**: a capacitor bank discharges through an R–L circuit; standard wave **8/20 µs** (arrester discharge), long **rectangular wave of about 2 ms** (line-discharge class), **4/10 µs high-current**. Peak currents 10–100 kA. **Switching surge generator**: Marx with a larger wave-shaping resistor, or a test transformer fed by capacitor discharge. **Tesla coil**: resonant transformer; **pulse transformers**. Transformers are tested with full-wave and chopped-wave impulses.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** A 20 µF capacitor charged to 25 kV stores W = ½ × 20 × 10⁻⁶ × (25 × 10³)² = **6.25 kJ**.

**Example 2.** Rule-of-thumb arrester energy: a 10 kA, 8/20 µs impulse with a 25 kV residual voltage dissipates roughly 25 kV × 10 kA × 20 µs ≈ **5 kJ** (order of magnitude).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing current and voltage wave notations.
- Ignoring inductance of the earth return.

scenes.text: A lab must test a 245 kV transformer with lightning impulse and AC withstand.

steps.title: Design workflow
steps.body: Required LI withstand: assume 1050 kV peak (245 kV class; check the standard tables). Marx stage voltage 100 kV, η = 0.9: n = 1050/(0.9 × 100) = 11.7 ⇒ **12 stages**. AC withstand (assume 460 kV rms): resonant set with winding capacitance C ≈ 3 nF at 50 Hz ⇒ L = 1/(ω²C) = 1/(314.16² × 3 × 10⁻⁹) = 3377 H (impractical) ⇒ use variable frequency (e.g., 200 Hz: L = 211 H) or compensating reactors.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: Stored energy: C_s per stage 0.5 µF/12 = 41.7 nF: W = ½ × 41.7 × 10⁻⁹ × (1.2 × 10⁶)² = **30 kJ**. Resonant test current at 460 kV and 200 Hz with 3 nF: I = ωCV = 1256.6 × 3 × 10⁻⁹ × 460 × 10³ = **1.73 A**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Neglecting utilisation factor η.
- Choosing 50 Hz resonance with tiny C (reactor too large).

lessons.title: Sphere gaps and electrostatic voltmeters

scenes.text: Two polished 25 cm metal spheres in a gap give the most trusted peak voltage reading in a HV lab.
But weather changes the answer, so a correction is needed.

steps.title: Sphere gap
steps.body:
A sphere gap measures **peak** voltage of AC, DC and impulse (accuracy ± 3 % for gap ≤ 0.5 D, D = sphere diameter). Standard tables (IEC 60052) give breakdown voltage for sphere diameters 2–200 cm at 20 °C, 760 mmHg. **Air density correction**: V = δ·V_table with **δ = 0.386 p/(273 + t)** (p in mmHg, t in °C); for large gaps use a humidity correction too. Precautions: spheres polished and dust-free, series damping resistor (100–1000 kΩ) to limit current and avoid pitting, clearance from earthed objects ≥ 2 D, and 5 breakdowns average. Limit: gap spacing ≤ D/2 ensures nearly uniform field; for d > 0.5 D accuracy drops.
**Electrostatic voltmeter**: attracted-disc type; force F = ½ ε₀ A (V/d)² ⇒ reads rms (or DC) with deflection ∝ V²; draws negligible current (high impedance, capacitance ~ 10–100 pF); used up to 600 kV with enclosures; frequency independent.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Table value 150 kV (peak) at standard air; p = 740 mmHg, t = 35 °C: δ = 0.386 × 740/308 = 0.927 ⇒ actual breakdown = 150 × 0.927 = **139.1 kV**. So if a lab shows a gap breaking at 139.1 kV in those conditions, it is equivalent to 150 kV at standard conditions: V_standard = V_meas/δ.

**Example 2.** Electrostatic voltmeter: A = 10 cm², d = 1 cm, V = 20 kV rms: F = ½ × 8.854 × 10⁻¹² × 10⁻³ × (2 × 10⁶)² (using V/d = 20 × 10³/10⁻² = 2 × 10⁶ V/m) = ½ × 8.854e-15 × 4e12 = **0.0177 N** (rms-based mean force).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using rms values with a peak-reading sphere gap table.
- Forgetting δ correction at altitude.
- Using gap/diameter ratio above 0.5.

steps.title: Practice
steps.body: Always take the average of at least three consecutive breakdowns at the same setting, with 1-min intervals.

activity.prompt: Sphere gap calibrated at 150 kV (standard conditions). Ambient p = 740 mmHg, t = 35 °C. The breakdown voltage in these conditions in kV?

lessons.title: Lab: Voltage dividers — resistive, capacitive and Chubb–Fortescue

scenes.text: A divider must turn kilovolts into a safe signal without distorting the wave.
Stray capacitance and inductance cause the errors.

steps.title: Dividers and rectifier methods
steps.body: **Resistive divider**: ratio (R₁ + R₂)/R₂; used for DC and AC at low frequency; problems: power dissipation (limit current ~ 1 mA ⇒ R₁ large), stray capacitance (response time ≈ RC/6 for distributed C), loading. **Capacitive divider**: ratio (C₁ + C₂)/C₁ with C₁ (HV, small) and C₂ (LV, large); no heating, good for AC and impulse; compressed-gas capacitors (stable, loss free). **Damped capacitive/RC dividers** for impulses give flat response. **Chubb–Fortescue method**: the current through a capacitor C is rectified; average current I_av = 2 f C V_m ⇒ **V_m = I_av/(2fC)**; peak voltage; includes frequency and waveform. **Potential transformer/CVT** for ≤ 400 kV AC; **generating voltmeter** for DC and AC with no direct connection (induced current from a rotating vane).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** R₁ = 100 MΩ, R₂ = 100 kΩ: ratio = (100 + 0.1)/0.1 = **1001**; 500 kV ⇒ 499.5 V at the output; current = 500 kV/100.1 MΩ = **4.99 mA** (power 2.5 kW!). So resistive dividers are limited to ~ 100–300 kV.

**Example 2.** C₁ = 100 pF, C₂ = 0.1 µF = 100 000 pF: ratio = (100 + 100 000)/100 = **1001**.

**Example 3.** Chubb–Fortescue: C = 100 pF, f = 50 Hz, I_av = 1 mA: V_m = 10⁻³/(2 × 50 × 10⁻¹⁰) = **100 kV** peak.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using a resistive divider on impulses without compensation.
- Forgetting that the LV arm (C₂) is large to give small ratio but also has to withstand test surges.
- Not placing a matching resistor in coaxial cable measurement.

lessons.title: Lab: Impulse measurement — CRO, shunts, Rogowski coils and peak voltmeters

scenes.text: The impulse is gone in 50 µs, so a digital recorder captures it.
Coaxial cable and divider must match to avoid ringing.

steps.title: Measuring fast transients
steps.body:
**Impulse voltage**: damped capacitor divider + coaxial cable terminated with its surge impedance + digital impulse recorder (≥ 100 MS/s, 8–12 bit, high bandwidth); peak voltmeters (diode–capacitor with discharge resistor) for peak. **Impulse current**: **shunt** (coaxial low-inductance resistor): V = I R (R in mΩ); **Rogowski coil** (air-cored coil around conductor): output **v = M di/dt**, integrated electronically; **magnetic links**; **Hall-effect probes**. **CRO**: deflection sensitivity; a trigger delay since the wave front can be too fast; sampling rate ≥ 10 × bandwidth.
**Wave parameters**: front time T₁ = 1.67 × (t₉₀ − t₃₀) for lightning impulse; time to half-value T₂; peak overshoot allowed ≤ 5 %.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Shunt: R = 10 mΩ, impulse current 10 kA ⇒ V = 100 V (need an attenuator before the recorder).

**Example 2.** Rogowski: M = 1 µH; current rises 10 kA in 8 µs ⇒ di/dt = 1.25 × 10⁹ A/s ⇒ v = 10⁻⁶ × 1.25 × 10⁹ = **1250 V** before integration.

**Example 3.** Lightning impulse from t₃₀ = 0.30 µs and t₉₀ = 1.00 µs: T₁ = 1.67 × 0.70 = **1.17 µs** (within 1.2 ± 30 %).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using 10–90 % rise instead of 1.67 × (t₉₀ − t₃₀).
- Ignoring cable reflections and ground loops.
- Forgetting calibration of the full measuring system.

lessons.title: Lab: Schering bridge, insulation resistance and polarisation index

scenes.text: A bushing's tan δ at 10 kV is measured with a Schering bridge.
A rising tan δ trend warns of moisture or ageing.

steps.title: Dielectric loss measurement
steps.body: **Schering bridge**: C_N (standard, gas-filled, loss-free) and C_x with loss resistance r_x; balance: **C_x = C_N R₄/R₃**; **tan δ = ω C₄ R₄** (C₄ variable, R₃ variable). The HV side is shielded (Wagner earthing) to remove stray effects; safe LV arms. **Dielectric loss** P = V² ω C_x tan δ. Typical new transformer bushings: tan δ < 0.5 % (0.005). **Insulation resistance** (megger, 1–5 kV DC): **polarisation index PI = R(10 min)/R(1 min)**; PI < 1 danger, 1–2 questionable, 2–4 good (> 4 very good); also DAR = R(60 s)/R(30 s). **Capacitance and tan δ trending** by frequency-domain spectroscopy (FDS) and return voltage methods.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the wrong arm for R₄ in the tan δ formula.
- Testing a hot or wet specimen without temperature correction.
- Interpreting a PI without considering temperature and surface leakage.

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone — partial discharge measurement and NDT

story.title: The PD test on a 33 kV transformer

scenes.text: During the test the PD detector shows 500 pC at 1.5 U_m/√3; the limit is 300 pC.
The team must identify, locate and decide.

steps.title: PD and NDT
steps.body: **Partial discharge** is a localised breakdown of part of the insulation. **Apparent charge** q = ΔV·(C_a + C_b) ≈ ΔV·C_k (pC) measured by a coupling capacitor and detector per IEC 60270; PD inception voltage (PDIV) and extinction voltage (PDEV). Equivalent void model: C_c (void), C_b (series), C_a (rest). Detection: electrical, acoustic (ultrasonic), UHF (GIS), optical, DGA (gas). Factory acceptance PD limit for a transformer is typically 100–500 pC at the specified level (standard-dependent). **NDT of insulation**: DGA, FRA, SFRA, tan δ, IR/PI, return voltage, thermography, ultrasound. **Pattern**: phase-resolved PD (PRPD) differentiates voids, corona, surface discharge.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** C_a = 500 pF; detector reading ΔV = 10 mV ⇒ q = 500 × 10⁻¹² × 10 × 10⁻³ = 5 × 10⁻¹² C = **5 pC**.

**Example 2.** PD at 500 pC > 300 pC limit ⇒ fail: locate by acoustic sensors on the tank, then inspect/dry-out/re-impregnate.

**Example 3.** Test voltage: phase voltage for a 36 kV max system, 1.5 U_m/√3 = 1.5 × 36/1.732 = **31.2 kV**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calibrating the PD detector after the test instead of before.
- Ignoring external corona from the test circuit.
- Judging PD by magnitude alone, without pattern or location.

lessons.title: Lightning phenomenon, stroke parameters and shielding

story.title: The tower that was struck twice

scenes.text: A 220 kV line trips repeatedly at the same tower during the monsoon.
The stroke current and footing resistance decide whether the insulator flashes over.

steps.title: Lightning
steps.body:
Charge separation in cumulonimbus clouds (ice/graupel collisions) produces a cloud base potential of 10–100 MV; a **stepped leader** descends, an **attachment** forms and a **return stroke** carries a high current. Typical parameters: median first-stroke peak current ≈ 30 kA (range 3–200 kA), front time 2–5 µs (steepness 20–40 kA/µs), time to half value 50–75 µs; about 20–25 % of flashes have multiple strokes; negative flashes ≈ 90 %. Keraunic level (thunder-days/year); ground flash density N_g ≈ 0.04 T_d^1.25 per km²/year.
**Effects on lines**: direct strike to phase conductor (V = I Z/2); strike to tower/ground wire (**back-flashover** when I R + L di/dt exceeds insulator withstand); **induced voltages** from nearby strokes (usually < 300 kV, important for distribution lines). **Protection**: overhead ground (shield) wires with shielding angle ≈ 20–30°, low tower-footing resistance (< 10 Ω), counterpoise, line arresters, rods, Franklin rods/mast for substations.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Direct stroke 30 kA to a phase conductor with Z = 400 Ω: current splits in the two directions, so V = I Z/2 = 30 × 400/2 = **6000 kV**, far above any insulator ⇒ flashover.

**Example 2.** Back-flashover: tower footing R = 10 Ω, I = 30 kA ⇒ resistive rise 300 kV (plus inductive part) — if the insulator string withstand is ≈ 1000 kV the line survives for I up to about 100 kA at 10 Ω (ignoring L di/dt), but with 50 Ω footing the limit falls to 20 kA.

**Example 3.** Thunder days T_d = 40: N_g = 0.04 × 40^1.25 = 0.04 × 100.6 = **4.0 flashes/km²/yr**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the factor ½ when the stroke current splits.
- Ignoring tower inductance on fast fronts.
- Specifying shielding by angle alone on EHV lines without checking with an electro-geometric model.

lessons.title: Lab: Travelling waves — reflection, transmission and Bewley lattice

scenes.text: A 100 kV surge on an overhead line reaches a cable junction.
Part is reflected, part transmitted — the numbers follow from the surge impedances.

steps.title: Wave equations
steps.body: For a lossless line: **surge impedance Z = √(L/C)**; **velocity v = 1/√(LC)**. Overhead line: Z ≈ 300–500 Ω, v ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s; cable: Z ≈ 30–50 Ω, v ≈ 1.5–2 × 10⁸ m/s. At a junction Z₁ → Z₂: **transmission coefficient τ = 2Z₂/(Z₁ + Z₂)**, **reflection coefficient ρ = (Z₂ − Z₁)/(Z₁ + Z₂)**, τ = 1 + ρ. Termination: open end (Z₂ = ∞) ρ = +1 (voltage doubles); short circuit ρ = −1; matched ρ = 0. **Bewley lattice diagram** tracks multiple reflections: each reflection at the sending end uses ρ_s, at the receiving end ρ_r. Through a lumped shunt capacitor C: wave front is slowed (time constant Z C/2), through series inductor L is steepness reduced.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Z₁ = 400 Ω (line), Z₂ = 50 Ω (cable), V = 100 kV: τ = 100/450 = 0.2222 ⇒ transmitted = **22.2 kV**; ρ = (50 − 400)/450 = −0.7778 ⇒ reflected = **−77.8 kV**. Check: 100 − 77.8 = 22.2 ✔.

**Example 2.** Open end: ρ = 1 ⇒ 100 kV incident reflects 100 kV ⇒ total 200 kV at the open end (the reason transformer terminals see doubled surges).

**Example 3.** Line L = 1.3 mH/km, C = 8.8 nF/km: Z = √(1.3 × 10⁻³/8.8 × 10⁻⁹) = **384 Ω**; v = 1/√(LC) = **2.96 × 10⁵ km/s**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using ρ with wrong order (Z₁ − Z₂).
- Forgetting that transmitted wave in the cable also reaches the cable end and reflects.
- Forgetting velocity differences in cable and overhead sections.

activity.prompt: Line Z1 = 400 Ω meets cable Z2 = 50 Ω. A 100 kV surge arrives. Transmitted voltage in kV (1 decimal)?

lessons.title: Lab: Switching overvoltages, TOV and surge arresters

scenes.text: Closing a breaker on an unloaded long line produces a switching surge of 2–3 pu.
A ZnO arrester clamps it.

steps.title: Overvoltages
steps.body:
Classification (IEC 60071): continuous power-frequency voltage; **temporary overvoltages (TOV)** (earth-fault: 1.3–1.7 pu in effectively earthed systems, load rejection, resonance, ferroresonance; seconds); **slow-front (switching)** overvoltages (energisation, reclosing, fault clearing, capacitor switching; typically 1.5–3 pu at EHV, limited by pre-insertion resistors, controlled switching and arresters); **fast-front (lightning)**; very-fast-front (GIS disconnector). 1 pu = U_m √2/√3.
**Surge arrester**: metal-oxide (ZnO) gapless, highly non-linear V–I (I = kV^α, α ≈ 25–50), no follow current; ratings: **rated voltage U_r** (TOV capability, 10 s), **MCOV** (continuous operating voltage), nominal discharge current (5, 10, 20 kA), residual (protective) voltage at that current, line discharge class, energy capability (kJ/kV). Selection: U_r ≥ k_e U_m/√3 (k_e = earth-fault factor, 1.4 for non-effectively earthed).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** U_m = 245 kV: 1 pu = 245 × √2/√3 = **200.0 kV** peak; a 2.5 pu switching surge = **500 kV**.

**Example 2.** Earth-fault factor 1.4: TOV = 1.4 × 245/√3 = **198 kV rms**: choose arrester U_r ≥ 198 kV (the standard 198 kV rating exists).

**Example 3.** Protective ratio/ margin: BIL 1050 kV, arrester residual 500 kV ⇒ margin = 1050/500 − 1 = **110 %** (before separation correction).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using U_r equal to the phase voltage (arrester would fail on TOV).
- Forgetting that arresters limit but cannot remove overvoltage.
- Confusing MCOV with rated voltage.

activity.prompt: 245 kV (U_m) system: peak phase-to-earth voltage (1 pu) in kV?

lessons.title: Lab: Insulation coordination — BIL, margins and arrester placement

story.title: Will the arrester protect the transformer 20 m away?

scenes.text: The arrester clamps at 500 kV at its terminals, but the transformer is 20 m away.
Reflections add voltage at the transformer: the separation effect.

steps.title: Concept
steps.body: **Insulation coordination** selects insulation strength (BIL — basic lightning impulse insulation level; BSL — switching impulse level) of equipment relative to expected overvoltages and arrester characteristics, with acceptable risk. Standard LI withstand (examples, IEC): 12 kV → 75 kV; 36 kV → 170 kV; 145 kV → 650 kV; 245 kV → 950/1050 kV. **Protective margin = (BIL/V_protective − 1) × 100 %** ; recommended ≥ 20 % (≥ 15 % for switching). **Separation effect**: voltage at equipment **V_eq = V_arr + 2 S l/v** (S = incoming surge steepness in kV/µs, l = arrester–equipment distance, v = wave velocity ≈ 300 m/µs). **Statistical coordination**: risk of failure for a given overvoltage distribution and insulation strength distribution.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** V_arr = 500 kV, S = 1000 kV/µs, l = 20 m: 2 × 1000 × 20/300 = 133.3 kV ⇒ V_eq = **633.3 kV**; margin = 1050/633.3 − 1 = **65.8 %** ✔.

**Example 2.** At l = 80 m: rise 533 kV ⇒ V_eq = 1033 kV ⇒ margin 1.6 % ✘ (fails the 20 % rule). Arrester must be moved closer or a second arrester added.

**Example 3.** Maximum permissible distance for a 20 % margin: V_eq ≤ 1050/1.2 = 875 kV ⇒ 2 S l/v ≤ 375 ⇒ l ≤ 375 × 300/2000 = **56.25 m**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Ignoring the separation distance (including lead length of the arrester).
- Applying 50 Hz ratings to impulse levels.
- Forgetting altitude correction for external insulation.

activity.prompt: V_arr = 500 kV, surge steepness 1000 kV/µs, distance 20 m, v = 300 m/µs. Transformer voltage V_eq in kV (1 decimal)?

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone — protect a 132/33 kV substation

scenes.text: A utility audits a 132/33 kV substation after a transformer bushing failure.
The audit must check shielding, grounding and arrester placement.

steps.title: Audit method
steps.body: 1. Determine the lightning and switching levels (BIL 650 kV for 145 kV class). 2. Select arresters: U_m = 145 kV, k_e = 1.4 ⇒ U_r ≥ 1.4 × 145/√3 = 117 kV ⇒ choose 120 kV; residual voltage at 10 kA ≈ 300 kV (typical). 3. Compute the margin including separation: S = 1000 kV/µs, l = 15 m: ΔV = 100 kV ⇒ V_eq = 400 kV ⇒ margin = 650/400 − 1 = 62.5 %. 4. Verify shielding by masts/shield wires; earth-grid resistance (< 1 Ω for large substations), step/touch potentials. 5. Add line entrance arresters and shield the last 1–2 km of line (good footing resistance).

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: Required Ur: 1.4 × 145/√3 = 117.2 kV ⇒ 120 kV. If l increased to 50 m: ΔV = 2 × 1000 × 50/300 = 333 kV ⇒ V_eq = 633 kV ⇒ margin = 650/633 − 1 = **2.7 %** ✘. Remedy: second arrester at the transformer terminal.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Overlooking grounding resistance.
- Using the arrester's rated voltage as the protective level.
- Not protecting both ends of an open breaker.

lessons.title: Formula and key-point sheet

story.title: The night before the HV exam

scenes.text: A single sheet with every formula in High Voltage Engineering.
Grouped by unit for quick revision.

steps.title: Breakdown
steps.body:
- Townsend: I = I₀e^(αd)/[1 − γ(e^(αd) − 1)]; breakdown γ(e^(αd) − 1) = 1.
- Paschen: V_b = f(pd); air min ≈ 300–330 V; uniform air ≈ 30 kV/cm peak; SF₆ ≈ 2.5 × air.
- Streamer: αx ≈ 18–20. Impulse ratio = V_imp/V_ac,peak.
- Peek: V_c = 21.1 m δ r ln(D/r) kV (rms phase); P = (241/δ)(f + 25)√(r/D)(V − V_c)² × 10⁻⁵ kW/km/phase; δ = 0.386p/(273 + t).
- Composite dielectric: E₁/E₂ = ε₂/ε₁; E₁ = Vε₂/(ε₂d₁ + ε₁d₂).
- Cable: E_max = V/(r ln(R/r)); optimum R/r = e. Thermal: W = ωε₀ε_r tanδ E². Life V^n t = const.

steps.title: Generation and measurement
steps.body:
- Cascade: n V₁. Resonance: L = 1/(ω²C); V = QV_in; kVA_source = kVA_test/Q.
- CW: V₀ = 2nV_m; ΔV = (I/fC)(2n³/3 + n²/2 − n/6); ripple = (I/fC)n(n + 1)/2.
- Marx: V = nV; C_s = C/n; W = ½C_sV². T_f ≈ 3R₁C₁C₂/(C₁ + C₂); T_t ≈ 0.7(R₁ + R₂)(C₁ + C₂). LI 1.2/50 µs; SI 250/2500 µs; current 8/20 µs.
- Sphere gap: V = δ V_table; Divider ratio resistive (R₁ + R₂)/R₂; capacitive (C₁ + C₂)/C₁; Chubb–Fortescue V_m = I_av/(2fC).
- Schering: C_x = C_N R₄/R₃; tan δ = ωC₄R₄; PI = R₁₀/R₁. Rogowski v = M di/dt. T₁ = 1.67(t₉₀ − t₃₀).

steps.title: Overvoltage
steps.body:
- Z = √(L/C); v = 1/√(LC); τ = 2Z₂/(Z₁ + Z₂); ρ = (Z₂ − Z₁)/(Z₁ + Z₂). Open end ρ = 1, short −1.
- Stroke V = IZ/2; N_g = 0.04T_d^1.25.
- 1 pu = U_m√2/√3; TOV = k_e U_m/√3.
- Margin = BIL/V_p − 1 ≥ 20 %; V_eq = V_arr + 2Sl/v.

lessons.title: Lab: Breakdown voltage of transformer oil

scenes.text: A technician draws a sample from the transformer drain valve.
The test set raises voltage at 2 kV/s until the oil sparks over.

steps.title: Aim, apparatus and procedure
steps.body: **Aim**: to find the dielectric strength (breakdown voltage, BDV) of transformer oil. **Apparatus**: oil test set (0–60/100 kV AC, 50 Hz) with test cell having two polished spherical or VDE electrodes, **2.5 mm gap**, transparent cup (~ 400 ml), gap gauge, sample bottle. **Procedure**: clean the cell with dry lint-free cloth, set 2.5 mm gap, fill with the oil sample without bubbles, wait 5 min, raise voltage steadily (2 kV/s) until breakdown, note kV, stir gently and wait 2 min; repeat six times; average the last 5 (discard the first, per many methods).

steps.title: Observation and calculation
steps.body:
| Test | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| BDV (kV) | 38 | 42 | 41 | 44 | 40 | 43 |
Mean of tests 2–6 = (42 + 41 + 44 + 40 + 43)/5 = **42.0 kV**. BDV ≥ 30 kV ⇒ oil acceptable for service in a 33 kV-class transformer (limits depend on the standard and class). Dielectric strength = 42 kV/2.5 mm = **16.8 kV/mm** (rms).

steps.title: Precautions
steps.body:
- Avoid bubbles and moisture pick-up while sampling.
- Do not touch the electrodes; clean after each test.
- Keep the area clear and use the safety interlock.

Stir gently, rest 2 minutes and repeat six times
Average the readings and compare with the limit

lessons.title: Lab: Sphere-gap calibration and impulse generator wave shaping

scenes.text: The sphere gap is used to calibrate a divider.
A small Marx generator is tuned for the 1.2/50 µs wave.

steps.title: Aim and procedure
steps.body: **Aim**: calibrate a voltage measuring system against a standard sphere gap and observe impulse wave shapes. **Procedure**: (1) Set up 25 cm spheres, spacing 2 cm; record temperature and pressure and compute δ. (2) Raise AC voltage, note the divider reading at spark-over; repeat 3–5 times. (3) Compare with the standard table corrected by δ. (4) Impulse: charge the generator to 10 kV per stage; fire; record the wave on the digital recorder; adjust R₁ for front time and R₂ for tail time.

steps.title: Observations
steps.body:
Table peak value (25 cm spheres, 2 cm gap) ≈ 59 kV at standard conditions (as an example value; use the standard table). δ = 0.386 × 750/(273 + 30) = 0.955 ⇒ expected 56.4 kV. Divider reading (peak) 56.0 kV ⇒ error −0.7 % (acceptable < 3 %).
Impulse: C₁ = 25 nF, C₂ = 1 nF ⇒ choose R₁ = 416 Ω, R₂ = 2331 Ω for 1.2/50 µs.

steps.title: Precautions
steps.body:
- Use series resistor, ground the spheres via the damping resistor.
- Apply impulse only with all personnel behind barriers.
- Discharge capacitors with the grounding stick.

lessons.title: Lab: Schering bridge — tan δ of a bushing and viva

scenes.text: The examiner hands you a bushing sample and a bridge.
You must measure and explain.

steps.title: Aim and procedure
steps.body: **Aim**: measure capacitance and tan δ of a specimen with a Schering bridge. **Apparatus**: HV supply with test transformer, standard gas capacitor C_N, bridge arms R₃ (variable), R₄ (fixed 1000/π Ω type) with variable C₄, null detector (vibration galvanometer/ electronic null), guard/ground connections. **Procedure**: connect, energise at 10 kV (or specified), balance by adjusting R₃ then C₄, repeat; compute C_x and tan δ.

steps.title: Safety
steps.body: Always ground HV parts with the earth stick; keep the interlock; never touch the test object during voltage application.

items.q: Why is a gas-filled standard capacitor used?
items.a: It has negligible loss (tan δ ≈ 0) and a stable capacitance, so all loss in the bridge is attributed to the specimen.
It removes the effect of stray capacitances to earth which would otherwise affect the balance.

items.q: What does an increasing tan δ with voltage indicate?
items.a: Presence of partial discharge or ionisation in voids.

items.q: Why do we use impulse tests when AC tests are done?
items.a: Different stress phenomena: AC examines thermal/dielectric loss and PD; impulses examine fast-front surge withstand.
Streamer forms when the avalanche contains about 10⁸ electrons (αx ≈ 18–20).

scenes.text: A typical paper has derivations, a few numericals and one design problem.

steps.title: Typical question types (original style)
steps.body: 1. Derive Townsend's current growth equation and the breakdown criterion. 2. Explain the suspended particle theory. 3. A single-core cable of 1.2 cm core radius and 3.6 cm sheath radius operates at 150 kV peak: find E_max and the optimum R/r. 4. A 6-stage Cockcroft–Walton circuit: find output and ripple. 5. Design a Marx generator for 960 kV. 6. A 400 Ω line meets a 100 Ω cable: find reflected and transmitted waves. 7. Explain insulation coordination.

steps.title: Solved question
steps.body:
**Q.** Cable E_max: V = 150 kV, r = 1.2 cm, R = 3.6 cm. E_max = 150/(1.2 × ln 3) = 150/(1.2 × 1.0986) = **113.8 kV/cm**. If R is fixed at 3.6 cm, the best core radius is r = R/e = 1.324 cm, giving E_max = 150/1.324 = 113.3 kV/cm — only slightly below 113.8, so the given design is already near optimum.
**Q.** Waves: τ = 2 × 100/500 = 0.4 ⇒ 40 kV transmitted for 100 kV incident; ρ = (100 − 400)/500 = −0.6 ⇒ −60 kV reflected.

lessons.title: Power system structure, thermal and hydro stations

scenes.text: Coal burns in a boiler at a thermal station; steam spins a turbine coupled to an alternator generating at 11–25 kV.
A step-up transformer raises it to 220/400 kV for transmission; substations step it down to 11 kV and finally 415/230 V at your home.

steps.title: Structure
steps.body: A power system has four parts: **generation → transmission (132 kV and above) → sub-transmission (33/66 kV) → distribution (11 kV, 415/230 V)**. Thermal plants use the **Rankine cycle**: boiler, superheater, turbine, condenser, feed pump. Overall efficiency = (electrical output)/(heat input) = η_boiler × η_cycle × η_turbine × η_alternator, typically 30–40 %. Hydro power: **P = ρ g Q H η** (ρ = 1000 kg/m³, Q in m³/s, H = net head in m).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1 (thermal).** A station delivers 200 MW burning 90 t/h of coal of calorific value 20,000 kJ/kg. Heat input = 90,000 × 20,000 = 1.8×10⁹ kJ/h = 5×10⁵ kW = 500 MW. η = 200/500 = **40 %**.

**Example 2 (hydro).** Q = 20 m³/s, H = 100 m, η = 0.9. P = 1000 × 9.81 × 20 × 100 × 0.9 = 17.66×10⁶ W = **17.66 MW**.

**Example 3.** Energy in a reservoir: 5×10⁶ m³ at 80 m head, η = 0.85: E = ρgVHη = 1000×9.81×5×10⁶×80×0.85 = 3.335×10¹² J = **926 MWh**.

steps.title: Why hydro matters
steps.body: Hydro plants start in minutes, so they serve **peak load** and spinning reserve; thermal and nuclear plants have high start-up cost/time and serve **base load**. Pumped-storage plants pump water uphill at night and generate at peak.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using gross head instead of net head (after penstock losses).
- Mixing kW and MW, or using Q in litres/s.
- Forgetting that 1 kWh = 3600 kJ when converting heat input.

activity.prompt: Hydro plant: Q = 10 m³/s, net head 50 m, overall η = 0.85. Output in kW? (use g = 9.81)

quiz.q: Thermal power stations use which thermodynamic cycle?
quiz.why: Steam plants operate on the Rankine cycle (boiler–turbine–condenser–pump).
P = ρgQHη, so power rises with both flow and head.

quiz.q: Which plants usually serve the peak load?
quiz.why: Hydro units start quickly and follow load; nuclear and coal are base-load.

lessons.title: Nuclear, gas and renewable generation

scenes.text: A wind farm engineer estimates how much of the wind's kinetic energy a turbine can capture.
Meanwhile a PHWR reactor makes heat by fission of uranium.

steps.title: Key relations
steps.body: **Nuclear:** fission of one U-235 atom releases ≈ 200 MeV (3.2×10⁻¹¹ J). 1 kg of U-235 completely fissioned ≈ 8.2×10¹³ J ≈ 2.3×10⁷ kWh. Components: fuel, moderator, control rods, coolant, shielding. **Wind:** P = ½ ρ A v³ C_p, with Betz limit C_p ≤ 16/27 = 59.3 %. **Solar PV:** P = η × irradiance × area. **Gas turbine (Brayton) combined cycle** reaches 55–60 % efficiency by using exhaust heat in a steam cycle.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Rotor radius 40 m, v = 12 m/s, ρ = 1.2 kg/m³. A = π×40² = 5026.5 m². Wind power = 0.5×1.2×5026.5×12³ = 5.21 MW. With C_p = 0.4: **2.085 MW**.

**Example 2.** PV panel 1.6 m², 18 % efficiency, irradiance 1000 W/m²: P = 0.18×1000×1.6 = **288 W**.

**Example 3.** Power doubling wind speed: P ∝ v³ ⇒ 8 times.

steps.title: Exam tip
steps.body: Cube law and Betz limit are favourite one-mark questions. Note India's wind cut-in is about 3–4 m/s and rated about 12–15 m/s.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using diameter instead of radius in A = πr².
- Applying Betz limit on top of C_p (C_p already includes it).

lessons.title: Load curves and load factors

scenes.text: At 7 pm lights, TVs and cooking push the city demand to its daily peak.
The load dispatcher plots demand against time: the load curve.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- **Load curve:** demand vs time; area = energy. **Load-duration curve:** loads sorted in descending order.
- **Maximum demand (MD)**, **average load** = energy/time.
- **Demand factor** = MD / connected load.
- **Load factor** = average load / MD (≤ 1).
- **Diversity factor** = Σ individual MDs / simultaneous (group) MD (≥ 1).
- **Plant capacity factor** = actual energy / (installed capacity × time).
- **Plant use factor** = energy / (capacity × hours of operation).
- **Utilisation factor** = MD / installed capacity.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Energy 2400 MWh in 30 days (720 h), MD 5 MW. Average = 3.333 MW; **LF = 0.667**.

**Example 2.** Connected load 80 MW, MD 50 MW ⇒ demand factor 0.625.

**Example 3.** Four feeders with MDs summing to 120 MW, simultaneous MD 80 MW ⇒ diversity factor 1.5.

**Example 4.** 60 MW plant generates 210 GWh/yr: capacity factor = 210/(60×8.76) = 210/525.6 = **0.40**.

steps.title: Why higher LF is good
steps.body: Higher load factor spreads fixed charges over more kWh, so cost per unit falls. Higher diversity factor reduces the required generating capacity and the cost per kW of capacity.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing diversity factor < 1 (it is always ≥ 1).
- Using 8760 h for a monthly calculation.

Sum of individual maxima ≥ simultaneous maximum.

lessons.title: Cost of generation and tariffs

story.title: Why the bill has two parts

scenes.text: A factory's bill lists a demand charge in ₹/kVA and an energy charge in ₹/kWh.
The utility must recover fixed capital cost and running fuel cost.

steps.title: Cost components
steps.body: **Fixed cost** (interest, depreciation, salaries) depends on capacity; **running (energy) cost** depends on kWh. Depreciation: straight-line = (C − S)/n; **sinking-fund** annual instalment q = (C − S)·i / ((1+i)ⁿ − 1). **Tariffs:** flat rate; block rate; **Hopkinson two-part** (a ₹/kW + b ₹/kWh); **Doherty three-part** (adds fixed charge per consumer, c); maximum-demand tariff; power-factor tariffs (kVA-based).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:

lessons.title: Power factor correction and the Indian grid

scenes.text: A workshop with many induction motors runs at 0.7 lagging and pays a low-PF penalty.
The engineer installs a capacitor bank to cancel part of the reactive power.

steps.title: Theory
steps.body: Inductive loads draw reactive power. For load P at pf cosφ₁ raised to cosφ₂: **Q_c = P (tanφ₁ − tanφ₂)** kVAR. Benefits: lower current, lower I²R loss, better voltage regulation, more kW available from the same kVA. **Indian grid:** five regional grids synchronised as one national grid at **50 Hz** (Southern grid joined in Dec 2013); transmission levels 765, 400, 220, 132 kV; IEGC frequency band 49.90–50.05 Hz.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 500 kW at 0.7 lag to 0.95 lag. tanφ₁ = 1.0202, tanφ₂ = 0.3287 ⇒ Q_c = 500×0.6915 = **345.8 kVAR**.

**Example 2.** Before: S = 500/0.7 = 714 kVA; after: 500/0.95 = 526 kVA; the kVA fall of 188 kVA releases capacity.

**Example 3.** Line current falls from S/(√3V) proportional: 714→526, i.e. 26 % lower, loss falls to (526/714)² = 54 %.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using cosφ instead of tanφ in the Q_c formula.
- Over-correcting to leading pf, which raises voltage and risks resonance.

lessons.title: Line resistance, skin and proximity effect

scenes.text: Conductors sag and heat in May; their resistance rises, and so do losses.
At 50 Hz current crowds toward the surface of thick conductors — the skin effect.

steps.title: Theory
steps.body: DC resistance **R = ρ l / A**. Aluminium ρ ≈ 2.82×10⁻⁸ Ω·m, copper 1.72×10⁻⁸ Ω·m at 20 °C. Temperature: **R₂ = R₁ (T + t₂)/(T + t₁)** with T = 234.5 °C (copper), ≈ 228 °C (aluminium). **Skin effect** (current pushed to the surface) and **proximity effect** (neighbouring conductors distort distribution) raise AC resistance above DC. Skin effect increases with frequency, conductor diameter and permeability; stranding and ACSR (steel core carries little current) address it.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using mm² directly in SI formulas (convert to m²).
- Believing skin effect exists in DC; it does not.

lessons.title: Inductance of a single-phase line

scenes.text: A current in a conductor makes flux inside it and around it.
Sum of internal and external flux linkages gives inductance.

steps.title: Derivation outline
steps.body: Internal flux linkage of a solid round conductor: λ_int = (μ₀/8π) I = **(1/2)×10⁻⁷ I** Wb-t/m (independent of radius). External linkage from r to D: 2×10⁻⁷ I ln(D/r). Total per conductor: L = 2×10⁻⁷ [1/4 + ln(D/r)] = **2×10⁻⁷ ln(D/r′) H/m**, where **r′ = r e^(−1/4) = 0.7788 r** (the GMR of a solid conductor). For a two-wire single-phase line the loop inductance is **L = 4×10⁻⁷ ln(d/r′) H/m**.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** d = 3 m, r = 1 cm. r′ = 0.7788 cm. ln(300/0.7788) = ln(385.2) = 5.954. Per conductor: 2×10⁻⁷×5.954 = 1.191 mH/km; loop = **2.382 mH/km**.

**Example 2.** Loop reactance at 50 Hz = 2π×50×2.382×10⁻³ = 0.748 Ω/km.

**Example 3.** Doubling spacing adds only 4×10⁻⁷ ln 2 = 0.277 mH/km to the loop.

steps.title: Exam tip
steps.body: Spacing enters through a logarithm, so L varies slowly with d. Remember loop = 2 × per-conductor.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using r instead of r′.
- Forgetting the factor 2 for the loop.

lessons.title: Three-phase inductance, GMD, GMR and bundling

scenes.text: A 400 kV tower has three bundled phases in a horizontal row.
Every third of the route the phases swap places: transposition.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body: For a transposed three-phase line: **L = 2×10⁻⁷ ln(GMD/GMR) H/m per phase**, with **GMD = (D₁₂ D₂₃ D₃₁)^(1/3)**. For a bundle of n sub-conductors, GMR_b: two sub-conductors **√(r′ d)**; three at triangle corners **(r′ d²)^(1/3)**; four at square corners **1.09 (r′ d³)^(1/4)**. Bundling raises GMR, lowering L (and X), raising C and reducing corona and radio interference.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Horizontal spacing 4, 4, 8 m: GMD = (4×4×8)^(1/3) = 5.04 m. r = 1.5 cm ⇒ r′ = 1.168 cm. L = 2×10⁻⁷ ln(504/1.168) = 2×10⁻⁷×6.067 = **1.213 mH/km**; X = 0.381 Ω/km.

**Example 2.** Two-conductor bundle, r′ = 1 cm, d = 40 cm: GMR_b = √(0.01×0.4) = **6.32 cm**.

**Example 3.** Using GMR_b = 6.32 cm with GMD 5.04 m: L = 2×10⁻⁷ ln(504/6.32) = 0.876 mH/km, 28 % less than single conductors of same r′.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using GMR of the bundle but forgetting to use the geometric mean of all distances between phase bundles.
- Mixing cm and m inside the logarithm (units must match).

lessons.title: Capacitance and charging current

story.title: A line that draws current with no load

scenes.text: A 200 km 400 kV line is energised with the far end open.
It still draws leading current — the line is a long capacitor.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body: Using Gauss's law: single-phase **C_ab = π ε₀ / ln(d/r)** F/m; capacitance to neutral **C_n = 2π ε₀ / ln(d/r)**. Transposed 3-phase: **C_n = 2π ε₀ / ln(GMD/r_b)** F/m with ε₀ = 8.854×10⁻¹² F/m. Charging current per phase **I_c = ωC V_ph**. Earth raises C slightly (image charges). For bundles use bundle GMR with r instead of r′ (r_b).

steps.title: Why it matters
steps.body: Charging current and Ferranti rise on lightly loaded EHV lines are controlled by shunt reactors.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using r′ (GMR) in capacitance; capacitance uses the physical radius.
- Using line voltage instead of phase voltage.

lessons.title: Surge impedance and surge impedance loading

story.title: The natural loading of a line

scenes.text: Planners ask how much power a line can carry without needing reactive support.
The answer is the surge impedance loading.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body: For a lossless line, **Z₀ = √(L/C)** (Ω) and **SIL = V_L² / Z₀** (MW with V_L in kV). At SIL the reactive power absorbed by the series inductance equals that generated by shunt capacitance; voltage profile is flat. Typical Z₀: 400 Ω for single-conductor lines, 250–300 Ω for bundled lines. Bundling lowers Z₀ and raises SIL (SIL ≈ 515 MW for 400 kV, ≈ 2250 MW for 765 kV in typical designs).

steps.title: Exam tip
steps.body: Loadings above SIL make the line inductive (absorbs vars, voltage sags); below SIL the line is capacitive (Ferranti rise).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using per-kilometre L and C but then mixing mH with nF without converting.
- Thinking SIL depends on length (it does not for a lossless line).

lessons.title: Short transmission lines: regulation and efficiency

scenes.text: A 33 kV feeder serves a small town 20 km from the substation.
The town complains of low voltage in the evening; the engineer computes regulation.

steps.title: Model
steps.body: Lines up to ~80 km (below 69 kV in some texts, up to 80 km generally) are 'short': shunt capacitance ignored, so series impedance Z = R + jX only. **V_S = V_R + I Z**, **I_S = I_R**, i.e. A = D = 1, B = Z, C = 0. **Regulation = (|V_S| − |V_R|)/|V_R| × 100** (at constant V_S, receiving voltage rises to V_S at no load). **Efficiency = P_R/(P_R + 3I²R)**. Approximate drop: ΔV ≈ I(R cosφ ± X sinφ) (plus for lagging).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 3-phase, Z = 8 + j12 Ω per phase, load 5 MW, 0.8 lag, V_R = 33 kV. I = 5×10⁶/(√3×33,000×0.8) = **109.35 A**; V_R(ph) = 19,053 V. I = 87.48 − j65.61 A; IZ = 1487 + j525 V. V_S = 20,540 + j525 ⇒ |V_S| = 20,547 V (35.6 kV line). **Regulation = (20,547 − 19,053)/19,053 = 7.84 %**.

**Example 2.** Loss = 3×109.35²×8 = 0.287 MW. η = 5/5.287 = **94.6 %**.

**Example 3.** For leading pf 0.8 the regulation can become negative (voltage rises).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using line voltage in the per-phase equation.
- Using the line-to-line voltage drop approximation with the wrong sign of X sinφ for leading loads.

lessons.title: Medium lines: nominal-T and nominal-π, ABCD

scenes.text: Over 150 km the charging current is no longer negligible.
Engineers lump the shunt admittance at the middle (T) or split at the ends (π).

steps.title: Constants
steps.body: **Nominal π:** A = D = 1 + YZ/2, B = Z, C = Y(1 + YZ/4). **Nominal T:** A = D = 1 + YZ/2, B = Z(1 + YZ/4), C = Y. Always **AD − BC = 1** for passive reciprocal networks. Then V_S = A V_R + B I_R, I_S = C V_R + D I_R. At no load, V_R,NL = V_S/A; regulation = (V_S/A − V_R,FL)/V_R,FL.

steps.title: Exam tip
steps.body: Always check AD − BC = 1; it catches arithmetic errors. Reverse cascade: ABCD of two networks in series multiply (matrix product).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Placing the full Y at the receiving end (that is the 'end-condenser' method, not π).
- Using Y/2 in the T formula for B.

lessons.title: Long lines: hyperbolic solution and lossless lines

scenes.text: Voltage and current travel along a long line as waves.
At 50 Hz a quarter wavelength is about 1,500 km.

steps.title: Equations
steps.body: Per-km z = r + jωL, y = g + jωC. **γ = √(zy) = α + jβ**, **Z_c = √(z/y)**. **V = V_R cosh γx + I_R Z_c sinh γx; I = I_R cosh γx + (V_R/Z_c) sinh γx.** ABCD: A = D = cosh γl, B = Z_c sinh γl, C = sinh γl / Z_c. Equivalent π: Z′ = Z_c sinh γl = Z(sinh γl/γl), Y′/2 = (1/Z_c) tanh(γl/2). **Lossless line:** α = 0, β = ω√(LC), Z_c = √(L/C); A = D = cos βl, B = jZ_c sin βl, C = j sin βl / Z_c. Wavelength λ = 2π/β; velocity v = 1/√(LC).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using degrees vs radians inconsistently in βl.
- Forgetting that γl is complex for lossy lines: use cosh(a + jb) = cosh a cos b + j sinh a sin b.

lessons.title: Power transfer and series compensation

story.title: How much can a corridor carry?

scenes.text: Two regions exchange power through one line.
Planners ask the maximum power and how to raise it.

steps.title: Power angle relation
steps.body: For a lossless line of reactance X: **P = V_S V_R sin δ / X**, P_max at δ = 90°. Reactive power received **Q_R = (V_S V_R cos δ − V_R²)/X**. Series compensation with fraction k: X_eff = (1 − k) X, so P_max increases by 1/(1 − k). Steady-state stability limit corresponds to δ = 90°; practical operating δ ≤ 30–40°.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** V_S = V_R = 220 kV, X = 100 Ω, δ = 30°: P = 220²/100 × 0.5 = **242 MW**; P_max = 484 MW.

**Example 2.** 40 % series compensation: X = 60 Ω; P_max = 48,400/60 = **806.7 MW**.

**Example 3.** At 242 MW, with k = 0.4, δ = asin(242×60/48,400) = asin(0.3) = 17.5°; the angle drops, improving stability margin.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using phase voltage with 3-phase power formula; with line voltages P is total 3-phase MW.
- Compensating 100 % (resonance); practical levels 30–70 %.

lessons.title: Sag and tension in overhead lines

scenes.text: Between two towers a conductor hangs in a curve called a catenary, approximated by a parabola.
In summer it expands and sags more; in winter tension is higher.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body: Level supports, span l, weight per metre w, horizontal tension T: **S = w l² / (8T)**; length of conductor **L = l + 8S²/(3l)**. Unequal levels (height difference h): x₁ = l/2 − T h/(w l), x₂ = l − x₁ (x₁ from the lower support to the lowest point); **S₁ = w x₁²/(2T), S₂ = w x₂²/(2T)**. With ice (w_i) and wind (w_w) per metre: **w_t = √((w + w_i)² + w_w²)**. Minimum ground clearance fixes tower height.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the wrong support as the origin of x₁.
- Adding wind and ice weights arithmetically instead of vectorially.

lessons.title: Insulators and string efficiency

story.title: The disc closest to the wire

scenes.text: A suspension string of discs holds the live conductor away from the grounded tower.
The disc nearest the conductor carries the highest voltage and fails first.

steps.title: Theory
steps.body: Types: **pin** (up to ~33 kV), **suspension** (disc strings), **strain** (dead-end), **shackle** (distribution), stay. Porcelain, toughened glass, polymer (composite). Each disc has self-capacitance C and shunt capacitance to earth/line of k·C (k ≈ 0.1–0.2). Voltage distribution (n = 3, from the cross-arm end): V₂ = V₁(1 + k), V₃ = V₁(1 + 3k + k²). **String efficiency = V_total / (n × V_max)**, V_max across the disc nearest the line. Improve by grading discs, guard ring, longer cross-arm.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** n = 3, k = 0.2: V₂ = 1.2 V₁, V₃ = 1.64 V₁; total 3.84 V₁; efficiency = 3.84/(3×1.64) = **78.05 %**.

**Example 2.** 132 kV line: V_ph = 76.21 kV; V₁ = 76.21/3.84 = 19.85 kV, V₃ = **32.55 kV**.

**Example 3.** With k = 0: efficiency 100 % (ideal).

steps.title: Why not 100 %
steps.body: Shunt capacitance diverts charging current so the lower discs carry more current and hence more voltage.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating V₁ as the disc nearest the conductor (it is nearest the cross-arm in this convention).
- Using line voltage across the string instead of phase voltage.

lessons.title: Corona

scenes.text: On a wet night, a faint violet glow and hiss appear along an EHV line.
It causes power loss and radio interference.

steps.title: Theory
steps.body: Corona occurs when the surface gradient exceeds the breakdown strength of air (30 kV/cm peak = 21.1 kV/cm rms at NTP). **Critical disruptive voltage (phase, rms): V_c = m_o g_o δ r ln(D/r) kV**, r and D in cm, m_o = surface factor (0.8–1.0). Air density factor **δ = 3.92 b/(273 + t)**. **Visual critical voltage: V_v = m_v g_o δ r (1 + 0.3/√(δ r)) ln(D/r)**. **Peek's loss: P = (241/δ)(f + 25)√(r/D)(V − V_c)² × 10⁻⁵ kW/km/phase**. Reduce by larger/bundled conductors, hollow conductors, spacing.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using metres for r and D in V_c (the constants assume cm; the ratio D/r is dimensionless but r multiplies).
- Using line voltage in Peek's formula.

activity.prompt: r = 1 cm, D = 400 cm, m_o = 0.85, δ = 1, g_o = 21.1 kV/cm. Critical disruptive voltage (LINE, kV)?

quiz.why: b in cm Hg, t in °C.

lessons.title: Underground cables: construction, capacitance, stress

scenes.text: Inside a city, 11 kV and 33 kV supply goes underground.
A cable is a concentric capacitor with copper inside and a metallic sheath outside.

steps.title: Theory
steps.body: Parts: conductor (Cu/Al), insulation (paper, PVC, XLPE), metallic sheath (lead/aluminium), bedding, armouring, serving. Types: belted (up to 11 kV), screened (H-type, Hochstadter; SL), pressure cables (oil-filled, gas) for EHV; XLPE for 11–400 kV. **Capacitance** (single core): **C = 2π ε₀ ε_r / ln(R/r) F/m**. **Insulation resistance: R_i = (ρ/2π l) ln(R/r)**. **Max stress at conductor surface: g_max = V/(r ln(R/r))**; most economical radius r = R/e (g_min = V/ r... gives g_max = e·V/R). Dielectric loss = ωCV² tanδ.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** r = 1 cm, R = 2.5 cm, ε_r = 3.5: C = 5.563×10⁻¹¹×3.5/ln 2.5 = 1.947×10⁻¹⁰/0.9163 = 2.125×10⁻¹⁰ F/m = **0.2125 µF/km**.

**Example 2.** V = 33 kV (phase, rms): g_max = 33/(1×0.9163) = **36.0 kV/cm**.

**Example 3.** Optimum r = R/e: with R = 2.5 cm, r = 0.92 cm, g_max = 33/(0.92×1) = 35.9 kV/cm, the minimum possible for this R.

steps.title: Exam tip
steps.body: The optimum r makes ln(R/r) = 1; g_max = V/r. This is the minimum stress for fixed V and R.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using diameter in place of radius.
- Forgetting ε_r in C.
