lessons.title: Grading of cables

scenes.text: The insulation next to the conductor is overstressed while the outer layers hardly work.
Grading spreads stress evenly across the dielectric.

steps.title: Methods
steps.body: **Capacitance grading:** layers of different ε_r, highest permittivity nearest the conductor. For equal maximum stress in each layer: **ε₁ r₁ = ε₂ r₂ = …**. **Intersheath grading:** thin metallic sheaths held at intermediate potentials by tappings; for equal maximum stress in two layers: V₁/(r₁ ln(r₂/r₁)) = (V − V₁)/(r₂ ln(R/r₂)).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** r₁ = 1 cm, ε₁ = 5, ε₂ = 3: r₂ = 5×1/3 = **1.667 cm**.

**Example 2 (intersheath).** V = 66 kV, r₁ = 1, r₂ = 2, R = 4 cm: ln(r₂/r₁) = ln(R/r₂) = 0.6931 ⇒ V₁/(0.6931) = (66 − V₁)/(1.3863) ⇒ 2V₁ = 66 − V₁ ⇒ **V₁ = 22 kV**; g = 31.7 kV/cm.

**Example 3.** Ungraded: g_max = 66/(1×ln 4) = 47.6 kV/cm — grading cuts stress by one-third.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Putting the highest-ε layer at the outside (should be at the inside).
- Missing the fact that intersheaths can be damaged by voids and rarely used now.

lessons.title: Radial distributors and voltage drop

story.title: The last house on the lane

scenes.text: Houses along a lane are fed from one transformer; the last house sees the lowest voltage.
The engineer adds the drops section by section.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body: Distribution systems: **radial** (one path, cheap, low reliability), **ring/loop** (two paths, more reliable), **interconnected**. A distributor has no intermediate tappings other than loads; a feeder has none at all. Statutory voltage variation ±6 % (LV, India). For a distributor fed at one end, current in each section = sum of all loads beyond it; voltage drop = Σ I_section × R_section (DC or unity pf).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 2-wire DC distributor, 300 m, fed at A with 100 V. Loop resistance 0.05 Ω per 100 m. Loads: 20 A at 100 m, 30 A at 200 m, 10 A at 300 m. Section currents: 60, 40, 10 A. Drops: 3.0 + 2.0 + 0.5 = 5.5 V ⇒ end voltage **94.5 V**.

**Example 2.** Total power loss = 60²×0.05 + 40²×0.05 + 10²×0.05 = 180 + 80 + 5 = **265 W**.

**Example 3.** If all 60 A were concentrated at the far end, drop = 60×0.15 = 9 V — worse; concentrated loads at the end give maximum drop.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the load current at a point instead of the sum of all downstream loads.
- Forgetting that 2-wire means go AND return resistance.

lessons.title: Ring mains and distributors fed at both ends

scenes.text: A town ring main is fed from two substations so a fault in one section does not black out everyone.
Where does the voltage dip lowest?

steps.title: Method
steps.body: For a distributor fed at both ends with equal end voltages, take moments about one end to find the feed current at the other: **I_A × L = Σ I_k × d_k (distance from B)**. Then trace the currents; the point where current changes direction is the **point of minimum potential**. Ring main = distributor fed at the same point (both ends joined) — cut at the feed point and treat as a two-end distributor.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** AB = 200 m, both ends 230 V; loop resistance 0.1 Ω/100 m. Loads: 100 A at C (50 m from A), 60 A at D (150 m from A). Moments about B: I_A×200 = 100×150 + 60×50 = 18,000 ⇒ **I_A = 90 A**, I_B = 70 A.

**Example 2.** A→C: 90 A × 0.05 = 4.5 V. Current beyond C is −10 A (flows from D to C) ⇒ C is the lowest point: V_C = 230 − 4.5 = **225.5 V**. Check from B: B→D 70×0.05 = 3.5 V, D→C 10×0.1 = 1 V ⇒ 225.5 V ✓.

**Example 3.** Power loss = 90²×0.05 + 10²×0.1 + 70²×0.05 = 405 + 10 + 245 = 660 W.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Taking moments about the wrong end and swapping I_A and I_B.
- Assuming minimum voltage is always the middle of the line.

lessons.title: AC distributors, voltage drop and Kelvin's law

story.title: Which cable size is cheapest to own?

scenes.text: A thicker cable costs more but wastes less energy.
Lord Kelvin gave the balance in 1881.

steps.title: Theory
steps.body: AC drop (per phase, approx): **ΔV ≈ I (R cosφ + X sinφ)** for lagging pf. **Kelvin's law:** the most economical conductor area is where annual cost of energy loss = annual interest + depreciation on the conductor cost. With annual cost C = P + Q A + R/A, minimum at **Q A = R/A ⇒ A = √(R/Q)**. Limitations: neglects insulation, current varying with time, and ignores that voltage drop limits usually decide size.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 3-phase 4-wire feeder 0.5 km, R = 0.05 Ω, X = 0.04 Ω per phase, I = 100 A, pf 0.8 lag: ΔV ≈ 100(0.05×0.8 + 0.04×0.6) = **6.4 V**, i.e. 2.8 % of 230 V.

**Example 2 (Kelvin).** C = 3000 + 40A + 160,000/A (A in mm², ₹/yr): A = √(160,000/40) = **63.2 mm²**; cost = 3000 + 2529.8 + 2529.8 = ₹8,059.6/yr.

**Example 3.** Kelvin's A is a minimum; standard size ≥ 63.2 mm² is chosen (70 mm²).

steps.title: Exam tip
steps.body: Kelvin's law: variable annual cost of copper (proportional to A) equals annual loss cost (proportional to 1/A).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using sinφ with a plus sign for leading loads.
- Taking Kelvin area without checking the voltage-drop and thermal limits.

lessons.title: Substations and busbar arrangements

scenes.text: An outdoor yard has a transformer, breakers, isolators and arresters.
A maintenance team must isolate one bay safely without a blackout.

steps.title: Equipment and layouts
steps.body: Types: step-up (generating), primary grid, secondary, distribution; outdoor air-insulated, indoor, **GIS (SF₆)**. Key equipment: **power transformer, circuit breaker (interrupts fault current), isolator (off-load, visible gap), earthing switch, CT, CVT/PT (instrument transformers), lightning arrester (ZnO), bus bars, protective relays, capacitor banks/reactors**. Busbar schemes: single bus (cheap, outage on maintenance), sectionalised single bus, double bus (selectable), main-and-transfer, **breaker-and-a-half**, ring/mesh. Sequence: close isolators first, then breaker; open breaker first, then isolators.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** A breaker-and-a-half bay has 3 breakers for 2 circuits: 1.5 breakers/circuit.

**Example 2.** CT ratio 800/1 A with relay current 1.25 A secondary ⇒ primary = 1000 A.

**Example 3.** CVT with 220 kV/√3 : 110 V/√3 ratio ⇒ secondary phase voltage 63.5 V when line is at rated voltage.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Operating an isolator on load (it cannot break current — arcing).
- Mixing CT (series, low-impedance secondary kept shorted) with PT (parallel, kept open-circuit safe).

lessons.title: Earthing and neutral grounding

scenes.text: A line technician steps near a faulted tower; current spreads in the soil.
The voltage between feet (step) and hand-foot (touch) must be limited.

steps.title: Theory
steps.body: Earthing: equipment earthing (safety) and system earthing (neutral). **Rod electrode resistance: R = ρ/(2π l) ln(4l/d).** Neutral grounding methods: **solid, resistance, reactance, resonant (Peterson/arc-suppression coil), ungrounded**. For a Peterson coil tuned to the line-to-earth capacitance C per phase: **L = 1/(3ω²C)**, which cancels the capacitive earth-fault current. Solid grounding gives largest fault current and lowest transient overvoltage (earth fault factor ≤ 1.4 for effectively grounded).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Peterson coil with C = 1 µF per phase at 50 Hz: L = 1/(3×314.16²×10⁻⁶) = **3.38 H**.

**Example 2.** Rod: ρ = 100 Ω·m, l = 3 m, d = 25 mm: R = 100/(2π×3)×ln(480) = 5.305×6.174 = **32.8 Ω**.

**Example 3.** Earth-fault current in ungrounded 11 kV system with C = 1 µF per phase = 3ωC V_ph = 3×314.16×10⁻⁶×6351 = 5.99 A.

steps.title: Why Peterson coils
steps.body: Arcing earth faults in overhead networks extinguish themselves when the inductive current balances the capacitive current; they are used in some 11–33 kV networks.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using ω = 50 instead of 2π×50.
- Forgetting factor 3 in the Peterson coil formula.

courses.summary: Formula sheet for Power Systems I, three standard laboratory experiments (Ferranti effect, insulator string efficiency, earth resistance), previous-year-style problems and a 20-question exam.
outcomes: Recall all key formulae of generation, line parameters, performance, insulators, cables

Solve exam-style numericals under time pressure

lessons.title: Formula and key-point sheet

scenes.text: You have one page to review everything in Power Systems I.
Cards help you recall the formula before you recall the derivation.

steps.title: Generation and load
steps.body:
- Hydro: P = ρgQHη. Wind: P = ½ρAv³C_p (Betz 16/27).
- Load factor = avg/MD; demand factor = MD/connected; diversity factor = ΣMD_i / MD_group ≥ 1.
- Capacity factor = energy/(capacity × hours).
- PF correction: Q_c = P(tanφ₁ − tanφ₂).

steps.title: Line parameters
steps.body:
- R = ρl/A, temp: (T + t₂)/(T + t₁).
- L = 2×10⁻⁷ ln(GMD/GMR) H/m; solid GMR = 0.7788 r.
- C_n = 2πε₀/ln(GMD/r) F/m; I_c = ωCV_ph.
- Z₀ = √(L/C); SIL = V²/Z₀; λ = 2π/β ≈ 6000 km.

steps.title: Performance and mechanical
steps.body:
- Short: A = D = 1, B = Z, C = 0. π: A = 1 + YZ/2, B = Z, C = Y(1 + YZ/4). T: B = Z(1 + YZ/4), C = Y. AD − BC = 1.
- Lossless long line: A = cos βl, B = jZ₀ sin βl. Ferranti: V_R = V_S/cos βl.
- P = V_SV_R sinδ/X.
- Sag = wl²/8T; string eff = V/(n V_max); V_c = m g δ r ln(D/r); Peek loss; cable C = 2πε₀ε_r/ln(R/r), g_max = V/(r ln(R/r)).
- Peterson L = 1/(3ω²C).

steps.title: Exam strategy
steps.body: Write the formula, substitute with units, box the answer. Check AD − BC = 1 for ABCD problems, and diversity factor ≥ 1, load factor ≤ 1.

steps.title: Aim and apparatus
steps.body: **Aim:** to observe the rise of receiving-end voltage on an unloaded transmission line model and verify V_R/V_S ≈ 1/cos βl. **Apparatus:** 3-phase variac, transmission-line model (π sections, L and C per section), 2 voltmeters, ammeter, switches, loading rheostat bank.

The ratio is constant, as expected from a linear model. Theory for βl = 0.321 rad: 1/cos(0.321) = 1.054.

lessons.title: Lab: Earth resistance and soil resistivity (Wenner method)

scenes.text: Before a substation is built, soil resistivity is measured at several spacings.
Four electrodes in a line, equally spaced a, are driven into the soil.

steps.title: Method
steps.body: Wenner: four equally spaced probes, spacing a; current passed through outer probes, voltage measured across inner ones. **ρ = 2π a R** (R = V/I), valid when electrode depth ≪ a. Fall-of-potential method for earth resistance uses the 62 % rule: potential probe at 62 % of the current-probe distance.

steps.title: Observation table
steps.body:
| a (m) | V (V) | I (A) | R = V/I (Ω) | ρ = 2πaR (Ω·m) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | 4.0 | 0.5 | 8.0 | 100.5 |
| 4 | 3.0 | 0.5 | 6.0 | 150.8 |
| 8 | 2.5 | 0.5 | 5.0 | 251.3 |

Resistivity increases with depth here — a wetter surface layer over drier soil.

steps.title: Precautions
steps.body:
- Probes must be in a straight line away from buried metal.
- Use a low-frequency (not 50 Hz) source or earth tester to avoid stray-current errors.

activity.prompt: Viva questions

items.a: The potential probe at 61.8 % of the distance lies at the point where the electrode's resistance area meets the zero-potential plane, giving the true electrode resistance.

items.q: Why does resistivity change with season?
items.a: Moisture and temperature change ion mobility in soil; wet soil has lower resistivity.

items.q: Why not use ordinary DC to measure earth resistance?
items.a: Polarisation and electrolytic effects distort readings, so AC at a non-mains frequency is used.

items.q: What is acceptable substation earth resistance?
items.a: Typically below 1 Ω for large substations, 5–10 Ω for small ones, as per design standards.

steps.title: Problem 1 (10 marks)
steps.body: A 3-phase 50 Hz overhead line has conductors of radius 1 cm at horizontal spacing 3 m, 3 m, 6 m (transposed). Find (a) inductance per km per phase. GMD = (3×3×6)^(1/3) = 54^(1/3) = 3.78 m; r′ = 0.7788 cm; ln(378/0.7788) = ln(485.4) = 6.185; **L = 1.237 mH/km**; X = 0.389 Ω/km. (b) C_n = 2πε₀/ln(378/1) = 5.563×10⁻¹¹/5.935 = **9.37 nF/km**.

steps.title: Problem 2 (10 marks)
steps.body: A 132 kV short line has Z = 6 + j15 Ω per phase and delivers 40 MW at 0.85 lag at 132 kV. I = 40×10⁶/(√3×132,000×0.85) = **205.8 A**. Drop ≈ 205.8(6×0.85 + 15×0.527) = 205.8(5.1 + 7.9) = 2.68 kV per phase (approx) ⇒ about 3.5 % regulation on 76.2 kV.

steps.title: Problem 3 (5 marks)
steps.body: A station has MD 50 MW, energy 262.8 GWh/year. Load factor = 262.8×10⁶/(50×10³×8760) = **0.60**.
